articles.text: On Friday, September 11, the City of Piedmont will host a brief ceremony to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, a defining moment in our nation’s history. The commemoration will take place in front of the Fire Station and City Hall and will begin at 8:30 a.m. The event will allow residents to remember the lives lost and honor the service of first responders past and present. The community is invited to attend and participate in the honoring of the lives lost in the attack. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan and Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen will give brief remarks to open the ceremony. Following their remarks first responders and attending community members will stand for a minute of silent reflection. The Fire Department will lower the flag at half-mast from sunrise to sunset to mourn the lives lost. The flag at half-mast at the 20th anniversary event the Piedmont Fire Department held in 2021. A Celebration of Life is scheduled for John Morrison on Saturday, September 12, at 2 p.m. in the John Morrison Gymnasium at Piedmont Middle School, 740 Magnolia Avenue. The longtime middle school principal died on August 7, 2026, at the age of 84.

articles.text: Labor Day is a recognition of both the important role labor unions have played in the well-being of our nation and its working families and of the value of work itself. It is on the value of work, and its corollary, the value of rest, that I would offer a few thoughts. The creation stories of Genesis celebrate the goodness of the world we inhabit. Included in that goodness are work, toil, labor and rest. In the first story human beings, having been created in the image of God, are given the work of being fruitful and multiplying, of filling the earth and exercising dominion “over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the air and over every living thing that moves upon the earth.” The questions “How well have we done in the work given us?” as well as “How well are we doing in that work?” are worthy of serious consideration. The answers must include the recognition that the exercise of dominion has often been mistakenly understood as exercise of domination and that our labors have thus undermined, rather than enhanced, the well-being of God’s creation. Still, there is meaning, purpose and joy to be found in “tilling and keeping” the earth, as the second story of creation describes the work we have been given. Wendell Berry, who died this week at age 92, said it well. “The care of the Earth is our most ancient and most worthy, and after all our most pleasing responsibility. To cherish what remains of it and to foster its renewal is our only hope.” Tilling and keeping the earth takes many forms. As Wendell’s life demonstrated, it includes sinking our hands into the soil, putting our hearts into our words, putting our best into our communities and putting our souls into our relationships. Whether we are employed or not, Labor Day, like the stories of creation and like the testimony of Farmer Berry, reminds us that we, all of us, are here because we have something to give and that there is a time both to give of ourselves, and to rest from giving. Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland.
articles.title: Of Labor Day and Labor

articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) on Tuesday, September 29, for a candidate forum. It will feature candidates on the Piedmont City Council ballot in the November 3, 2026, General Election. The forum will be held at 7:00 p.m. in the City Council chambers and in overflow space as needed. It will include the following five candidates running for three positions: Nancy Beninati, Sunny Bostrom-Fleming, Adam Hundt, Tom Ramsey, and Bill Reichle. Piedmont voters can learn more about the City Council forum at lwvpiedmont.org. Registration is required to attend the live forum, as space is limited. The forum will also be broadcast and recorded on KCOM. After the forum, the recording will be available on LWVP’s website, on LWVP’s YouTube channel, and through the websites of KCOM and the City. A LWVP representative will moderate the forum. It will include questions from the public. On September 22 until 5 p.m., voters may submit questions by filling out the online form on the event description pages on LWVP’s website. Questions will be reviewed to ensure a range of topics and issues. Visit the Election Resources page (https://bit.ly/4ymy5xS) to learn about WHAT’s on your ballot and HOW, WHEN, and WHERE to vote. A ballot will be mailed to every registered voter starting October 5. Ballot dropoff locations will open October 6. If you have moved or changed your party or your name, you can update your registration online. The last day to register to vote is October 19. There are three ways to vote in Alameda County: 1) mail your ballot, 2) drop off your ballot at a secure ballot drop-box in the county, or 3) vote in person or drop off your ballot at any vote center in the county. The list of vote centers will be updated as the Registrar of Voters confirms the sites. There will likely be a ballot drop-box in central Piedmont next to the mailbox near the Piedmont Community Church. There will likely be a vote center in Piedmont at the Veterans Memorial Building at 401 Highland Avenue. A limited number of additional early 10-day in-person Alameda County vote centers will also be open starting October 24. A limited number of additional early 4-day in-person Alameda County vote centers will also be open starting October 31. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked on or before Election Day. articles.text: This past week the fencing around the Piedmont Park tot lot has been removed marking the completion of the new ADA path and landscaping. The next stage of the project will include installing new swings and a nature play area funded by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. According to the city, there is a delay on the manufacturer’s end in delivering the new swing set. The city expects the swings to arrive in November. The new path cuts through the former grassy area between the Exedra Plaza and Piedmont High School campus, connecting with the path in front of the tot lot. Fresh grass has been planted on the left side of the path, while the right side has playground wood chips. The location where the swings will be installed is currently a dug-out hole surrounded by cement stairs with signage and tape to keep the public from entering. The sand surrounding the area has been removed and will be replaced with ADA fiber matting. During installation of the new swings, the climbing structure, The new ADA path with wood chips and newly planted grass on either side. lawn area, Exedra Plaza, and restroom will remain open. The memorial benches are within the construction zone and will be reinstalled after the project is completed. Modernscape Innovations was awarded the $156,364 contract to complete the first stage of this project. The swing equipment and ADA fiber matting installation is anticipated to be awarded separately via a California Multiple Award Schedule (CMAS) agreement. The swings will be bucket swings similar to the original swings. Once the equipment arrives in November, installation will take two weeks to complete. This project is in response to the longstanding community request to rebuild the swings that were removed in 2024 due to structural rot. The current plan is to expand the swing zone to meet modern safety requirements. The dug-out area where the new swing equipment and ADA fiber matting will be installed.

articles.text: More than 25 years ago, a few community members dedicated themselves to bringing a new pool to Piedmont. Josh Bernstein, Russ Hafferkamp, and Clarence Mamuyac identified the community’s need for aquatics and worked to bring a new pool to the “There just wasn’t enough pool space,” said Bernstein. “Piedmont was and is still one of the only school districts in our area that doesn’t have their own At first, the group wanted to help the School District build a pool on campus, but were eventually shot down due to the School District’s concern over liability and maintenance. They decided to set their sights on the Piedmont “It became apparent that we had a much broader interest in aquatics in Piedmont than the pool (Piedmont Swim Club Pool) could really sustain. We had a new developing water polo team, we had a really good high school aquatics program, and there was a growing number of new families that wanted to have the same aquatic experiences that were available in Orinda, Lafayette and Moraga,” said Hafferkamp, then the assistant coach of Cal’s At the time, the Swim Club’s Pool was unfit to host aquatic sports. It was considered a “relic,” and the group believed it needed to be addressed. They proposed renovations to accommodate aquatic sports and expand space for swimmers. “We contacted Clarence Mamuyac, who was a very active architect in the aquatics field and lived in the community, and he was supportive of the idea. He helped us build a 3D model of what the facility would look like with drawings and renderings, and we had a series of public meetings and public presentations inside the community about our plan,” said Hafferkamp. Not everyone was supportive of this plan to renovate the pool and there was pushback from the leaseholders of Piedmont Swim Club. “We were met with equal parts opposition, equal parts support, and equal parts apathy. “Apathy kind of won the day,” said Hafferkamp. “The problem was the Piedmont Swim Club. They had the lease from the city on the pool, and they didn’t want to make any changes. What they had done at the time was remove the gutters from the old Piedmont pool during a renovation project, which rendered the old swimming pool unfit for swimming competition,” Bernstein explained. “They were trying to force the swim teams out, and it worked. They couldn’t hold swim meets at the old Piedmont swim club. That became a problem because we had the swim team here in town, and the kids were working out in this substandard pool. They (Piedmont Swim Club) were afraid they were going to lose their swim club, and they wouldn’t have any place to swim during construction.” Their project and ideas were shut down. It took years before the community would think about a new pool again. It was only when the swim club lost its lease to the city that the idea of a new pool gained traction. “Eventually, they lost their lease, and that’s when things started to change. Once the Recreation Department (under Mark Delventhal) took things over, there was an opportunity,” Bernstein said. There was a community movement of those who recognized the value of aquatics; many of whom were previously against the idea of a pool were now on board. “The community recognized the future value of aquatics, and the reality that the old pool was a relic and needed to be addressed,” said Hafferkamp. A new pool was approved, and after years of planning and construction, the Community Pool was built. Bernstein and Hafferkamp believe the work they did with Mamuyac paid off. “I think that the homework that we did in the beginning helped when Betsy Andersen came along, and she was able to really take it from this concept that we had to a real project,” said Bernstein. He and Hafferkamp were very appreciative of the work Mayor Andersen and the city did to bring this project to fruition. When Bernstein showed up for the pool’s opening day, he reflected on the years of hard work his group put into the idea of a new pool. Seeing it completed was an emotional moment Josh Bernstein gives a thumbs-up on the opening day of the Community Pool. for him. “I got choked up on the first day when we came to go swimming. It was such a long time coming. To see that concept that started in our kitchen become a reality and such an unbelievably impressive reality. It was an emotional experience for me,” said Bernstein. The two plan to enjoy the new pool for as long as it exists. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223 Daycare Boarding Training Grooming 2101 Mandela Pkwy Oakland, CA (510) 547-3647

articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting on Wednesday, September 9 at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall. Interim Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans will preside over his first meeting since rejoining the district in August. Evans’ return to start the school year has stabilized things in the district so that August could be about new teachers and new classes. The school board will announce its plans to begin the search for a new superintendent by submitting a request for proposals (RFP) from education executive search firms or individuals to provide consulting services for a national search. The board aims to publicly announce the new superintendent by December 9, 2026. The permanent role of superintendent would start on January 1, 2027. Teachers, parents and students have benefited from Evans’ steady hand. “I can’t believe some of the high school students remember me from four years ago. To hear them say ‘welcome back, Dr. Evans’ made me feel like I was back home,” Evans said. The meeting will feature a check presented to the board by the Piedmont Education Foundation. The Parcel Tax Committee is also slated to be recognized by the board. The presentation of the evening will put Beach Elementary School in the spotlight as Principal Anne Valva talks about test results, and the school culture in 2026. This school board meeting will be held at City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue and can be seen remotely at Zoom.us/wc/83297005216 and on KCOM local Channel 27.

articles.text: Good morning and welcome to KidNuz. Today is Wednesday, September 9th, 2026 and we begin with… A sacred piece of 9/11 history now on the final leg of its cross country journey. Organized by the son of a fallen New York firefighter, the 21-foot long, 16-thousand pound steel beam from the South Tower of the World Trade Center made 35 stops in 21 states to help kids better understand the magnitude of that day in 2001… and ensure future generations “Never Forget” the souls lost and the sacrifices made. This Friday, it will join a procession through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel as part of remembrances marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks. The beam’s final appearance will be at the Giants-Cowboys game at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. For more on the impact of the tour and the importance of learning about 9/11, check out a special episode we dropped last weekend. You can find it wherever you get your podcasts. Sticky fingers have struck France… again. Early yesterday, thieves stole four paintings by the famed artist Renoir from a small museum on the French Riviera. The escape wasn’t flawless; the burglars dropped two of the paintings during their getaway. Still, the ones they did make off with… are worth millions. The brazen theft comes less than a year after the high profile heist of crown jewels from the Louvre in Paris, many of which are still missing. Are you ready for some football? Tonight, for the first time in a decade, the season is opening with a Super Bowl rematch: It’ll be the Seahawks vs the Patriots, with New England quarterback Drake May hoping to avenge the 16 point drubbing by Sam Darnold last February. articles.text: gone to the birds, at least temporarily. As it does every September, the Gateway Arch in St. Louis, Missouri is turning off its lights at night to keep our fine feathered friends from getting sidetracked as they head south for winter. According to the National Park Service, the arch sits smack dab in the middle of one of the nation’s busiest bird highways: the Mississippi Flyway. Many of the avian aviators travel at night and the lights can be disorienting, sending them in the wrong direction or, sometimes, even into the sides of buildings. Come October, once most of the birds have safely winged their way to warmer destinations, the Arch will light back up, before bowing to nature again in May for their long return trip home. If only all elections could be this friendly. When a recent town council showdown in Arizona ended in a 67-to-67 tie, local officials turned to a century old state law to break it: a game of chance. It could be any game, like rock paper scissors, marbles or straws, but Gila Bend decided its two candidates would draw cards, high card wins. And it’s a good thing they considered the possibility of another deadlock, because — improbably — both candidates drew 3s. It was pre-determined that spades would trump other suits, which one of the two wanna-bees had and clinched the win. Gila Bend is far from the first town to decide a race by chance. So far, the movie’s made 2.4 billion dollars worldwide and capped a really good summer run for Hollywood, which saw domestic ticket sales up more than 22-percent over last summer. Still to come: if you like ice cream — and honestly who doesn’t — we have found what could be the perfect job. The Seahawks and Patriots, a Super Bowl rematch • Why is St. Louis’ famous arch dark for the month of September? The pay: $10,000 a month for three months of globetrotting in search of the latest, greatest and wackiest frozen concoctions. Ultimately, the goal is to help Snoop pick out his next ‘flavor.’ Do you have what it takes? The job requirements include speaking English, a valid passport, and the availability to travel for the next three months. At least a few dozen students have confirmed their excitement and attendance. • 7:00 p.m. — PHS Homecoming Football Game at Witter Field. Join us for continued conversation as we cheer on the Highlanders. For more info and questions, please reach out to Drew Preston, Class President (Andrew.Preston5@gmail.com; 510-410-1851). Good morning and welcome to KidNuz. Today is Wednesday, September 9th, 2026 and we begin with… A sacred piece of 9/11 history now on the final leg of its cross country journey. Organized by the son of a fallen New York firefighter, the 21-foot long, 16-thousand pound steel beam from the South Tower of the World Trade Center made 35 stops in 21 states to help kids better understand the magnitude of that day in 2001… and ensure future generations “Never Forget” the souls lost and the sacrifices made. This Friday, it will join a procession through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel as part of remembrances marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks. The beam’s final appearance will be at the Giants-Cowboys game at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. For more on the impact of the tour and the importance of learning about 9/11, check out a special episode we dropped last weekend. You can find it wherever you get your podcasts. Sticky fingers have struck France… again. Early yesterday, thieves stole four paintings by the famed artist Renoir from a small museum on the French Riviera. The escape wasn’t flawless; the burglars dropped two of the paintings during their getaway. Still, the ones they did make off with… are worth millions. The brazen theft comes less than a year after the high profile heist of crown jewels from the Louvre in Paris, many of which are still missing. Are you ready for some football? The NFL is back — and not just with any game. Tonight, for the first time in a decade, the season is opening with a Super Bowl rematch: It’ll be the Seahawks vs the Patriots, with New England quarterback Drake May hoping to avenge the 16 point drubbing by Sam Darnold last February. For celebration, and perhaps emphasis, the Seahawks will raise their championship banner just before kickoff, which is 5:20 p.m. Pacific Time. A famed US landmark has Welcome to KidNuz gone to the birds, at least temporarily. As it does every September, the Gateway Arch in St. Louis, Missouri is turning off its lights at night to keep our fine feathered friends from getting sidetracked as they head south for winter. According to the National Park Service, the arch sits smack dab in the middle of one of the nation’s busiest bird highways: the Mississippi Flyway. Many of the avian aviators travel at night and the lights can be disorienting, sending them in the wrong direction or, sometimes, even into the sides of buildings. Come October, once most of the birds have safely winged their way to warmer destinations, the Arch will light back up, before bowing to nature again in May for their long return trip home. If only all elections could be this friendly. When a recent town council showdown in Arizona ended in a 67-to-67 tie, local officials turned to a century old state law to break it: a game of chance. It could be any game, like rock paper scissors, marbles or straws, but Gila Bend decided its two candidates would draw cards, high card wins. And it’s a good thing they considered the possibility of another deadlock, because — improbably — both candidates drew 3s. It was pre-determined that spades would trump other suits, which one of the two wanna-bees had and clinched the win. Gila Bend is far from the first town to decide a race by chance. According to the New York Times, local elections have come down to poker games, straw-drawing and, earlier this month in Hawaii, names tucked into plastic eggs and picked from a woven basket. held on to the top spot at the box office over the holiday weekend, marking its sixth straight week at #1. So far, the movie’s made 2.4 billion dollars worldwide and capped a really good summer run for Hollywood, which saw domestic ticket sales up more than 22-percent over last summer. Still to come: if you like ice cream — and honestly who doesn’t — we have found what could be the perfect job. The Seahawks and Patriots, a Super Bowl rematch • Why is St. Louis’ famous arch dark for the month of September? Rapper, singer, and allaround businessman Snoop Dogg is hiring what could be everyone’s dream job: International ice cream taster. The pay: $10,000 a month for three months of globetrotting in search of the latest, greatest and wackiest frozen concoctions. Ultimately, the goal is to help Snoop pick out his next ‘flavor.’ Do you have what it takes? The job requirements include speaking English, a valid passport, and the availability to travel for the next three months. articles.text: On Sunday, August 23, more than 100 Girl Scouts and their families gathered in Piedmont Park to kick off the new scouting year at the annual ice cream social and sing-along. The ice cream social was hosted by Head-Royce and Piedmont High School tenth grade Senior Troop 33587, who served scoops of vanilla, chocolate, and rainbow sherbet with a variety of toppings, including sprinkles, whipped cream, crushed Oreos, and chocolate chips. While enjoying their ice cream on the lawn, PHS twelfth grade Ambassador Troop 30713 led the girls in singing traditional Girl Scout songs. This year’s singalong was the final time for these Ambassadors to host the yearly tradition before they graduate. The Ambassador Scouts belted out classic camp tunes, starting with “Make New Friends” and diving into lively repeat-after-me songs like “There Was a Great Big Moose.” The younger scouts were invited to lead the group with songs they picked like “Over the Deep Blue Sea.” Service Unit 303 Girl Scouts gathered in a friendship circle to close the event as the girls are ready for a year of building courage, confidence and character. Girl Scouts kicked off the new scouting year with an ice cream social and sing-along event in Piedmont Park. articles.text: Registration is underway for the Fall 2026 session, with classes beginning September 14. Piedmont Adult School offers a wide range of community classes designed to make learning enjoyable and accessible for adults of all ages. Whether you want to explore a big idea, discover a new practice or simply taste some really good chocolate, there’s still time to join us and learn something new and valuable this fall. Spaces are still available for classes including: • Understanding Modern Art — Make more sense of what you see in museums and galleries! Explore the artists, ideas and movements that shaped modern art and learn some of the vocabulary that can make looking at and talking about art more enjoyable. No previous art background is needed. • Philosophy as a Way of Living — Explore how ideas from some of the world’s great philosophical traditions can help us think about the questions that matter in everyday life, from our values and choices to what gives life meaning. • Mindfulness in Motion: Zen and the Japanese Sword (Budo Zen) — Discover a different approach to mindfulness through movement. This class combines Zen meditation with Iaido, a classical Japanese sword art practiced with bokken (wooden swords). Through guided sword movements, concentration and meditation, you’ll explore ways to develop greater focus, awareness and inner calm. No martial arts or meditation experience is necessary. • Wild Chocolate: Taste the Amazon — Taste four premium chocolates made from sustainably sourced Amazonian cacao and discover how where cacao grows influences its flavor. A certified chocolate taster will guide you through the tasting while sharing the story of chocolate that supports rainforest preservation and local communities. • Eat for Your Body Type — Learn more about your individual body type and explore how making thoughtful food choices can support your health and well-being. Come learn something new, expand your horizons, and meet great people at Piedmont Adult School this fall! Register today at piedmontadultschool.org or call 510-594-2655 for more information.

articles.text: Sophomore Girl Scout Troop #33587 started their scouting year by camping for two nights at Point Reyes the last weekend of August. They started at the Palomarin Trailhead and hiked 5.5 miles in with an elevation gain of about 1,000 feet to Wildcat Campground. This was their 24th camping trip as a troop and the longest backpacking hike so far. The hike took the girls past Bass Lake and through forests lit by the setting sun. The girls arrived at the campsite in the dark and were greeted by the moon rising over a ridge and Venus glowing in the west over the Pacific Ocean. By day, the girls were visited by a fox, an elk and flocks of California Quail. The girls also earned merit badges by drawing in nature as part of the Mind, Body badge. Juliette Edesses (left) and Emma Syhabout Photos by Carolyn Pan Girl Scouts in Troop #33587 take the Palomarin Trail towards Wildcat Campground in Point Reyes. Pictured are Victoria Mbise (left), Emma Syhabout, Juliette Edesses and Charlotte Phung. Troop #33587 backpacked 5.5 miles to reach Wildcat Campground in Point Reyes. Victoria Mbise (left), Charlotte Phung, Emma Syhabout and Juliette Edesses stop for a photo as the sun sets over Bass Lake. A gray fox walks by Piedmont Girl Scouts during their backpacking trip in Point Reyes. Troop #33587 leader Stacy Readall looks south from Point Reyes with the setting sun highlighting the Pacific Ocean.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont High hosted its first water polo match since 2019 on September 3 against James Logan. Staff Photos Thursday, September 3 was a monumental day for Piedmont High’s water polo team. The boys’ team hosted James Logan HS at the Piedmont Pool for a regular season match, marking the first time the team has done so since 2019. The Highlanders fell in double-overtime 8-7 to the Colts, but the game result hardly impacted the team’s joy on Thursday night. For people who have been connected to the program, like coach Rik Krumins who was an assistant coach on that 2019 squad, playing at home was an emotional experience. “We all worked so hard for this. I love this sport, and the fact we’re here is kind of weird. There are a lot of people who put blood, sweat, tears into this facility. One thing I talked with the team about was past teams were literally knocking on doors to tell people,” Krumins said. Piedmont’s current players were in elementary school the last time the school hosted a water polo match. “Tonight means a lot to everyone. We’ve had to commute long distances for practice, but the team has so much passion and everyone was willing to do it. This is definitely going to help get more people involved, younger people involved, and grow the program,” senior Colin Amen said. The Highlanders’ match against James Logan was a battle of two D2 North Coast Section qualifiers, and Thursday certainly had a playoff atmosphere. According to online records, Piedmont High has never hosted a playoff game at the Piedmont Pool. Before the closure, PHS received high playoff seeds from 2016 to 2019, but still played each match at pools outside Piedmont. For this year’s team, hosting a NCS match would be a major step forward. “It would mean so much to host a playoff game. Having that crowd really riles us up; it takes the intensity to a whole new level,” said junior Rylan Patty. “I’ve rarely heard a home crowd before. It’s great; I tried to get a lot of my friends to come out here. A lot of people don’t know how big water polo is to our community, but it’s a big sport in Piedmont. We have an awesome culture and it’s nice to share that with people,” Colin Amen said. Hearing a home crowd at Rylan Patty scores one of his three goals against James Logan. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team captured its first win of the season with a 28-0 shutout of St. Mary’s at Witter Field on Friday, September 4. It was a strong defensive day for the Highlanders who had five quarterback sacks, four tackles for loss, and an interception. It marked the school’s first shutout since October 2024 when they beat Dougherty Valley 41-0. “We probably could’ve played a cleaner game, but it’s hard to complain about a 28-0 shutout. The defense played really well, so it was good to see them rallying around and tackling. We’re a young team, and momentum is big for a young team, so now it’s about keeping the guys focused,” Coach Jordan Seiden said. It was a good response for PHS following its season-opening loss to Napa, where the winning side gained 314 yards on the ground. “During practice this week, we knew we had to work on the run game. We knew that if we stopped the run, we’ll be able to defend the pass and we really trust our pass coverage. We really just worked on defending the run so we can force them to pass,” senior linebacker Colby Hong said. Senior running back Rehan Mumtaz had his way with the Panthers’ defense, switching the field and putting opposing players on skates. He recorded 130 rushing yards on 12 carries, to go along with three receptions for 50 yards and two touchdowns. “We usually start off the season pretty slow, but once we find our zone, things really get going. Our line blocked so well today, I can’t give enough gratitude to them. Running becomes instinct at this point, I’ve practiced so many times that finding the lanes becomes second nature,” Mumtaz said. Game Recap St. Mary’s opened the game with a long drive down to Piedmont’s nine-yard line, but their series stalled on 4th-and-4. The Highlanders turned over on downs at their own 41, but wasted no time getting the ball back. On the Panthers’ first play, Piedmont’s Owen Curran intercepted a long pass at their own 12 with 20 seconds left in the first quarter. Staff Photos Diego Hurwitz (2) celebrates a touchdown with Henry Brennan (6) and Mason Gray (28). Rehan Mumtaz during his 35-yard touchdown reception against St. Mary’s. He had two touchdown catches, 130 rushing yards, and 50 receiving yards.

articles.text: Piedmont has boosted its record to 10-4 overall. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split its last two matches over the past week. They shut out Redwood Christian 3-0 on Tuesday, September 1 at Binks Rawlings Gym Two days later they fell to Salesian 3-2 in a heated five-set match bout 3-2 at Salesian in Richmond. The results improves Piedmont’s record to 10-4 overall, which eclipses last year’s total of nine wins. “When we’re at our best, we’re getting pressure from all three hitting spots. It starts with our middles and opens up. We continue to see them just getting better,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. Despite the loss to Salesian, outside hitter Maika Ting had a strong performance, logging a season-high 24 kills. “Maika’s been super consistent and has shown great improvement in terms of knowing when to take a little bit off and when not to,” Glass said. 3-0 over Redwood Christian It was a clean 3-0 sweep for Piedmont over the Eagles, winning by scores of 25-9, 25-14, 25-14. In the first set, PHS established an 18-5 lead at one point, including two kills by Maika Ting, Sofia Meyer, and Charlotte Bailey. Fiona Olsen and Lucia Dorsey also had individual kills and blocks. Piedmont continued the momentum into the second set, leading 9-0 until Redwood Christian got its first point. The run included three aces by Carina Vora, a block by Dorsey, and another kill by Olsen. RCHS inched closer to make it a 12-7 deficit, but PHS extended to 24-12 from there before the Eagles added two more points. Both teams traded points in the third set with PHS leading 5-4. From there, Piedmont scored seven straight points to lead 12-4. The Highlanders extended the lead to 22-7 before Redwood Christian inched closer to 24-14. PHS closed the game with a thunderous kill by Olsen. Final stats: Olsen recorded seven kills and one block. Ting recorded four kills, six digs and two assists. Bailey recorded two kills. Allyson Huynh recorded one kill, five digs and one assist. Izara Dando recorded two kills. Hazel Schaeffer recorded one ace and five digs. Meyer recorded four kills, two aces and three digs. Nora Trombi recorded two kills, one ace, two digs and seven assists. Olivia Stevens recorded five kills, one ace and three digs. Staff Photos Fiona Olsen led Piedmont with seven kills against Redwood Christian. Maika Ting had 24 kills against Salesian. Dorsey recorded four kills and two blocks. Vora recorded five aces, one block, six digs and 15 assists. Mia Bechtel recorded two aces, six digs and four assists. 3-2 loss to Salesian Piedmont won the second and fourth sets, Match scores were 25-19, 18-25, 25-19, 24-26, 15-12. In the fourth set, both sides traded the lead multiple times until PHS built a 22-18 cushion. However, the Pride went on a four point run to tie it at 22-22. PHS had set-point at 24-23, but an error tied things up. After that, Piedmont scored two straight with a kill by Dorsey and a lane violation by Salesian to force a fifth set. Salesian took control in the fifth set to hold match-point at 14-9, but PHS scored three straight to make things interesting at 14-12. To end the match, Salesian called the number of its tall middle hitter, finishing with a spike. Final stats: Ting recorded 24 kills, six aces and eight digs. Bailey recorded five kills, two blocks and one dig. A. Huynh recorded 35 digs and 11 assists. Dando recorded four kills. Meyer recorded eight kills. Stevens recorded five kills, and five digs. Dorsey recorded five kills, three blocks and three digs. Vora recorded two aces, 20 digs and 26 assists. Bechtel recorded nine digs and 11 assists. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Moraga for the St. Mary’s Invitational at St. Mary’s College on Saturday, September 5. The boys team came away with an eighth place finish out of 25 schools, while the girls placed 10th of 24 teams. “Overall, it looked like what it was – the first race of the season,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “We saw a lot of good things, but we also learned some things about how we need to race better. We had runners who were aggressive early, but had a harder time maintaining that momentum through the second mile.” Senior Alex Schleuning led the way for the Highlanders in 26th of 178 runners in 10:47.02 on the two-mile course. Piedmont’s top-four runners were separated by just 14 seconds. Dresden Schulte-Sasse was next in, finishing 36th in 10:51.57. Sophomore Dylan Wallway was 46th in 10:58.79, senior Aaron Bennett was 53rd in 11:01.35, while sophomore Blake Riiff rounded out the top five in 113th in 11:59.60. “Alex, Dresden, Dylan and Aaron were separated by only 14 seconds. Having four runners that close together gives us a really good group to work with as we continue building toward the championship portion of the season,” Zirkelbach said. The girls’ squad was notably without three top runners, seniors Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray, and sophomore Kelsey Coleman. Sophomore Camille Hauser led the team placing 46th of 166 runners in 13:19.95. Alex Schleuning led the way for Piedmont, finishing 26th of 178 runners. “Camille Hauser ran 13:42 here last year, so she improved by approximately 23 seconds from her freshman season,” Zirkelbach said. Piedmont had all five of its best runners within 53-seconds of each other. Right behind Hauser was senior Cora Brozowski-Schrader in 47th with a time of 13:21.42. Junior Nikita Gorelik finished 55th in 13:29.41, fellow junior Viviane Oesterer was 69th in 13:50.26, while sophomore Madeleine Ewen rounded things out in 83rd in 14:13.06. “We have always put a lot of emphasis on developing a strong pack rather than relying on one or two runners at the front, and this gives us a good group to continue developing,” Zirkelbach said. Dresden Schulte-Sasse was second in for PHS, placing 36th. Staff Photo Camille Hauser (1048) led the girls’ varsity team, finishing 46th of 166 runners.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team split its last two games, bringing their record to 2-5 overall. The Highlanders claimed a narrow 14-13 win over San Leandro at Witter Field on Thursday, September 3, and lost 38-0 to St. Ignatius of San Francisco at home on Saturday, September 5. Saturday’s game against St. Ignatius was Piedmont’s inaugural “Battle of the Bay” Highlander Showcase, which featured four games where one East Bay school took on one school from San Francisco. “A tournament like this is really good because we’re playing and watching more football. We’ve installed a lot in a little bit of time, so we’re looking forward to seeing how things look at the end of the season with the experience we’ve gained,” said defensive coordinator Hayley Adams, who filled in for coach Beth Black on Saturday. “This tournament means we’re taking this sport seriously. When the program started four years ago, it wasn’t very serious at first. Now, we’re here to play football and win games,” said quarterback Edie Elmquist. Against the San Leandro Pirates, PHS held an initial 8-0 lead after Agatha Filha-Gama recorded a safety late in the first quarter before Edie Elmquist hit Cea’naiya Alexander for a seven-yard touchdown midway through the second. San Leandro scored to end the first half. “Naiya was on the outside and was open in the corner. We’re moving the ball well; we’re working on blocking, seeing what the defense is doing, and then figuring out how that affects our plays and what we do,” Elmquist said. The Pirates went ahead 13-9 late in the third quarter, but Piedmont found the winner late in the game. Nearing the final minute Kate Tong had one interception and three pass defenses against San Leandro. Staff Photos Nea Mafi scored the gamewinning touchdown against San Leandro on an improvised 26-yard cutback run. of action, running back Nea Mafi made the play of the game. With the ball at SL 26, Mafi took an initial run to the left side, but turned the other direction with defenders converging on her. Using her speed, Mafi sprinted the opposite way to avoid pressure, evaded one defender, and then broke to the end zone to make it 14-13. 14-13 over San Leandro After back-and-forth possessions through the first quarter, Piedmont pinned San Leandro deep with a punt late in the first quarter. It led to Filha-Gama recording a sack in the end zone to give her team a 2-0 lead. Piedmont took over at their 25 midway through the second for its next score. Elmquist converted a critical 3rd-and-7 with an eight yard quarterback keeper, while Mafi later converted a 3rd-and-3 with an eight yard carry. On 3rd-and-goal from the SLHS seven, Elmquist stepped back for pass, initially looking left before turning to the right to find Alexander running a corner route for the touchdown, making it 8-0. San Leandro scored on its ensuing possession on 4th-andgoal from the 19 to end the quarter down 8-7. In the third quarter, San Leandro drove all the way down to Piedmont’s three, but the Highlanders held them without a touchdown. SLHS scored to end the third quarter after starting possession at Piedmont’s 25, scoring after four plays to go up 13-7. PHS had a chance to score after an interception by Kate Tong started a series at the Pirates’ 19, but Piedmont stalled out at the 23 following a penalty. Piedmont’s game-winning score came on the third play of its series. At the San Leandro 26, Mafi took a handoff to the Cea’naiya Alexander had a touchdown reception against San Leandro.

articles.text: William Bridges (4) Jeb Burden (81) Jojo Logwood (28) Although the Highlanders conceded a 26-13 loss to Casa Grande last week, their performance gave Highlander fans hope. The defense was quite strong and the offense picked up towards the end of the game. The Highlander defense came out in the first drive on fire. They set the tone on the first play of the game with a ferocious tackle for loss by Lethi Havea setting the Gauchos back 3 yards. The bottom line for the offense in the first half was turnovers. With two costly fumbles early in the game, the Gauchos put Piedmont on their heels with a passing TD and one touchdown on a run. With the Highlanders needing to score to stay alive, freshman Will Dietrich showed his speed and agility, taking the kickoff 70+ yards and putting the Highlanders in a prime position to go into halftime with some momentum. Along with his long kickoff return. Dietrich put the Highlanders in great position on just about every kickoff when he touched the ball despite playing with an injury. A combination of smart coaching by head coach Pouyan Assadi and quick runs by Ernie Hildreth enabled the Highlanders to convert on a fourth down with two seconds left in the first half. With an extra point by Gael Fierro the halftime score was 20-7. Special teams player Jojo Logwood came in with a full head of speed from the linebacker position and was able to block two CG extra points. With the Highlander defense trying to set the tone like they did in the first half, things were looking up as two penalties against Casa Grande’s offense resulted in a first and 25 on their own 20-yard line. But two miscues by Piedmont’s defense allowed a 23-yard catch, followed by a quarterback scramble to pick up the first down. It didn’t take long for the Gauchos to rip off a 54-yard touchdown run, the third TD of the game. With a Logwood extra point block the score was 26-7. Piedmont dominated the fourth quarter. Playing in Petaluma against a strong opponent, Piedmont showed grit and determination on both sides of the ball. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2026-27 season with Legally Blonde The Musical, based on the popular 2001 film, running September 11 through October 11. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods, a sorority president who enrolls at Harvard Law School after being dumped by her boyfriend and ultimately proves herself while working on a case. No’eau Kahalekulu directs the production, with choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes and music direction by Camden Daly. The production features a 25-person company of Bay Area performers. “If you loved this movie in 2001, I promise it’s even more fun with a live band and an audience. The show moves at a whip fast pace and is full of laughs and seriously impressive dance and vocals,” said Kimberly Dooley, Artistic Director of Berkeley Playhouse. “Legally Blonde defies stereotypes and celebrates female teamwork, empowerment and above all else...authenticity.” Kahalekulu said the character of Elle Woods has remained a favorite since the film’s release. “Elle Woods has been my comfort character since 2001. If she can get into Harvard and keep her sparkle, the rest of us can handle whatever’s in front of us,” said director No’eau Kahalekulu. “We’ve all gotten a little scared to be big and silly and sincere in public lately. This production is an invitation back into it. Like the show says, being true to yourself never goes out of style.” Scenic design is by Sarah Phykitt, with costumes by Ashley Renee and lighting by Sophia Craven. The musical is based on the novel Legally Blonde by Amanda Brown and the 2001 film of the same name. The cast also includes two dogs: Latke the Pomeranian, making a theatrical debut as Bruiser Woods, and Stella, a three-year-old French bulldog mix, as Rufus. Tickets are available through Berkeley Playhouse online at https://berkeleyplayhouse.org/. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods. Music Lessons │ Band Instrument Rentals │ Sales and Repairs

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will celebrate the opening of its 104th season with the 51st annual Opera in the Park, a free outdoor concert this Sunday, September 13, at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. The concert begins at 1:30 p.m. and will feature the San Francisco Opera Orchestra conducted by Music Director Eun Sun Kim, along with singers from the company’s upcoming 2026-27 season. Scheduled performers include sopranos Eleonora Buratto, Sofia Gotch, Mary Hoskins, Toni Marie Palmertree and Heidi Stober; tenors Joshua Guerrero and Christopher Sokolowski; baritones Amartuvshin Enkhbat, Thomas Mole and Gabriel NatalBáez; and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn. The program will include arias and ensembles by composers including Verdi, Puccini, Donizetti, Glinka, Weber and Richard Strauss, as well as a selection from a movie musical. San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock will emcee the concert. The event, presented by the San Francisco Chronicle, typically draws more than 10,000 people to Golden Gate Park. Established in 1971 by former Opera General Director Kurt Herbert Adler, Opera in the Park has featured performers including Luciano Pavarotti, Montserrat Caballé, Marilyn Horne and Renata Scotto. A picnic contest, introduced last year, will return, with judges selecting the best-decorated or most elaborate picnic spread during the first half of the concert. Food and beverages will also be available for purchase. Children and families can visit Bearitone the Opera Bear’s Club House for coloring, crafts and lawn games. The event is free and does not require tickets. For more information, call (415) 864-3330 or visit sfopera. com/operainthepark. The free concert is held at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Opera
articles.title: SF Opera performs free concert in Golden Gate Park this Sunday

articles.text: Ramona Kelley in Oakland Ballet’s performance Luna Mexicana Oakland Ballet Company will perform Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Día de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on October 30 and November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission, Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza . Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Tickets are available online now. Visit https://oaklandballet. org to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony opens its 2026–27 season with Inheritance on Sunday, October 18, 2026, at 4 p.m. It marks the return of Music Director Laureate Kent Nagano to the orchestra for the first time since 2009. Held at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts (10 10th St, Oakland), the season-opening concert brings together works by Felix Mendelssohn and the world premiere of Vater unser by Argentine composer Alex Nante, a work dedicated to Berkeley Symphony and Nagano. The program opens with Mendelssohn’s The Hebrides (Fingal’s Cave), followed by the premiere of Vater unser. Pianist Mari Kodama then joins the orchestra for Mendelssohn’s Piano Concerto No. 1. The program concludes with Mendelssohn’s Symphony No. 5, “Reformation,” whose finale is built on the chorale “Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott.” “In Vater unser, Bach’s melodies become a point of departure for an unbound process of orchestral amplification and harmonic elaboration,” said Nante. “One of my main interests as a composer is the evocation of light in sound, whether in meditative or ecstatic atmospheres.” Nante began his series of Bach-inspired works at Nagano’s encouragement, as the composer and conductor have collaborated frequently in recent years. Nagano led Berkeley Symphony for 31 years, from 1978 to 2009, shaping the orchestra into an internationally recognized Photo by Antoine Saito Conductor Kent Nagano is renowned for interpretations of clarity, elegance, and intelligence, with a repertoire spanning the classical, romantic, and contemporary eras. ensemble known for adventurous programming and commitment to living composers. His return to the podium reunites Nagano with an orchestra whose artistic identity he helped define for more than three decades. “As Berkeley Symphony looks toward its future, it is especially meaningful to welcome Kent Nagano back to the orchestra he helped shape,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton. “Kent remains a wonderful friend and champion of Berkeley Symphony, and we’re delighted to have him with us for this season opener. His return connects us to the orchestra’s history while reminding us that an inheritance is not simply something to preserve – it’s a foundation to build on as we imagine our future.” Berkeley Symphony’s 2026-27 season features three Mainstage Concerts and two Chamber Concerts, including two premieres. The next Mainstage Concert features Berkeley-born composer Gabriella Smith’s Desert Ecology, a response to the realities of climate change, on February 27 and 28, 2027. Following orchestra tradition, living artists make up over half of the season’s composers. Subscription packages and individual tickets are on sale now, with single tickets starting at $20. The season offers a full subscription (all three mainstage concerts plus both chamber concerts) and a mainstage subscription (all three mainstage concerts). Tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by phone at (510) 841-2800.
articles.title: Kent Nagano returns to Berkeley Symphony podium in Oct.

articles.text: Photo by Gary Sexton Installation view of Contemporary Painting in Papua New Guinea: Mathias Kauage and His Family. A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through December 6. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea. He exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The local exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moresby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Georgina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art in Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/papua-new-guinea-mathias-kauage.
articles.title: Mathias Kauage exhibition now on display at de Young

articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 15. Now in its 15th year, the three-night festival brings illuminated art installations to the gardens surrounding Lake Merritt. The event has drawn more than 12,000 visitors since its launch in 2012. This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays throughout the gardens, along with live entertainment, an art market, children’s activities and food and beverage vendors. Additional activities include a costume contest for children and adults, an artists awards program and a kids zone. The festival’s food court will feature local food trucks and vendors, along with beer and wine gardens. Proceeds from ticket sales benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a nonprofit volunteer organization formed in 2004. The organization works with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization and programming of the gardens at Lakeside Park. The seven-acre collection of themed gardens includes the Bonsai Garden, Sensory Garden, Toddler Garden and Urban Edible Garden, among others. FGLM volunteers provide maintenance assistance as the city’s gardening staff has been reduced over time. The Autumn Lights Festival is the organization’s largest annual fundraiser. Tickets and additional information are available through the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt at https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/about/. Crystal Gardens by Studio One Art Center, 2025
articles.title: Autumn Lights Festival returns to Lake Merritt Oct. 15 - 17

Following orchestra tradition, living artists make up over half of the season’s composers. Subscription packages and individual tickets are on sale now, with single tickets starting at $20. The season offers a full subscription (all three mainstage concerts plus both chamber concerts) and a mainstage subscription (all three mainstage concerts). Now in its 15th year, the three-night festival brings illuminated art installations to the gardens surrounding Lake Merritt. The event has drawn more than 12,000 visitors since its launch in 2012. This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays throughout the gardens, along with live entertainment, an art market, children’s activities and food and beverage vendors. Additional activities include a costume contest for children and adults, an artists awards program and a kids zone. The festival’s food court will feature local food trucks and vendors, along with beer and wine gardens. Proceeds from ticket sales benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a nonprofit volunteer organization formed in 2004. The organization works with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization and programming of the gardens at Lakeside Park. The seven-acre collection of themed gardens includes the Bonsai Garden, Sensory Garden, Toddler Garden and Urban Edible Garden, among others. By Allyson Aleksey A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through December 6. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea. He exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The local exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moresby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Georgina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art in Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. Two crashed into the twin towers of the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon, and one was brought down in rural Shanksville, Pennsylvania, by the extraordinary will of the onboard passengers. Known simply as 9/11, it is a day that will forever be remembered and memorialized. The moving and heartfelt film Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close opens with what has become an iconic image of 9/11: the falling man. We bear witness to an individual dropping some 106 stories through the air, unable, we assume, to escape a consuming fire and so chooses this unimaginable final outcome. Another image captured in the film, one that will forever be with us, is the scene of a brick wall. It’s only been a few days since the Twin Towers collapsed. In the dark of night the camera slowly moves from right to left, revealing countless photographs of the missing, along with hand-written messages, many a desperate plea to call home. Many years ago, I knew one of the important Spanish dipThe Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet lomats of the 20th century. He was the Duke of Baena, and even though I knew him very well I always referred to him as “Your Excellency.” The Duke’s diplomacy was one of his strong points. One time he had a heated meeting with Generalissimo Franco. Diplomacy probably saved him from execution. I need his advice now on how to answer my opinion of pop music. One famous musician of the past responded by saying: “I like some of it very much.” The two concerts I attended were Tom Rigney’s fiddle concert with his ensemble known as Flambeau, and a concert entitled “Paris in Piedmont” presented by SonoMusette. The music was worlds apart, but the concerts shared many things in common. Each ensemble was thoroughly professional. They love to perform. It was most enjoyable to see their seamless timing as they moved from one musical selection to another. The mature audience was appreciative and enthusiastic from the outset. It is very gratifying to see things like this. But there was one drawback. Both concerts were so loud that the music was deafening. The volume was artificially created by artificial amplification not artistic ability. As I said before, the audience loved everything. It didn’t matter that they were becoming deaf. They loved it all. I, however, value my hearing and decided to depart. The music was still audible through closed doors while I was across the street. articles.text: High above Napa Valley, on the rugged slopes of Pritchard Hill, Chappellet Winery occupies a place that is both physically and historically distinctive. Founded by Donn and Molly Chappellet in 1967, the family winery was one of the pioneers of Napa Valley’s modern wine era and helped establish mountain vineyards as a source of some of California’s most distinguished Cabernet Sauvignon. Donn Chappellet came to winemaking with an ambitious goal: to produce wines that could stand alongside the great First Growths of Bordeaux. After selling his interest in a successful food-service company, he and Molly moved their family to Pritchard Hill, then an isolated and largely unproven piece of Napa Valley. Following the advice of legendary winemaker André Tchelistcheff, they planted vines on the steep, rocky terrain. It was hardly an obvious choice. Pritchard Hill is considerably warmer and more rugged than much of the valley floor, with elevations at the Chappellet estate ranging from about 800 to 1,800 feet. But those difficult conditions turned out to be an advantage. The thin, well-drained soils and varied elevations and exposures naturally limit vine vigor and produce small quantities of intensely flavored grapes. Today the estate is divided into 48 vineyard blocks, each reflecting differences in soil, slope and exposure. Chappellet’s first commercial Cabernet Sauvignon appeared in 1969, establishing a tradition that remains at the heart of the winery. Although the original vineyards also included Chenin Blanc, Riesling, Chardonnay, Gamay and Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon gradually became the estate’s signature. The winery’s Pritchard Hill Cabernet Sauvignon is now its flagship wine, produced from the finest fruit on the mountain. The winery itself is almost as memorable as the wines. Built in 1968, the unusual pyramid-shaped structure was designed by artist Ed Moses and architect Dick Keith. Partly hidden among the trees, it has become one of Napa Valley’s most recognizable winery buildings. Winemaker Phillip Corallo-Titus, who returned to Chappellet in 1990, has guided the estate’s winemaking for decades, emphasizing vineyard expression and the distinctive character of Pritchard Hill. In an era when many Napa wineries have become corporate enterprises, Chappellet offers something increasingly rare: a family, a mountain and a clear sense of place. Its greatest achievement may be proving that Pritchard Hill was not merely a difficult place to grow grapes, but one of Napa Valley’s extraordinary sources of Cabernet Sauvignon. is one of the biggest most powerful Pinots I have had in ages. Broad, silken and rich in the mouth it flows through a deep saturated and anise-tinged finish that lingers with firm, finegrained tannins and a juicy core of intensely concentrated fruit flavors. The finish is long and satisfying. Very impressive. • 2025 Chappellet Chenin Blanc $75 Chappellet has been producing Chenin Blanc long before it became the trendy hot grape in California. The wine shows a golden color with a faintly greenish hue. The palate sits at a medium to full-bodied weight, offering a plush yet mineral-driven core with peach and pear flavors. The fruit is tight and textured at this early stage. Juicy and mouthwatering, it finishes with a squeeze of fresh lemon, delivering freshness and drive. • 2025 Chappellet Pinot Noir Apple Lane Vineyard $70 Hailing from the Russian River Valley this inky dark Pinot Chappellet makes a classic style Cabernet Sauvignon. • 2022 Chappellet Cabernet Sauvignon $95 The wine opens with complex aromas of plums, blackberries, tobacco and currants. The oak is well-integrated. On the palate, the wine is full-bodied, richly tannic and very deep, with a layered, concentrated core of fruit framed by chalky tannins. The wine has great structure and should last for a couple of decades in the cellar. The Chappellet Cabernet Franc was the top wine of the tasting. • 2022 Chappellet Cabernet Franc $115 Hints of tar, sage and black pepper accent cassis and black cherries in this medium-to-fullbodied effort. Rich and concentrated, it’s supple, even creamy up front, then more velvety textured on the long, soft finish. Delicious but it will improve with time in the cellar. • 2022 Chappellet Las Piedras $95 This Bordeaux-style blend uses all five of the traditional Bordeaux grapes. It offers up aromas of dark berries, chocolate, plums, espresso and earth. It is medium-bodied deep and fleshy with a rich lively core of fruit, powdery tannins and a long, penetrating finish. The perfect partner to a grilled steak or lamb chops. articles.text: A new program called Weavers is getting Piedmont seniors and teens together for social visits aiming at intergenerational connectivity. The Piedmont chapter of Weavers was tested from April to June with more than 40 participants, thanks to the help of founding members and Piedmont students Allyson Huynh and Luca Laforte. Gloria Lee of Oakland founded the program along with Kristin Richmond, the co-founder of Revolution Food. Lee, who lectures at Cal and Stanford, contacted Ken Li, the Crew Advisor of Piedmont Community Service Crew to get the program off the ground. She was then introduced to PHS juniors Huynh and Laforte, meeting in March to discuss the launch. Huynh started a Weavers’ Instagram to recruit teenagers to participate and went door to door in Piedmont to find interested seniors. Lee explained the origination of the program. “My sons Corbin and Asher really benefited from their friendship with an older neighbor, who first invited them over to bake cookies when they were four and six years old,” she said. Richmond’s son Caleb similarly started a window washing business and noticed that the older adults hiring him enjoyed chatting more than they cared about clean windows. The Piedmont program in the spring started with six weekly visits between “Weavers,” teens, and “Silvers” (seniors), and each visit lasted 60-90 minutes. “We think it’s really important that these relationships are mutually beneficial. We saw other well-meaning programs out there that treat one person in the relationship as someone who needs Olivia Tran (left), Mary Carter, Dick Carter, and Elly Mak. to be taken care of — but no one really wants to be the recipient of charity,” said Lee. Helping one another and building community is at the forefront of this work. “While Weavers are able to lend a hand to Silvers with technology support, gardening, and light organizing. I have found that people really do enjoy just talking. It makes a difference in your day just to have a good long conversation with someone,” said Huynh. In the Spring pilot of Piedmont and Oakland region, there were 23 Weavers and 23 Silvers. Piedmont’s Dick and Mary Carter signed up for the program because they like the concepts of intergeneration connection and people helping one another. They also joined because of the recommendation to join from longtime friend Ken Li. “Just meeting and talking with these delightful, energetic young people is delightful,” said Dick Carter. “I think older adults who don’t have much contact and communications with teenagers would especially benefit and enjoy the program. However, everyone can benefit from having more contact with people who are different from them.” Carter also spoke of a reaffirmation that the future is in good hands after the meetings, a comment echoed by many of the Silvers participating. “Intergenerational community to me feels like everyone, regardless of age, having positive relationships,” said Huynh. “It feels like everyone coming together and being friends, making memories, and having fun. Having this kind of community is super important because really, everyone benefits.” “Weavers will have the opportunity not only to demonstrate their skills but also have those skills validated by an older adult with lots of life experience. One of the important things about this program is that both sides contribute and both sides benefit,” said Lee. All participants of the spring pilot signed up again for the fall sessions which begins this month. Teenagers and seniors who want to learn about the program can visit beaweaver.com or call 510-788-0260. Gael Pardi (left) and Asher Breeden. Nava Shaham (left) and Olivia Bailey. Co-founder Kris Richmond leads a focus group with Silvers (seniors) in Mill Valley, the site of the program’s second pilot.

articles.text: Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group drew 50 walkers and seven K-9 best friends to the Exedra for Part 2 of a walk they had enjoyed in early August. Mary Carter was back to lead, again drawing on her former Wildwood School Piedmont history lessons and Ann Swift’s 2007 Cottages and Castles – The Centennial Houses of the City of Piedmont for a second visit to historical, pre-1906 San Francisco Earthquake Piedmont homes. Swift’s book describes 173 of the city’s historic homes that qualified in 2007 as Piedmont Centennial Homes. August’s walk covered mostly Hillside Avenue; this one turned to Highland and Bonita. Mary started up Highland at 636, commonly known as “The Ghirardelli House,” one of the more noteworthy and beautiful homes in central Piedmont. George and Grace Howell built a Mission Style home there before 1903, then hired A.W. Smith to build a larger Tudor next door at 630 Highland on a lot they owned. In 1905 they sold 636 to Joseph and Ellen (Ellie) Ghirardelli, the son and daughter-inlaw of Domenico Ghirardelli, the Italian-trained chocolatier who emigrated from Genoa to Uruguay in 1838, came north for the Gold Rush, and founded his chocolate company where Ghirardelli Square stands today. Joseph, born in 1852, was the third of the Ghirardellis’ eight children. He worked in the family business and was in Santa Cruz when the 1906 earthquake struck. With no transportation available back to the East Bay, he set out on foot and died of a heart attack on the way. He never lived in the Highland Avenue house, which was then being remodeled from Mission Style to the Colonial Revival we see today. Ellie and their two daughters moved in once the work was finished. Back up Highland, the group passed 1900 Oakland Avenue — “The Rackliffe House,” built in 1899 with captivating witch’s cap turrets — and, across the street, the turreted Queen Anne at 225 Highland. John and Annie Hendry sold lots there to Maggie Perry in 1897; she built the house in 1898 and rented to the Hendrys, who eventually bought it from her. A 1910 proposal to line the street with retail stores set off a battle among the neighbors, and the widening that followed in 1911 claimed Annie’s front garden. She had the house put on rollers and moved with a significant setback so that her garden would never again be violated. At Highland’s corner with Moraga Avenue stands 7 Highland, built in 1907 by Frank C. Havens’ Piedmont Development Company to showcase homes and sell lots in Piedmont. Current homeowner Patty Edmonds came out to tell the walkers her family’s history with it: her mother and stepfather lived there 55 years until their passings, and Patty and her husband, Art, moved in later. She said the couple recently noticed a bulge around the front entrance and discovered the wire support for the stucco exterior had fully deteriorated after 120 years. It has been replaced, and the exterior will be painted soon to complete the project. Down Moraga and up Bonita, the walkers noted 24 Bonita, built in 1904 with deep eaves and brown shingles, and 42 Bonita, built in 1905 — a “hybrid house,” Mary said, originally wood-sided Colonial Revival until brown shingles added sometime after 1926 gave it a Craftsman look. Its owner, spotting half a hundred visitors outside, came out to see what was going on; the words “Wednesday Walkers” explained everything. He provided a little more information about the home but declined to be identified for this report. Farther along, 112 Bonita is a “twin house” to a Hillside home built in 1905. The Queen Anne “Berkenfeld House” at 227 Bonita has rooftop gargoyles, spindle work posts, corbels, and window panels. Its initial owner was one of the original Piedmont volunteer firefighters, who helped save a house at 116 Hillside — and possibly the block — during Among those participating were Moya Robinson with K-9 best friend Petunia, Albert Chen, Bill Ahern, Juliane Jacqueline, Kristin Howard, Audrey Sung, Matt Truesdell, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Rich Harms, Matt Gerhardt, Judy Love, Debbie Powell, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Cathy Laymon, Peggy Shultz, Noemi Alvarado, Vicki Trimbach, Pat Nicholas, Jim Kuo, Brian Hamlin, Denny McGee, Mary Ann Barnes, Greg Keller, Claudine Bach, Caskey Weston, Melba Yee, Chuck Oraftik, Rick Eigenbrode, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mark Davis, Sherry Jacobs, Mary Carter, Charlene Louie, Mary Henderson, Alan Jolly, Sanghi Wagner, Dan Sedonis, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friend Brie, Pat Keller, Bern Schild, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Christine Cumbelich with K-9 best friend Kobe, Anne Gritzer, Iris Chavarria, Al Chen with K-9 best friend Sherlock, and Eli Messinger walking with them for the first time.
