articles.text: Gary Laymon, 68, of Piedmont, California, passed away peacefully on July 24, 2026 after a nearly two-year journey with cancer. He was a cherished husband, father, son, brother, neighbor, colleague, and friend and he will be deeply missed. Gary was born in 1958 to Rose and Maurice Laymon in Indianapolis, Indiana. They moved to the Bay Area, where his younger sister, Nancy, was born in 1961. The young family lived between Mount Tamalpais and Mount Diablo, eventually settling in Danville. The Laymons were involved in their local church, and Gary loved going to the youth group. He also enjoyed singing in the church choir, bowling, playing golf, and doing yard work when he wasn’t pulling goofy pranks with his friends. He graduated from Monte Vista High School in 1976, and began pursuing a degree in Landscape Architecture at Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo that fall. After graduating, Gary landed a job with Guzzardo & Associates, a landscape architecture firm in San Francisco, where he would spend the next 46 years. He began attending First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley in the ’80s, meeting many dear friends and was involved in several fellowship groups. Through a young adult group, he met Cathy Ives, who invited him to a party marking the anniversary of the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. His world was rocked as through some blessed misread signals each believed the other to be flirting, and suddenly Gary saw his friend in a new light. They were together ever since the “Great Misunderstanding,” marrying October 3rd, 1992, and welcoming Emily in 1996, Claire in 1999, and Elissa in 2002. Gary was a devoted father, known for his silliness, humor, and sense of adventure. He shared with his daughters his love of the ocean, music, gardens, art, bike riding, and travel creating countless memories along the way. As a young family, the Laymons enjoyed bike rides in wine country, hikes in the East Bay Hills, annual trips to Half Moon Bay’s pumpkin patches, Disneyland trips, summer musicals at Woodminster theaters, sports games, innumerable dance recitals, and summers with extended family at Mount Hermon, where Gary had gone as a child. As the girls grew older, the family traveled together to France, Spain, and Italy, went wine tasting and bike riding, toured an excessive number of gardens and art museums, and took thousands upon thousands of photos. In 2000, Gary became partner and owner at The Guzzardo Partnership with his long-term colleague Paul Lettieri. Gary was passionate about landscape design and loved working with clients to bring projects to life. He also enjoyed mentoring and teaching colleagues who were newer to the profession. Any drive in the car with Gary inevitably included him pointing out the many, many projects he had worked on over the years. In his free time, Gary painted with acrylics, moving through phases of vineyards, palm trees, scenes from his travels, Gary with his paintings at the Piedmont Art Walk Piedmont resident Gary Laymon died on July 24, 2026, at age 68. surfboards and abstract pieces inspired by his favorite jazz compositions. He loved sharing his art, displaying it at church and participating in the Piedmont Art Walk over several years. Gary’s faith was integral to his life. He started the day with Bible study and prayer. He saw needs and felt led to help. He was known for being kind, humble, gentle, grateful and generous. He was involved in several projects at church and led work groups at CityTeam Oakland, an organization near and dear to his heart. Mostly, Gary loved the routine of the life he loved: commuting to work in SF by bike and ferry, church on Sunday with Cathy by his side and being the last to leave the sanctuary, never having chatted with quite enough people; drinking Peet’s coffee every morning from a cup he painted when the kids were young at Color Me Mine; creating immersive scenes from scripture in his garage-turned-studio space with his paint brush; marveling at the miracle of streaming music on Spotify; calling out “sunset alert!” in the house when the view was too stunning to miss; working hard in the yard, always wanting to make things more beautiful. It was never enough to marvel at something alone. Gary wanted to share his awe, share his vision, and share the beautiful things he created to the fullest extent possible. Gary is survived by his wife, Cathy Laymon of Piedmont; his daughters, Emily West (Nick) of San Diego, Claire Laymon of Piedmont, Elissa Laymon of San Francisco; his mother, Rose Laymon, of Walnut Creek, and his sister, Nancy Laymon, of Chico. He was preceded in death by his father, Maurice Laymon. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made in Gary’s memory to CityTeam Oakland. Gary with his family (from l to r) Nick, Emily, Cathy, Gary, Claire, Elissa
articles.title: Remembering Gary Laymon: Creating Beauty, Sharing Joy

articles.text: James Richard Saunders, Jr., known as Jim to family and friends and “Pops” to his grandchildren, passed away peacefully at his home in Piedmont, California on July 11, 2026, surrounded by family. He was 82 years old. Jim was born on August 5, 1943, in Omaha, Nebraska. He grew up in Menlo Park, California, where he attended Menlo-Atherton High School. He went on to graduate from Johns Hopkins University before earning his medical degree from the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. While at Menlo-Atherton, Jim met Lynn, who would become his wife and lifelong partner. They were married for 59 years and built a life together while raising their three children and, in later years, enjoying the company of their six grandchildren, all of whom live within a mile. Jim practiced internal medicine for more than 40 years, spending the majority of his career with Oakland Medical Group. He took great pride in the lasting relationships he built with his patients, many of whom remained with him throughout his career. Medicine was more than a profession to Jim; it was a passion he cared deeply about and approached with dedication, compassion, and integrity. Outside of medicine, Jim had a lifelong love of the outdoors and stayed active through running, cycling, and hiking. He was a devoted Oakland sports fan and always knew the latest scores. Whether following the A’s, RaidJames Richard Saunders passed away peacefully on July 11, 2026. He was 82 years old. ers, or Warriors, he enjoyed keeping up with his teams through every season. Jim was also well known for his quick wit and sense of humor. Jim is survived by his devoted wife, Lynn; his son, Vince Saunders and his wife, Michelle, and their children, Henry and Charlie; his son, Jamie Saunders and his wife, Teebie, and their children, George and Jane; and his daughter, Ashley Stevanovic and her husband, Andreja, and their children, Luka and Nicholas. He was preceded in death by his parents, James and Marion Saunders, and his sister, Joanne. Jim will be remembered as a dedicated physician, a loyal friend, and a devoted husband, father, and grandfather. His family will miss his humor, his steady presence, and the many ways he quietly showed his love over the years. In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that donations be made to the charity of your choice in Jim’s memory.
articles.title: James Richard Saunders, Jr., MD

The Colts maintained the two goal advantage to lead 5-3 through the second, including Patty assisting Wilson for a goal and Patty scoring via a 5-meter penalty. In the third, PHS tied the match at 5-5 with two minutes left. Wilson assisted Patty for a goal with 3:21 left before Henry Stein scored with two minutes left. However, JLHS scored 30 seconds later to take a 6-5 lead into the fourth. Patty drew a 5-meter penalty early in the fourth, leading to Stein scoring with 5:23 left. Patty then gave PHS a 7-6 lead with 1:52 left in the fourth. But with 16 seconds left, James Logan scored the equalizer to force overtime. Both teams went scoreless through the first period, including Wilson hitting the crossbar with a minute left. Graham Smith had a shot saved nine seconds into the second period of overtime. Something has happened, but he is just fine and everyone has been told to remain in place. Message two has an edge of uncertainty to it, yet remains reassuring. There are six calls in all, each seeming more fraught than the previous one, until the last message (“hello…are you there? Are you there?”) abruptly stops, followed by a long moment of silence. Oskar, who has turned on the television, watches in disbelief as the towers fall, as if in slow motion, each vanishing into billowing clouds of dust. Horrified, he runs to his room and crawls under his bed, waiting for his mother, Linda (Sandra Bullock), to return from work. Finally she arrives, and knowing what has occurred coaxes him out and into her arms. Oskar is incapable of accepting the loss of his father, his grief immeasurable, and when his mother has an empty-casket funeral, he refuses to attend, observing the ceremony from a distance, his denial palpable. Loud & Close Continued from page 16 Hanks), a call from the 105th floor of one of the towers where he has been attending a meeting. Something has happened, but he is just fine and everyone has been told to remain in place. Message two has an edge of uncertainty to it, yet remains reassuring. There are six calls in all, each seeming more fraught than the previous one, until the last message (“hello…are you there? Are you there?”) abruptly stops, followed by a long moment of silence. Oskar, who has turned on the television, watches in disbelief as the towers fall, as if in slow motion, each vanishing into billowing clouds of dust. Horrified, he runs to his room and crawls under his bed, waiting for his mother, Linda (Sandra Bullock), to return from work. Finally she arrives, and knowing what has occurred coaxes him out and into her arms. Oskar is incapable of accepting the loss of his father, his grief immeasurable, and when his mother has an empty-casket funeral, he refuses to attend, observing the ceremony from a distance, his denial palpable. And so a year passes, and finally, reluctantly, Oskar enters his father’s den and begins to look through his things. And when taking down a box, he knocks a blue vase off the shelf, breaking it. Among the fragments he discovers a small envelope with the name “Black” written on it. Inside he finds an unusual, corrugated key. Oskar holds the key in his hand, and it is in that moment that he becomes convinced that the key fits a lock, a box perhaps, that contains a message from his father. And thus we learn, through flashbacks, that over the years Thomas has created what he called “reconnaissance expeditions,” a scavenger hunt of sorts, which sends Oskar out into the streets of New York in search of what they call “the sixth borough.” And so attaching the key to a lanyard, which he wears around his neck, Oskar is inspired to begin a similar expedition. He starts by looking through a massive NYC phone book, and finds that there are 472 Blacks listed. His mission, kept a secret from his mother, is to visit all of them, asking if they recognize the key. His first stop is at the home of Abby Black (Viola Davis), and it’s during his conversation with her that he mentions he has been tested for Asperger’s Syndrome with inconclusive results. We know that Oskar is precocious, at times brusque, highly verbal, but we soon learn that Thomas’ expeditions were about much more than simply a sixth borough hunt, but a way of sending his son into a world in which he is inherently uncomfortable. Abby has no idea about the key, and so Oskar continues, from Black to Black, showing each of them the key, and using his father’s vintage camera takes their photograph, which he keeps in a notebook. To refer to Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close as a work of art may verge on hyperbole. And yet, doesn’t it represent the use of images and narrative as only film can, to explore the depths of grief and loss while focusing on the emotions of a young boy who struggles to find meaning in what he angrily judges is meaningless. The key becomes a metaphor for Oskar’s arduous and at times fraught search for answers to questions that are timeless: to what purpose? To what end? And, ultimately, why? Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close. Directed by Stephen Daldry. Starring Thomas Horn, Tom Hanks, Sandra Bullock, Max von Sydow. 2 hrs, 9 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Although the median home value has risen, so has the Consumer Price Index (CPI). If elected, I will work to reduce monthly bills and increase home values through access to affordable electrification and energy efficiency programs. I will also work to lower the upfront cost of home upgrades that have a positive return on investment and improve our health by reducing exposure to gas. I tackle fiscal responsibility first because a solid financial foundation is required to deliver on any other priority. Currently, inflation and rising labor costs outpace our revenues. They will continue to lead the classroom in its new home, bringing continuity and stability to the transition. The new location offers a light-filled, calm and inviting setting for the school’s play-based approach to early childhood learning. PPS remains the only licensed preschool of its kind in the area built around social-emotional learning as a core part of its curriculum. A day at Piedmont Play School Each day at PPS blends structured and child-led play, giving children space to explore, build friendships, and develop independence alongside caring, familiar teachers. PPS’s play-based, mixedage curriculum is intentionally designed to strengthen the social and emotional skills that matter most as children grow. Mixedage classes encourage younger children to learn from older peers and give older children opportunities to lead and mentor — building confidence, empathy, and communication skills. Educators increasingly point to strong social-emotional foundations as a key predictor of success when children enter TK and Kindergarten, where academic and behavioral expectations have never been higher. PPS’s approach is designed to help prepare children for that transition both academically and emotionally. Teacher Michelle Ritchie has been with Piedmont Play School since 2013. A Co-Op model built for busy families PPS operates as a light co-op by design. Families are asked to contribute in small, manageable ways rather than large time commitments, making it possible for working parents to still be present and engaged in their child’s classroom experience. Many parents describe their volunteer hours as some of the most rewarding time they spend with their kids. For PPS President & CEO June Groboske, the co-op model is about more than the preschool. It’s the starting point for a much longer relationship between families and their community. “Our co-op model is where a lifelong connection to our school community begins,” said Groboske. “PPS parents discover early on what meaningful school involvement looks like. Working side by side with teachers and other parents gives families a firsthand appreciation for the school, classroom, and community dynamics, helping parents learn how to best support teachers and students alike. That strong foundation naturally carries forward — so many of our PPS parents go on to serve as parent board officers, school committee chairs, and active community leaders throughout PUSD.” With this move to Clarewood Drive, PPS parents, alumni, and teachers preserved a philosophy of early childhood education, a group of beloved teachers, and a place where families can be genuinely involved in their children’s earliest school experiences. The comfort in knowing the school will carry on, paired with genuine enthusiasm for what’s ahead, has echoed throughout the PPS community as the school settles into its new space. To learn more about PPS, please visit piedmontplayschool. org. Follow along: @piedmontplayschoolca on Instagram. Students enter Piedmont Play School at age 2 usually with enrollment designed as a two-year experience preparing them for Transitional Kindergarten or Kindergarten. articles.text: As fall begins, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to set aside time to complete a simple, easy-to-follow at-home wildfire evacuation exercise with their household. The exercise provides step-by-step instructions and discussion prompts in a short video that families, housemates, and neighbors can use to transform their wildfire “what ifs” into a tangible, actionable plan. The short exercise helps you spot gaps, talk through decisions, and walk away more confident about what to do if a wildfire comes. What to expect: • A realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont • Simple, pause-and-discuss prompts for each stage of • • • evacuation A downloadable worksheet to capture your household’s plan and next steps A calm, supportive narrator to walk you through the process Total time: 30-45 minutes Watch the video and download the worksheet at piedmont.ca.gov/ WildfirePlan. Find additional wildfire preparedness resources at piedmont.ca.gov/Wildfire. The at-home evacuation exercise is one part of the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. Last year, the department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/ Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving them a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide year-round public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. The department also recently led the development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a 5-year roadmap that identifies steps the city can take to reduce the effects of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole.
articles.title: Fire Dept. asks residents to complete wildfire evacuation plans

articles.text: Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions. For this year’s race, the Post will send one question every week to the candidates running for City Council in the November 3 election. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on Wednesday, September 16, and were asked to reply with a 200-word response. Week 4 question: What, in your view, are the city’s top 3 infrastructure needs? If elected to the council, which of these needs would you prioritize addressing? And why? Adam Hundt (AdamHundt.com) The top 3 infrastructure needs for Piedmont are: first, mitigating risk from hazards that could affect residents’ housing; second, the renovation and modernization of city buildings (including Police and Fire departments) and the improvement of sewer and storm drain infrastructure; third, the upkeep of roads and enhancements to crosswalks and bike pathways to ensure resident safety and mobility. First, I support the Fire Department’s outreach work with residents to address hazards by switching from gas to home electrification and managing vegetation on one’s property to reduce wildfire risk. Piedmont’s 2025 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) noted the near 100% likelihood of catastrophic wildfires occurring in the next year or every year. Second, aging infrastructure is not up to code and challenges city departments’ ability to provide resident services. Piedmont Police and Fire departments need modern facilities that adequately accommodate personnel and equipment. The Recreation Department, which provides programming for children, needs repair. Piedmont must improve its city sewers to meet obligations from a Consent Decree Order. The Regional Water Quality Control Board has stormwater management requirements. Third, Piedmont must continuously maintain its roads; enhance crosswalk, sidewalk, and path safety and accessibility for pedestrians and bicyclists; and reduce speeding. Tom Ramsey Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com) We live in a beautiful, historic town, but our infrastructure requires aggressive stewardship to keep Piedmont functioning at a high level. Three critical needs stand at the top: Sewers and Storm Drains: We lead neighboring cities in complying with federal sanitary sewer mandates, but 30% of the project remains. We must stay on track using State Revolving Fund low-interest loans, while preparing storm systems for El Niño. Pavement Management: Staff excels at securing state and county revenues, but rising construction costs outpace funding, causing our Pavement Condition Index (PCI) score to slip. We must inject more capital here; every dollar spent on maintenance saves up to ten dollars in future reconstruction. Aging Civic Buildings: Modernizing facilities far exceeds current revenue. I echo the Budget Advisory Committee’s guidance: ongoing planning, quantification, and strict prioritization are vital given long lead times. If elected, I will prioritize Pavement Management. While sewer compliance is mandated and facility upgrades require long-term planning, road maintenance offers the most immediate fiscal leverage. Letting streets deteriorate creates a compounding liability. Prioritizing preservation now protects tax dollars from being wasted on catastrophic road failures, keeping Piedmont safe and fiscally sound. Bill Reichle (ReichleforPiedmont.com) Given the age of our infrastructure, Piedmont has more maintenance and capital needs than available dollars. As a result, identifying, prioritizing, sequencing, and funding infrastructure projects is a continuous discussion between the city administrator, city council, and residents. articles.text: On Friday, September 18, the annual Medieval Faire was held at Piedmont Middle School. The Medieval Faire is an event for 7th graders as a way to experience what life was like during Medieval times. The school tradition dates back over 30 years. The students elected a king, queen, and nobility, and everyone dressed in period costumes. The monarchy and nobility made speeches welcoming everyone, and different classes performed during the “banquet” of cookies and juice. Lastly, everyone went to the pickleball courts where Medieval games were set up. One of the classes spent their social studies periods making games for the faire: Fortune Telling, Ring Around the Rosie, Donut on a String, Soak-a-Serf, Cornhole, and Hoop Rolling, taking place on the pickleball courts. Some of the most popular games were Soak-a-Serf, where someone stood in a pillory while others pelted them with sponges, and Donut on a String, a competition for the first to finish a donut suspended in the air by a string without their hands. Overall, most people thought that the fair was a fun way to see how it was in Medieval times, reinforcing the things they learned in social studies. (See additional articles and photos on pages 8 and 9)
articles.title: 7th Graders host annual Medieval Faire

articles.text: Racers prepare to enter the water with the help of parents. On Saturday, September 19, Piedmont hosted the Cardboard Boat Race at the Community Pool. Over 20 families came to the pool to build boats from scratch and race against other kids in their age group. The event took over the Activity Pool from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. Kids ages five through 12 designed and built a boat using cardboard, then launched it into the pool to see if it could make it across the water. Saturday’s event had three age brackets. Families had an hour and a half to build a cardboard The Heywood family won the age 7 & under competition with their boat and well-designed paddle.
articles.title: Piedmont’s Cardboard Boat Race brings families together

articles.text: I strongly recommend Piedmont voters support Measure GG on this November ballot. Measure GG is a “transfer tax,” a one-time assessment collected when property is sold or ownership is transferred. The current Piedmont transfer tax was set in 1993. It has not been updated in 33 years. The transfer tax is a one-time tax levied on a property at the time of sale and is often split between the buyer and the seller. Piedmont does not have sales tax or any significant commercial tax revenue, so the transfer tax is a critical source of income and represents 10% of the annual operating budget of the City. Proceeds from Measure GG will stay in Piedmont and support our core City services through the City’s General Fund. The City uses those revenues to partially pay for repair of aging City buildings, streets and sidewalks, parks, public safety and recreation. Our neighboring communities of Oakland, Berkeley, Emeryville, and Richmond have all increased their transfer taxes far higher than Measure GG. While Piedmont home prices have risen in the last few years, maintenance expenses and construction costs for roads, sidewalks and storm drains have risen even faster. As a former Councilmember and Mayor, and now Chair of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, I have had a front row seat to City revenues and expenditures for the past 14 years. I can attest that the City Council has taken, and continues to take, a conservative approach to budgeting and expenditures. A long-overdue increase in the transfer tax would provide the City with revenue to continue to provide essential services and maintain the basic City infrastructure upon which we all rely. Please join me in voting YES on Measure GG. – Bob McBain, Former Mayor Chair of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee

articles.text: I am writing in support of Measure GG, which will appear on the November 3 ballot. Piedmont is a remarkable community because of the things we have built and maintained together—excellent public safety, responsive police and fire services, beautiful parks, well-maintained streets and sidewalks, and the many community services that contribute to the quality of life we value so highly. Measure GG provides an important source of funding to help preserve those services for the future. The measure would increase Piedmont’s one-time real property transfer tax from 1.3% to 1.75% and is expected to generate approximately $1.5 million annually in additional general tax revenue. What I particularly appreciate about this approach is that it is a onetime tax paid when a property changes hands, rather than an annual tax on every Piedmont homeowner. The cost of the transfer tax can also be negotiated as part of a real estate transaction. For those of us who live in Piedmont, the value of our community is not simply the homes we own. It is the security of knowing that our police and firefighters are there when we need them. It is the quality of our parks, roads, sidewalks and public spaces. It is the investment we make in maintaining the infrastructure and services that make Piedmont such a special place to live. The City has identified significant ongoing needs, including aging buildings, infrastructure, parks, stormwater systems, roads and sidewalks, in addition to essential public safety and emergency services. I believe maintaining these services is an investment in the community we all care about. Measure GG provides an opportunity to help ensure that Piedmont continues to be the safe, beautiful and exceptionally well-served community we know and love. I encourage my fellow Piedmonters to vote YES on Measure GG this November. Sincerely, –Teresa Baum, Realtor
articles.title: A stronger Piedmont starts with protecting what makes our community special

It will feature candidates on the Piedmont City Council ballot in the November 3, 2026, General Election. The forum will be held at 7:00 p.m. in the City Council chambers and in overflow space as needed. It will include the following five candidates running for three positions: Nancy Beninati, Nancy Bostrom, Adam Hundt, Tom Ramsey, and Bill Reichle. Piedmont voters can learn more about the City Council forum at lwvpiedmont.org. Registration is required to attend the live forum, as space is limited. There will likely be a ballot drop-box in central Piedmont next to the mailbox near the Piedmont Community Church. articles.text: What is the Real Estate Transfer Tax? The transfer tax is a one-time assessment collected when property is sold or ownership is transferred. Transfer tax revenue in Piedmont funds day-to-day costs for police, fire, emergency response, public works, recreation, and other services, as well as the maintenance and replacement of aging infrastructure and facilities. Who pays the Transfer Tax? Piedmont’s transfer taxes are typically split equally between buyer and seller when a home is sold, although the parties may negotiate a different arrangement. How would Piedmont’s rate compare with neighboring cities? Measure GG would bring Piedmont’s rate more in line with neighboring cities. In Oakland, the rate is 1.75% for sales between $2 million and $5 million and 2.5% for sales above $5 million. In Berkeley, the rate is 2.5% for sales of $1.6 million or more. What prompted the City to update the transfer tax? Piedmont has had a local transfer tax since 1968. As other neighboring cities have modified theirs, Piedmont’s transfer tax has not changed since 1993, which was 33 years ago. The City is facing a long-term gap between the cost of maintaining existing city services, facilities, and infrastructure and the revenues available to support them. Piedmont has no significant revenue from retail, and the cost of rehabilitating City buildings, parks, streets, sidewalks, stormwater drains and other infrastructure are rising. The increase was recommended by the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, after the City Council asked that they explore options for addressing Piedmont’s long-term needs.
articles.title: Measure GG: Transfer Tax FAQ

articles.text: What would Measure GG do? Measure GG would increase Piedmont’s Real Estate Transfer Tax rate from 1.3% to 1.75% of the sale price of real property – from $13 to $17.50 per $1,000. If approved by a majority of voters, the new rate would take effect July 1, 2027. Measure GG is estimated to generate $1.5 million in additional revenue annually. Actual revenue will vary based on the number of sales and sales price.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Harvest Festival returns for its 28th year this Sunday, September 27. Attendees will enjoy a day of food, music, art, and community traditions throughout Piedmont Park from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. The festival kicks off the fall season for Piedmont families. The Edibles Contest has been part of the Harvest Festival since the beginning and remains its centerpiece. Each year, Piedmont’s community creativity and talent shine as tables fill with homemade breads, pies, cookies, jams, and homegrown produce. To enter, residents can download the entry form at piedmont.ca.gov/EdiblesContest and drop their entry off with a label at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:30 to 10 a.m. on the morning of the festival. This year’s Harvest Festival will feature an expanded Farmers’ Market, including local honey, flowers, vegetable starts, skincare products, and more. The Watermelon Eating Contest will return this year after last year’s success. Competitors will line up and eat a watermelon as fast as they can; the first one done wins. Sign-up is on-site, and the competition starts at 1 p.m. Scarecrow Alley will be crowded with student scarecrows to be auctioned. All auction proceeds benefit Beach, Havens, and Wildwood. For more information, contact the Piedmont Education Foundation: info@ piedmontedfoundation.org. The Harvest Festival will host an Art Show at the Tea House, featuring work from Piedmont artists. Those interested in becoming an exhibitor may contact Jane Reed Two local kids trying their best at the PEF Carnival Judges at last year’s Edibles Contest survey the food and make their decisions. at (510) 654-2670. The Kids’ Carnival features fun games like ring toss, alien invasion, Krazy Kan, and more. The carnival benefits Piedmont elementary schools. Families can buy their kids a wristband in advance at PiedmontStore.org. A wristband gets you unlimited carnival games, one walk-through at the Cake Hop, and one snow cone. Seven food trucks plus Oakland’s Line 51 Brewing will be available for attendees to enjoy. Piedmont’s community groups will host tables to showcase their organization with a “harvest” theme. The Harvest Festival is searching for volunteers. Shifts are available from 8:30 to 11:30 a.m. for set-up and 3 to 5 p.m. for event breakdown. Contact Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen at ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov to sign up. For more information, including vendor lists, schedules, edibles contest entry forms, and volunteer opportunities, visit piedmont.ca.gov/HarvestFestival.
articles.title: Annual Harvest Festival returns for the 28th year on Sunday

articles.text: The Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival celebrates its 25th year this Sunday, September 27. The festival will take place on an open stage in front of the Piedmont Community Hall starting at 11 a.m. This free city-sponsored event will be held in conjunction with the Harvest Festival and the School Carnival. For 25 years, the festival has celebrated Piedmont’s rich musical talent. This year’s performers will include the Piedmont High School Jazz Band, the Clifton Street Regulars, J Fleser and the Jaywalkers, and What Might Have Been. Each performance will last close to an hour. The festival will run alongside the Harvest Festival, providing Piedmont Park with music while people play games, visit community tables, and participate in competitions. The Jazz Festival will take a 30-minute recess at 1:00 p.m. for the Watermelon Eating Contest. To learn more about the Jazz Festival and the Harvest Festival, visit the city’s website: https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/ events/harvest_festival. The Clifton Street Regulars are one of the performers for this Sunday’s Jazz Festival.

articles.text: Mina Herrgott Girl Scout Troop #33521, made up of 15 high school juniors, will host a garage sale on Sunday, September 27, selling interesting used items from their homes to promote sustainability while fundraising for their activities. The garage sale will take place at 39 Craig Avenue, just a few blocks away from the park, from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m. The garage sale will coincide with the Harvest Festival, the yearly gathering of music and food in Piedmont Park. This gives people enjoying the Harvest Festival an opportunity to explore vintage clothes, children’s toys, sports gear, and handmade objects, from jewelry to ceramics. Girl Scout Troop #33521 was started in 2017 and has grown from a few students at Wildwood to almost 20 members from Piedmont and Oakland. They have done a variety of activities and gone on many adventures, ranging from camping to learning from Piedmont’s firefighters. Their earlier years were characterized by badge earning – first aid, babysitting, woodworking, eating healthy, and more. Many of the members completed a Silver Award in middle school. Girls spent more than 50 hours addressing a community issue. Two girls advocated to reduce food insecurity, another pair built a website about animal care, and one pair created a brochure to support new immigrants in the East Bay. Now students at Piedmont High School, Head Royce, and College Preparatory, they’re focused on volunteering and earning their Gold Awards, the most prestigious award in Girl Scouts and the next step after their Silver Award. Girl Scouts pursuing a Gold Award need to have at least 80 hours of work with prominent experts to create a profound, lasting impact on their community in an area of their choice. Some examples of Gold Award projects include supporting girls in a male-dominated sport, increasing excitement about math for kids, and educating people to empower introverts. Girl Scout Troop #33521 invites you to their Garage Sale Fundraiser. Please stop by to give these amazing items a new home and, in doing so, support these young entrepreneurs. articles.text: A local artist is live painting a piece for a guest at Drawn Together. Children’s Fairyland announces the return of its “artsiest party of the year.” Drawn Together will take place on Friday, September 25, from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. For this special evening, Fairyland opens exclusively to adults ages 21 and over, offering a rare opportunity for grown-ups to explore the magical world of Fairyland, a place typically reserved for children and their families. Tickets are now on sale. An intimate evening of live art, cocktails, and creative connection. The 21-and-over event invites art lovers to watch more than 50 local artists and industry professionals create original, Fairyland-inspired artwork live throughout the park. As the night winds down, the energy shifts into a wildly spirited art sale, where guests can take home a piece created that very evening for just $50. “It’s an open-air art gallery meets a bar meets a theme park meets a party meets an art sale,” said Fairyland’s Artistic Director Shannon Taylor of the one-ofa-kind event, which blends the whimsy of Fairyland’s storybook setting with a full slate of adult entertainment. Drawn Together is an adultsonly playground, featuring cocktails, food trucks, live art being made in real time by local visual artists, puppet shows, live music, tarot card readings, artists’ meet-and-greets, an infamously spirited art sale, and an evening showing of Fairyland’s current puppet production, The Three Little Pigs in the 1920s. Guests can explore Fairyland’s iconic storybook sets, from Willie the Whale to the Alice in Wonderland card maze. Tot-sized rides and animal areas will be closed for the evening. Guests who would prefer a guaranteed place are welcome to purchase a Patron Ticket. Patron Ticket holders will receive a numbered, limited-edition Children’s Fairyland print created exclusively for Drawn Together 2026, along with early entry to the event. It gives guests a chance to avoid the lines, speak with artists before the crowds arrive, and secure a piece of art early, all while donating to Children’s Fairyland. P roceeds f rom D raw n Together will support the people, programs, and spaces that make Children’s Fairyland magic possible year-round — from free field trips for under-resourced communities to hands-on workshops that bring creativity to life for young visitors. Tickets are $35 for general admission, $30 for members, and $100 for Patron. Tickets and event information can be found on Fairyland’s website: https:// secure.fairyland.org/4337/4338.
articles.title: An Adults-Only (21+) Evening of Live Art for Bay Area Artists

articles.text: The new phone policy at Piedmont High School, which forces students to keep phones and personal internet-connected devices in backpacks for the entirety of school days, has caused unforeseen consequences as students try to adjust to a different campus environment. After six weeks of the new policy, many students are expressing frustration over the restriction of their phones. According to the 2026-2027 student handbook, the current board of education policy limits cell phone usage during the school day to only a “dumb phone,” a phone equipped only with text and call features. Students began to see the new policy’s enforcement on day one of school, August 10, with cell phones being confiscated by school staff and Campus Supervisor Darnell Reed. “The phone policy has been very effective so far,” junior Cassidy Carter said. “Especially with the scaring tactic of phones being taken to the office, and the threat of having to turn your phone in every day at the beginning of the school day.” Many students are frustrated the policy was created to begin with, citing bigger issues that the school should be focusing on instead. “I don’t think it addresses an actual issue, if anything it’s more work for the teachers,” junior Maika Ting said. “They’re the ones having to enforce it and our old policy didn’t really have any issues.” With each violation of the phone policy, consequences increase. The first offense causes phones to confiscated for the day and comes with an email to parents. Further disciplinary action include revoking phone privileges for the remainder of the year, daily phone drop-offs, and assignments to progressive disciplinary. A fourth offense results in ineligibility for school activities. “The punishments are a little too harsh. It’s likely that many students will get their phones taken since we are slightly reliant on them,” Carter said. “It’s unfair to have to turn them in in the mornings on only the second offense.” Classes such as yearbook and journalism occasionally require cell phone use, which has caused frustration and difficulty when classes are given exceptions, according to students. “It’s necessary to have them on you at all times for pictures, interviews, or notes.” Carter said. “Administrators didn’t really understand that there was no need for a change.” Students also rely on their cell phones to contact family members throughout the day, and the phone policy limits their ability to do so. “I don’t think they [the administration] understand that students use their phones as a way to talk to their parents at school,” sophomore Olivia Nealon said. “Many people rely on lunch to talk to their parents about after school plans.” With lunch being the only period where students can go off campus and use their phones, there has been a decrease in students spending lunch on campus, changing the campus atmosphere in an unexpected way. Students said there are possible improvements to be made to make the policy more effective and sustainable for further years. “Having a hard reset for a number of phone offenses at different times throughout the school year would be better,” Carter said. “Or some other punishment that is a little more lenient for students.” Ayla Blanford is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student intern writer with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: PHS phone policy too spartan for some students

articles.text: Piedmont librarians published a Letter to the Editor in the September 2 Piedmont Post describing the imminent lose of the COMPASS program at the end of this school year. Educators and librarians are currently calling on state legislators to restore funding for the California Online Media Program for Access and Student Success (COMPASS), a statewide program that provides K-12 students and teachers with free access to high-quality, vetted online research resources. The 2026-27 state budget eliminates COMPASS funding after July 1, 2027, ending the state’s $5.5 million annual investment in the program. COMPASS databases include Encyclopedia Britannica, PBS videos, PebbleGo, Gale, National Geographic for Kids, ProQuest, and TeachingBooks. Media resources slated to be lost include encyclopedias, research databases, and scientific journals. “We cannot imagine doing our work of teaching media literacy and research skills without this program,” Piedmont librarians stated. Since 2018, COMPASS has provided free access to research and curriculum resources to California’s public schools. The program’s resources are verified by teachers and credentialed school librarians. Since its launch, the program has received over 700 million searches. California ranks 49th nationwide in school librarian staffing, with nearly 10,000 students for each librarian, according to research by the Institute of Museum and Library Services. Without librarians or research tools, K-12 students will have to fend for themselves. According to a CalMatters article the state allotted funds for COMPASS in earlier budget versions but is directing the funding elsewhere. Instead, $5 million of the funding is going toward the state’s new dyslexia screener. Read more at Calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2026/06/ school-libraries-california/ The cost of replacing COMPASS will be dramatically higher if schools and districts are required to purchase the resources independently. According to the California State Library, individual schools subscribing to comparable COMPASS materials would spend more than $216 million annually. To send Governor Newsom an email urging him to restore this resource visit: Saveschoollibrarians.org/compass2026.
articles.title: Librarians provide warning about upcoming state cuts

articles.text: Ariel Rodriguez Many high schools throughout the country will be hosting the PSAT in October, but what is the PSAT? PSAT stands for Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test, essentially the precursor to the SAT. Like the SAT, the PSAT is a digital, adaptive test that includes a Reading & Writing section and a Math section. Both the SAT and PSAT are 2 hours and 14 minutes long. There are also some major differences between the PSAT and the SAT. The PSAT is only offered once per year, in October, and is typically hosted by your high school. The SAT, on the other hand, is offered eight times per year at test centers throughout the country. The maximum scaled score on each section of the PSAT is 760; the maximum scaled score on each section of the SAT is 800. If you are a junior taking the PSAT, your scores could qualify you for National Merit Commendation or National Merit Semifinalist. Many schools will also allow sophomores to take the PSAT, but only scores from junior year can qualify for national merit recognition. Exact score cutoffs are determined by state in the year following the PSAT taken. So, a junior taking the PSAT Fall 2026 will not find out if they have received national merit commendation or semifinalist status until 2027. Commended students are typically within the top 3-4% of testers; semifinalists are typically within the top 1% of testers. Historically, California has been one of the states with the highest cutoffs. Students who are National Merit Semifinalists can apply to become National Merit Scholars. National Merit Scholar status makes you eligible for different scholarships: some from the National Merit Scholarship Corporation, some from private corporations, and others from colleges and universities themselves. While there are some perks for students who score in the top percentiles on the PSAT, for the vast majority of students, the PSAT mainly functions as a practice test. If the PSAT is being offered at your school, go ahead and take it and put in a good faith effort, but don’t put undue stress on this test. Instead, use it as an opportunity to gain more information that will empower you to understand how standardized tests may become part of the bigger picture for college admissions. Ariel is the Co-Director of College Consulting and Emily is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Ariel has worked in undergraduate admissions at both public and private universities. For more information, please visit www. studysmarter.com, email info@ studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.

articles.text: On Saturday, September 12, the Piedmont Makers hosted a season kickoff and watch party for the unveiling of the 2026-27 FIRST Tech Challenge theme at the new community robotics and maker space on 10th Street in FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) challenges middle and high school students to design, build and program robots to compete in a new game each year. Working with mentors, students develop engineering skills, teamwork and strategies for competition. A local non-profit dedicated to K-12 STEAM education, the Piedmont Makers offers hands-on learning opportunities through robotics, maker programs, teacher grants and community events. The organization has expanded beyond Piedmont, with programs serving over 1,000 students from 139 schools across the Bay Area during the 2026- 2027 season. Piedmont Makers’ programming starts in kindergarten and continues through high school. “It’s a really amazing program that impacts a lot of kids for a very long time,” says Paul Morrison, the co-leader of the Piedmont Makers FIRST Tech Challenge. The 7,000-square-foot 10th Street facility serves as a hub for the local maker and robotics community. The space provides a full-size robotics practice field and access to specialized equipment like CNC routers, and has hosted over 30 robotics teams throughout the Bay Area in the past year. Highlander Robotics, Piedmont Makers’ capstone high school team, first had the idea: a full-size, community-accessible robotics practice field. The team opened one at a temporary space in Oakland, giving Bay Area teams that used to drive to East Palo Alto for practice a home in the East Bay. When rent rose at that location, the team partnered with Piedmont Makers to find a long-term site. It was a period where you could be anyone from the Medieval Ages, from archbishops to the rats carrying the bubonic plagues. Everyone dressed in colorful attire. Some favorites were the plague doctors, dressed in deep, black robes (sable, if you may) and those horrifying crow masks. Another interesting garment to note was the riding cloak. It’s such a beautifully cut piece of fabric, trimmed at the ankle and crowning the shoulders, pinned together with an elegant brooch. With crow masks and cloaks discussed, I still must ask what could a medieval faire be without its fair share of fair maidens? There were several glamorous dresses, featuring deep blues and rich greens worn by our nobles and queen. These flowing dresses allowed for a very stately gait, present in all the faire’s activities. And although the faire is over, surely all medieval apparel will be remembered. articles.text: The Piedmont-based non-profit Orion Fund will host its 20th annual Golf Tournament and Banquet at Chardonnay Golf Club in Napa on Saturday, October 24. Tickets are affordable and go to the best of causes, supporting college students undergoing medical emergencies in California. The Orion Fund non-profit started at the behest of Piedmont moms two decades ago following the death of PHS graduate Orion Trott from cancer at the age of 21. They have awarded more than $850,000 to college students in times of urgent need. The Orion Fund provides grants for students amidst any health crisis including organ transplants, car crashes and cancer diagnoses. The Orion Fund primarily serves low-income students without family support, many of whom are first-generation college students and working while enrolled. “We put a safety net under them so that they can recover and complete a hard-won education,” said Orion Fund President Pam Hirtzer. Since the Orion Fund began in 2004 it has assisted 500 college students with grants, so kids battling an injury or setback can stay enrolled in college. The Orion Fund has sent tuition to more than 65 schools in California, supporting local kids of all demographics, under any medical crisis, for any academic pursuit. Grant winners have also applied their funds to keep their health insurance or pay their rent while ill. Twenty-seven grant recipients already selected for the next year depend upon the continued support of donors to the Orion Fund. “It is seriously difficult to fundraise for non-profits in this day and age. We can’t help everybody, and have to turn kids away that would otherwise qualify,” said Hirtzer. A tee-time in the October 24 golf tournament and a seat for the banquet dinner costs $165; this also includes cart rental and range balls. The shotgun start begins at 12:00 p.m. and at 5:00 p.m. there will be a banquet dinner, along with an auction, tournament awards and a golden raffle. This year’s top prize in the raffle is a goals. The Chardonnay Golf Course in Napa is the site of the 20th annual Orion Fund Golf Tournament on October 24.

Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Waking up before sunrise for practice. Carrying two backpacks from class to class. Finishing homework in the backseat of a car on the way to an away game. For student-athletes at Piedmont High School, the school day doesn’t always end when the final bell rings. Practices, games, and workouts can last well into the evening, leaving athletes scrambling to find time for schoolwork whenever they can. Water polo player senior Raffaello Banin said managing school work during the water polo season can be difficult, especially when games and practices take up much of the day. “I try to be super efficient overall when I have time to work and sometimes get homework done in the car on the way to games,” Banin said. For some athletes, that efficiency means less free time to relax. Basketball player senior Taylor White said her schedule requires her to fit schoolwork in whenever she gets the opportunity. “Managing school and a sport can be a challenge sometimes, but mostly I do my homework during my free periods, in the car while going home, and sometimes I set my alarm to wake up early in the morning to catch up on anything I missed,” White said. The challenge can become more complicated for athletes who compete outside of PHS. Many student-athletes participate in club sports, adding another layer to an already busy schedule. For volleyball player junior Olivia Stevens, the timing of the school and club seasons helps make the commitments more manageable. “School season is August-October and club is November-May, so it works out,” Stevens said. “For beach volleyball, it’s harder because it’s spring season and it overlaps [with club], but it’s still manageable.” Even when seasons do not directly overlap, the workload can be exhausting. White said club basketball is more laid back than her school season, but travel can make it demanding. During school basketball season, practices and workouts can add another physical challenge to the school day. “The school days can be tiring after a workout from the previous day,” White said. “Since we have workouts right after school, it just depends on my mood. But other than that, school season is exciting.” Despite the time commitment, athletes said their sports provide experiences that make the busy schedules worthwhile. For Banin, one of the biggest differences between club and school sports is the connection among teammates. Knowing teammates from school already creates a stronger sense of community. “School sports is a bigger commitment [than club sports], but the team is also more connected because we see each other every day,” Banin said. “Club is good though, because you meet new people and it’s fun.” White said basketball has given her the opportunity to build relationships while also competing against high-level competition athletes from around the country. “The experience and opportunity to travel across the country playing against some of the best competition and future college players is really exciting. I get to see how I match up against some of the best players,” White said. For PHS student-athletes, balancing academics and athletics often requires fitting study sessions and homework in whenever there is time , and achieving success both as an athlete and as a student requires physical and mental strength. The sacrifices that athletes make show up both in the classroom and on the field, the court, or the pool. Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: The double life of student-athletes

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team won one of four matches at the Vintage Valley Tournament at Vintage HS in Napa on Friday and Saturday, September 18-19. All three losses were separated by two goals or less; they fell 9-8 to Clayton Valley Charter and beat Marin Catholic 11-8 on the opening day, while losing 12-10 to Sequoia and 12-11 to San Marin the following day. The batch of results brings the Highlanders’ record to 5-6 overall with eight matches left in the regular season. It was a strong tournament for junior Henry Stein, who had 24 goals over the four-match span, including nine goals in their 12-11 loss to San Marin. Goalie Dylan Jerez was also instrumental in keeping the matches close, recording 35 saves throughout the tourney. Official quarter-by-quarter score lines were not provided for the tournament matches. 9-8 loss to Clayton Valley Charter Piedmont fell 9-8 in the opening match of the tournament. Clayton Valley led 4-0 through the first quarter and 6-2 by halftime. Then, Piedmont roared back in the third quarter with four unanswered goals to knot things up at 6-6 going into the final period. . However the Ugly Eagles outscored the Highlanders 3-2 in the fourth to win it. Final stats: Stein led with five goals and three assists. Rylan Patty had two goals, two assists, and two steals. Dylan Jerez finished with 11 saves, two steals, an assist, and scored once as a goalie. 11-8 win vs. Marin Catholic The Highlanders claimed its only win of the tournament 11-8 over Marin Catholic in their second match. Final stats: Stein had five goals and two assists. Patty had five goals, one assist, and one steal. Henry Van Den Bos had one goal and an assist. Oliver Hurwitz had one assist and one steal. Graham Smith had two steals. Travers Kemp had one steal. Raffi Banin had one assist. Jerez had six saves, four steals, and two assists. 12-10 loss to Sequoia Piedmont returned on Saturday and lost a narrow 12-10 battle to Sequoia. Staff Photos The boys’ water polo team won one of four matches at the Vintage Valley Tournament in Napa.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Newhall Community Park in Concord for the 2026 De La Salle Nike Invitational on Saturday, September 19. The Highlanders’ boys’ team finished 22nd of 31 schools, while the girls were 18th of 22. “The De La Salle Nike Invitational was our third meet of the season and another opportunity to see how our runners are progressing as we start to head into the middle of the season. We are still only in September. We are continuing to train, build durability and learn how to race,” explained coach Steve Zirkelbach. “The objective isn’t to be at our best right now—it is to keep progressing so that we are running our best when the important championship meets arrive later in the season. Saturday gave us another encouraging indication that we are moving in the right direction.” Junior runner Dresden Schulte-Sasse led PHS for the third straight meet. He finished 50th of 204 athletes with a time of 17:06.9 on the three-mile course. “Dresden led Piedmont over the three-mile course, becoming our No. 3 junior performance by a Piedmont runner at Newhall Community Park. Dresden gave us another strong performance at the front of the boys’ varsity team,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Schulte-Sasse was senior Alex Schleuning placing 99th with a time of 17:45.1. Junior Luca LaForte was 140th in 18:32, Dresden Schulte-Sasse led Piedmont’s boys’ team for the third straight meet. sophomore Blake Riif was 162nd in 19:07.6, while sophomore Rohan Seshan rounded out their best five runners in 164th, clocking a 19:13.8. “Alex Schleuning was our second finisher, followed by Luca LaForte. Blake Riiff continued his strong start to the season, and Rohan Seshan completed our scoring five. Our collective time of 91:45.4 was the No. 2 Piedmont varsity boys’ team performance at Newhall Park,” Zirkelbach said. The girls continue to run without marquee runners Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, and Kelsey Coleman. Junior runner Viviane Oesterer led the girls’ side, finishing 76th of 167 with a time of 21:13.7. “The front of our girls’ varsity group ran particularly well. Viviane Oesterer led Piedmont with a very good time for the three-mile course. She improved her previous Newhall Park best by approximately eight seconds and moved to No. 4 on Piedmont’s junior list at the event,” Zirkelbach said. Senior Cora Brozowski Schrader was next in for the Highlanders, placing 82nd, clocking a 21:24.1. Junior Nikita Gorelik was 96th in 21:45.3, sophomore Camille Hauser came in 120th in 22:55.7, while senior Annie Thornton rounded out their five scorers in 144th, 24:32.9. “Just behind Viviane was Cora Brozowski Schrader. Cora’s performance ranks No. 2 among Piedmont seniors at Newhall Park. Nikita Gorelik gave us a third runner near the front. That put Viviane, Cora and Nikita within approximately 32 seconds of one another. Developing that kind of grouping at the front of the team will be increasingly important as we move farther into the season,” Zirkelbach said. NEXT UP Piedmont has 11 days of rest before its first Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season on Wednesday, September 30 at Point Pinole Regional Park at 3:30 p.m. Alex Schleuning was the boys’ second best runner at the De La Salle Invitational. Viviane Oesterer (right) and Cora Brozowksi Schrader (left) were PHS’ top two female runners at the De La Salle Invitational.
articles.title: PHS cross-country team runs at De La Salle Nike Invitational

articles.text: Staff Photos Chiara Silvio (left) and Emma Chan locked down a 6-4, 6-0 win at No. 1 doubles against Berkeley. The Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team got its Western Alameda County Conference schedule started in a big way, dominating rival Berkeley 6-1 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Wednesday, September 16. PHS fell 4-3 to North Coast Section competitor Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco the previous day, September 15. Wednesday’s win over the Yellowjackets was a good display by the No. 1 doubles duo of Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio, claiming the school’s first win of the day in a 6-4, 6-0 victory. Chan is in her third varsity year and second straight year as the team’s No. 1 doubles starter after appearing alongside Samantha Huynh last season. “Because Chiara and I are really good friends, it’s easy have a connection on the court and coordinate our shots. I don’t need to tell her where to go, she’ll already be there. Obviously, like any new partner, it takes some adjusting to. At this point of the season, we’re getting more comfortable and coordinated,” Chan said. “We played a lot together growing up and we have good chemistry. I don’t have to worry about what she’s going to do next,” Silvio said. Silvio did well at the net against Berkeley, converting many smashes and volleys for points. “It’s been really nice because I can rely on Emma to be really aggressive. I think my net-play has gotten a lot better, I’ve gotten more comfortable and confident there,” Silvio said. “Her net play is great,” said Chan. “When Chiara gets her racket on the ball at the net, it’s really effective,”. The Berkeley win was an impressive display by freshman Maddy Huynh, moving up to the No. 2 singles spot with usual starter Faith Chin out. Huynh dominated in a clean sweep, 6-0, 6-0. “With Faith out we moved up Maddy. She has been really good and we have a lot of belief in her. She’s already a great player and is going to get even better,” said coach Jim Landes. 6-1 win over Berkeley Winning the first match of the day was the No. 1 doubles duo of Chan and Silvio. Leela Sivakumar quickly followed with a 6-0, 6-1 win at the No. 3 singles spot, while Ella Ruthven at the No. 1 singles spot won 6-1, 6-3 to five Piedmont its third win. Maddy Huynh clinched the day at No. 2 singles in her shutout victory, giving PHS its fourth Maddy Huynh, a freshman, moved up to No. 2 singles against Berkeley, winning in a 6-0, 6-0 clean sweep. win. After that, Berkeley got its only win of the day at No. 4 singles, where Ella Sharafi lost 6-4, 7-6 (7-5). Finishing the day was Ella Thomasson and Paige Chin winning 6-1, 6-4 at No. 2 doubles, while Penelope Welch and Mai Pham won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 3 doubles. 4-3 loss to Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont won one of four matches at singles with Faith Chin winning a barn burner in three sets at the No. 2 spot by scores of 6-3, 3-6, 10-8. Ella Ruthven lost 6-3, 6-0 at No. 1, Huynh lost a close match No. 3 in three sets by scores of 7-6 (9-7), 2-6, 10-4, while Sivakumar lost 6-2, 6-2 at No. 4. At doubles, PHS won two of three matches. Paige Chin and Thomasson won 6-2, 6-0 at No. 2, while Layla Reed-Miguel and Katie Pham won 6-3, 6-1 at No. 3. Chan and Silvio lost 6-0, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. pages.text: Wednesday, September 23, 2026 13 PHS cross-country team runs at De La Salle Nike Invitational By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Newhall Community Park in Concord for the 2026 De La Salle Nike Invitational on Saturday, September 19. The Highlanders’ boys’ team finished 22nd of 31 schools, while the girls were 18th of 22. “The De La Salle Nike Invitational was our third meet of the season and another opportunity to see how our runners are progressing as we start to head into the middle of the season. We are still only in September. We are continuing to train, build durability and learn how to race,” explained coach Steve Zirkelbach. “The objective isn’t to be at our best right now—it is to keep progressing so that we are running our best when the important championship meets arrive later in the season. Saturday gave us another encouraging indication that we are moving in the right direction.” Junior runner Dresden Schulte-Sasse led PHS for the third straight meet. He finished 50th of 204 athletes with a time of 17:06.9 on the three-mile course. “Dresden led Piedmont over the three-mile course, becoming our No. 3 junior performance by a Piedmont runner at Newhall Community Park. Dresden gave us another strong performance at the front of the boys’ varsity team,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Schulte-Sasse was senior Alex Schleuning placing 99th with a time of 17:45.1. Junior Luca LaForte was 140th in 18:32, Dresden Schulte-Sasse led Piedmont’s boys’ team for the third straight meet. sophomore Blake Riif was 162nd in 19:07.6, while sophomore Rohan Seshan rounded out their best five runners in 164th, clocking a 19:13.8. “Alex Schleuning was our second finisher, followed by Luca LaForte. Blake Riiff continued his strong start to the season, and Rohan Seshan completed our scoring five. Our collective time of 91:45.4 was the No. 2 Piedmont varsity boys’ team performance at Newhall Park,” Zirkelbach said. The girls continue to run without marquee runners Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, and Kelsey Coleman. Junior runner Viviane Oesterer led the girls’ side, finishing 76th of 167 with a time of 21:13.7. “The front of our girls’ varsity group ran particularly well. Viviane Oesterer led Piedmont with a very good time for the three-mile course. She improved her previous Newhall Park best by approximately eight seconds and moved to No. 4 on Piedmont’s junior list at the event,” Zirkelbach said. Senior Cora Brozowski Schrader was next in for the Highlanders, placing 82nd, clocking a 21:24.1. Girls’ tennis team bashes Berkeley 6-1 in league opener By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team got its Western Alameda County Conference schedule started in a big way, dominating rival Berkeley 6-1 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Wednesday, September 16. PHS fell 4-3 to North Coast Section competitor Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco the previous day, September 15. Wednesday’s win over the Yellowjackets was a good display by the No. 1 doubles duo of Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio, claiming the school’s first win of the day in a 6-4, 6-0 victory. Chan is in her third varsity year and second straight year as the team’s No. 1 doubles starter after appearing alongside Samantha Huynh last season. “Because Chiara and I are really good friends, it’s easy have a connection on the court and coordinate our shots. I don’t need to tell her where to go, she’ll already be there. Obviously, like any new partner, it takes some adjusting to. At this point of the season, we’re getting more comfortable and coordinated,” Chan said. “We played a lot together growing up and we have good chemistry. I don’t have to worry about what she’s going to do next,” Silvio said. Silvio did well at the net against Berkeley, converting many smashes and volleys for points. “It’s been really nice because I can rely on Emma to be really aggressive. I think my net-play has gotten a lot better, I’ve gotten more comfortable and confident there,” Silvio said. “Her net play is great,” said Chan. “When Chiara gets her racket on the ball at the net, it’s really effective,”. The Berkeley win was an impressive display by freshman Maddy Huynh, moving up to the No. 2 singles spot with usual starter Faith Chin out. Huynh dominated in a clean sweep, 6-0, 6-0. “With Faith out we moved up Maddy. She has been really good and we have a lot of belief in her. She’s already a great player and is going to get even better,” said coach Jim Landes. 6-1 win over Berkeley Winning the first match of the day was the No. 1 doubles duo of Chan and Silvio. Leela Sivakumar quickly followed with a 6-0, 6-1 win at the No. 3 singles spot, while Ella Ruthven at the No. 1 singles spot won 6-1, 6-3 to five Piedmont its third win. Maddy Huynh clinched the day at No. 2 singles in her shutout victory, giving PHS its fourth Maddy Huynh, a freshman, moved up to No. 2 singles against Berkeley, winning in a 6-0, 6-0 clean sweep. win. After that, Berkeley got its only win of the day at No. 4 singles, where Ella Sharafi lost 6-4, 7-6 (7-5). Finishing the day was Ella Thomasson and Paige Chin winning 6-1, 6-4 at No. 2 doubles, while Penelope Welch and Mai Pham won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 3 doubles. 4-3 loss to Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont won one of four matches at singles with Faith Chin winning a barn burner in three sets at the No. 2 spot by scores of 6-3, 3-6, 10-8. Ella Ruthven lost 6-3, 6-0 at No. 1, Huynh lost a close match No. 3 in three sets by scores of 7-6 (9-7), 2-6, 10-4, while Sivakumar lost 6-2, 6-2 at No. 4. At doubles, PHS won two of three matches. Paige Chin and Thomasson won 6-2, 6-0 at No. 2, while Layla Reed-Miguel and Katie Pham won 6-3, 6-1 at No. 3. Chan and Silvio lost 6-0, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team took a one-sided 40-14 loss to Aragon for Homecoming Night on Friday, September 18 at Witter Field. The result brings their record to 1-3. The Highlanders were dealing with several important injuries to starters going into the game. They were without running back Rehan Mumtaz, receiver and safety Diego Hurwitz, linebacker Max Fujimoto, cornerback Owen Curran, and starting linebacker and receiver Mason Gray left the game with an injury. “We had a lot of people out, but the effort was there. Our numbers are low and we have to get some bodies back. You see how it played out; those are all great players for us and heavy contributing starters. I was just hoping to get through this game healthy, but that’s football,” coach Jordan Seiden said. PHS’ young roster faced growing pains, including sophomore quarterback Cyrus Emanuelson tossing some interceptions. He was able to respond well in the game’s final drive, leading the Highlanders to a touchdown. “One thing about Cyrus that I love is he is unflappable. He shakes things off and is on to the next play. Being a young quarterback, he could’ve easily gone into a hole and tanked, but not Cyrus. He has a huge heart and loves the game, he’s just going to continue to grow. My message to Mateo Long scoring a touchdown for Piedmont. George Saunders reaches for a ball against Aragon. He scored Piedmont’s final touchdown. Staff photos Piedmont suffered a rough 40-14 loss to the Aragon with a bulk of its starters missing due to injuries. him is to just keep growing and keep getting better. That’s the same with the rest of the team,” Seiden said. Game Recap After a scoreless first quarter, Aragon scored on a 12-play, 71-yard series. They converted a 4th-and-goal from the four to make it 6-0 with 11:10 left in the second quarter following a missed extra point. Piedmont scored on its ensuing possession with an eight-play, 72 yard drive. It featured 37-yard pass from Cyrus Emanuelson to Gray on 3rd-and-10 from their own 45. After that, Colby Hong ran the ball 18 yards, while Emanuelson threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Mateo Long with 8:15 on the clock. A missed two-point conversion kept it deadlocked at 6-6. PHS had good field position after Henry Brennan recovered a fumble at Aragon’s 45, but Piedmont turned over on downs after gaining just four yards. From there, AHS blew the game open with 34 unanswered points. They scored twice more in the second quarter to lead 20-6 at the half, and extended to 40-6 with an interception return for a touchdown with 2:37 left in the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s final touchdown came with 1:12 remaining in the game. Starting at their own 42, the drive started with a 33 yard pass to George Saunders. On 2nd-and-10, Saunders took a 17-yard reception to the eight, and then connected with Emanuelson again for an eight-yard touchdown catch. Hong ran the ball in for a successful two-point conversion for a final score of 40-14. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-3 overall) visits Moreau Catholic in Hayward on Friday, September 25 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team came away with a one-sided 46-0 shutout of San Lorenzo on Thursday, September 17 at Witter Field. The result marked its third win in four games, bringing their record to 5-5 and 3-1 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. “The offense is coming along and the defense is improving every game. I think tonight was a good correction from our last loss, and the girls never wanted to leave the field,” said coach Beth Black. It was a strong game allaround for the Highlanders, logging six interceptions on the night by Sydney Latvala, Cory Minor, Maddie Lee, Skye Prata Baack, and two by Bea Nackley. “We’re forcing turnovers and we showed we’re hungry for the ball,” Black said. Prata Baack had a productive game with a touchdown reception and a one-point conversion on five receptions. She broke catches of 21-, 29-, 15-, and 12-yards. “It’s my first year playing, so it was hard to adjust in the beginning. Now, as a team, we’ve had so much time together and we’re feeling that connection. We’re able to execute, the energy was really good tonight. Getting to know each other and learn our styles of play is really helping,” Prata Baack said. Game Recap Piedmont’s Sydney Latvala recorded an interception on the second play of the game. Prata Baack then took a 21-yard reception to the Grizzlies’ five, but SLZ was able to nab an interception of its own. After forcing a punt, PHS got its first score of the game with 47 seconds left in the first quarter with an eight-play, 66-yard drive. It capped off with a nine-yard touchdown pass from Edie Elmquist to Cea’naiya Alexander on a corner route, making it 7-0 after a successful one-point conversion on a pass to Agatha Filha Gama. Bea Nackley grabbed an interception on San Lorenzo’s next drive, returning it to the one 18 seconds into the second quarter. On second down, Elmquist took a keeper up the middle for the touchdown with 10:26 left, making it 13-0 after an unsuccessful conversion. PHS’ defense forced a threeand-out, leading to six-play, 45 yard drive that resulted in a 19-yard touchdown run by Mafi, who also converted the one-point try on a run to make it 20-0 with 4:07 left in the half. Another three-and-out gave Piedmont a short field at the SLZ 31 with 1:46 remaining. After a 16-yard run by Elmquist, she hit Prata Baack for a 15-yard touchdown pass with 1:08 left. Elmquist converted the one-point try to make it 27-0. Staff Photos Skye Prata Baack celebrates a touchdown reception against San Lorenzo. Bea Nackley made two interceptions against San Lorenzo. Nea Mafi runs in a touchdown against the Grizzlies.

articles.text: Los Tranquilos Nipomo-based band Los Tranquilos perform at Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) this Friday. The free concert is part of the museum’s Friday Nights series. OMCA hosts free community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout the year, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. The band Los Tranquilos features brother duo Manny and JJ Martinez, as well as longtime friend Cameron Porter. Established in the summer of 2022, Los Tranquilos create both universal and historical tracks with sounds heavily inspired by 60s and 70s “romanticas” soul, psychedelia from Mexico and Latin America. The event continues in the museum’s amphitheater with Caja Mágica’s all-vinyl DJ set, featuring a vibrant selection of Latin American records from the ’60s and ’70s across a range of genres. Visitors can also connect with Bike East Bay in the museum garden to learn more about the organization’s efforts to create safer, more accessible streets throughout the East Bay. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Visit https://museumca.org/ to learn more. ®

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2026-27 season with Legally Blonde The Musical, based on the popular 2001 film, running now through October 11. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods, a sorority president who enrolls at Harvard Law School after being dumped by her boyfriend and ultimately proves herself while working on a case. No’eau Kahalekulu directs the production, with choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes and music direction by Camden Daly. The production features a 25-person company of Bay Area performers. “If you loved this movie in 2001, I promise it’s even more fun with a live band and an audience. The show moves at a whip fast pace and is full of laughs and seriously impressive dance and vocals,” said Kimberly Dooley, Artistic Director of Berkeley Playhouse. “Legally Blonde defies stereotypes and celebrates female teamwork, empowerment and above all else ... authenticity.” Kahalekulu said the character of Elle Woods has remained a favorite since the film’s release. “Elle Woods has been my comfort character since 2001. If she can get into Harvard and keep her sparkle, the rest of us can handle whatever’s in front of us,” said director No’eau Kahalekulu. “We’ve all gotten a little scared to be big and silly and sincere in public lately. This production is an invitation back into it. Like the show says, being true to yourself never goes out of style.” Scenic design is by Sarah Phykitt, with costumes by Ashley Renee and lighting by Sophia Craven. The musical is based on the novel Legally Blonde by Amanda Brown and the 2001 film of the same name. The cast also includes two dogs: Latke the Pomeranian, making a theatrical debut as Bruiser Woods, and Stella, a three-yearold French bulldog mix, as Rufus. Tickets are available through Berkeley Playhouse online at https://berkeleyplayhouse.org/. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods.
