articles.text: Photo courtesy of American Conservatory Theater The cast includes Danny Collins as Thornhill. American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) opens its 2026-27 season with a theatrical adaptation of Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest, showing onstage now through October 18. The production is adapted and directed by Emma Rice. Rice previously directed A.C.T.’s Brief Encounter and Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s The Wild Bride. Rice’s production uses seven performers, live music, movement and theatrical effects to tell the story of Roger Thornhill, an advertising executive who is mistaken for a Cold War spy and forced to flee across the country. The production features a 1950s-inspired soundtrack and a theatrical recreation of the film’s famous Mount Rushmore sequence. The cast includes Danny Collins as Thornhill, Evangeline Dickson as Mrs. Townsend and understudy, Patrycja Kujawska as Eve Kendall and others, Simon Oskarsson as Valerian and others, Katy Owen as the Professor and others, Bryony Pennington as Anna and others, and Karl Queensborough as Phillip Vandamm and others. Sam Archer will take over the role of Valerian and others beginning October 10. “What makes Emma Rice’s North by Northwest so exhilarating is that it isn’t trying to recreate Hitchcock’s film frame for frame,” said Andy Chan Donald, A.C.T.’s artistic producing director and acting artistic director. “Instead, it captures the wit, suspense, and cinematic scale of the original while embracing everything that makes live theater extraordinary.” “The result is a production that honors a beloved classic while becoming something entirely its own — a thrilling reminder that the stage can be every bit as breathtaking as the silver screen,” Donald added. The original North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant and Eva Marie Saint, follows Thornhill as he is pursued across the country after being mistaken for a government agent. Directed by Hitchcock and released in 1959, the film is widely regarded as one of the director’s major works. North by Northwest will run at A.C.T.’s Toni Rembe Theater now through October 18. Post-show conversations are scheduled for September 29, October 4 and 7. Pride Night will take place October 7, with an open-captioned performance on October 10. A tasting event is scheduled for October 6, and PlayTime, an interactive theater workshop, will take place before the October 17 matinee. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: A.C.T. presents North by Northwest now through Oct. 18

articles.text: 250 Years, Indigenous Futures installation view Haines Gallery at San Francisco’s Fort Mason presents 250 Years, Indigenous Futures, a group exhibition featuring work by eight Native American artists. The exhibition features Victoria Grace Canby, Jordan Ann Craig, Sky Hopinka, Brad Kahlhamer, Terran Last Gun, Jamie Okuma, Wendy Red Star and Keith Secola. The artists work across painting, drawing, sculpture, photography and film. The works draw from a wide range of sources, including Piikani painted lodges, Northern Cheyenne beadwork, the 1969- 71 occupation of Alcatraz Island by the Indians of All Tribes, the annual Crow Fair, horror films and archival photography. Among the artists featured is Marin-based Victoria Grace Canby, whose new works on paper depict the Three Sisters — corn, beans and squash — as a model of resilience, healing and collective care. Jordan Ann Craig’s paintings combine references to Northern Cheyenne beadwork and quillwork with the work of modernist painter Agnes Martin. Sky Hopinka’s film Sunflower Siege Engine connects the occupation of Alcatraz with Cahokia Mounds in Illinois, while Brad Kahlhamer’s Pima Air + Space features birds, horses and masked figures rendered in acrylic, ink and pencil on a bedsheet. Terran Last Gun created a series of works inspired by the geometric designs of Piikani painted lodges, while Jamie Okuma’s Of Love and Sacrifice: Motherhood combines intricate Payómkawichum (Luiseño) beadwork with imagery from the 2018 horror film Suspiria. The exhibition takes its title from the writings of Standing Photo courtesy of Haines Gallery Rock Sioux historian Philip J. Deloria and his colleagues, who have argued for understanding Native peoples through “the lens of futurity.” The exhibition similarly considers Indigenous creativity and knowledge as active forces shaping contemporary life and the future. Haines Gallery, a resident of Fort Mason since 2022, is dedicated to providing a platform for emerging and internationally established artists from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, North and South America. 250 Years, Indigenous Futures is on view now through Saturday, November 7, 2026 at Haines Gallery located in Building C, on the first floor of the Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture. Admission is free. Visit https://fortmason.org/ event/haines-gallery-250-yearsindigenous-futures/2026-09-22/ to learn more.
articles.title: Haines Gallery explores Indigenous futures in new group exhibition

articles.text: The San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Orchestra jointly announced last week that they have reached a tentative agreement on a new four-year contract. The agreement, reached on September 17 after a week of negotiating by both parties, spans August 1, 2026 through July 31, 2030 and is still subject to ratification, according to the company. The orchestra strike forced the cancellation of the September 12 opening-night performance of Simon Boccanegra, as well as the annual free Opera in the Park concert scheduled for September 13. The musicians’ strike also postponed the company’s annual fundraiser to November. San Francisco Opera’s 104th season opened this Tuesday, September 22, with Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra. Thea Musgrave’s Mary, Queen of Scots opens tomorrow, Thursday, September 24, in a new co-production directed by Stewart Laing and led by debuting conductor Clelia Cafiero. “I am deeply grateful that we have reached a tentative agreement on a new contract, one that addresses important structural changes while providing a fair agreement for our Musicians,” San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock said in a press release. “We look forward to welcoming our talented company members and guest artists, as well as our cherished patrons and donors, back to the theater. Most of all, we look forward to coming together again and reconnecting through the collective beauty of the arts,” Shilvock added. For more information about San Francisco Opera’s 2026–27 season, visit www.sfopera.com.
articles.title: SF Opera and orchestra reach tentative contract agreement

articles.text: Saturday, September 26 – November 1 Oakland Art Association gallery show Oakland Art Association presents Hopes and Dreams, a curated show that encompasses everyone’s most precious and intimate desires for the future. It can be a dream vacation, a dream come true, a dream for the future of the world or just your part of it. Hope knows no bounds, hope for change, for healing, a brighter future, or for world peace. OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties whose mission is to encourage artistic endeavor in the community, support public school art education, and arrange show venues for our members’ artworks. The Opening Reception will be from 1:00 – 4:00 p.m. on Saturday, September 26, free and open to all. For more information, see www.oaklandart.org. Saturday, September 26, 6:00 p.m. Ezequiel Barrera and Carl Blake piano recital As part of his residency in the SF Bay Area, virtuoso pianist and composer Ezequiel Sebastian Barrera from Mexico City will perform a recital, assisted by local pianist Carl Blake in a performance of Barrera’s Fantasia Mexicana for one piano-four hands. Ezequiel has performed extensively to critical acclaim in diverse venues around the world including US, Canada, Mexico, Central America, Chile, and Germany. The program includes works by Beethoven, Ravel, and Villa-Lobos as well as original compositions by Barrera. A wine reception will follow the recital to which everyone is cordially invited. $25 Advance tickets are available at https:// www.ticketsignup.io/Barrera. Sunday, September 27, 7:30 p.m. Festival Opera Vocal Salon Walnut Creek’s Festival Opera Association continues its 2026 season with the first of three events in this year’s Salon Series, which will celebrate the launch of Festival Opera’s new Resident Artist Program with a concert of arias and scenes featuring the exceptional talents of our inaugural class of resident artists, followed by a wine reception where you can meet the artists. Resident artist sopranos Marielle Leiboff and Rachel Nelson, mezzo-soprano Phoebe Dinga, tenor Spencer Greene, baritone Liam Daley, and pianist Daniel Lockert will showcase arias and scenes from operas composed by Verdi, Handel, Mozart, Strauss, Massenet, Bizet, Lehar, Leoncavallo, Tesori, and Bernstein. Doors will open at 7:00 p.m. Please buy advance tickets for this show or for the series at https://tinyurl.com/FestivalSalon1. Saturday, October 3, 7:00 p.m. Mads Tolling with Kenny Washington Two-time Grammy Award-winning Danish violinist Mads Tolling returns to PCA with prolific pianist John R. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington for the fourth time the three of them will perform together. The trio will perform their own music as well as that of composers Chick Corea, Ornette Coleman, and the group Toto, along with songs from the American Songbook, including the Temptations, Carol King, and jazz greats like Thelonious Monk and George Gershwin. Advance tickets are recommended, as this show is likely to sell out, and are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/jazzviolin, and doors will open at 6:30 p.m. Friday, October 9, 6:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture A Friday night Extravaganza! Art historian Michael Stehr presents a spirited, illustrated 50-minute lecture exploring Michelangelo’s work in his hometown of Florence, Italy. At the age of 29, he would put the finishing touches on his David, likely one of the most recognizable sculptures in Western Art. As he moved through his forties, this sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance would continue to yield sculptural masterpieces and explore the art of architecture at San Lorenzo, the parish church of the Medici family. In 1534, he moved to Rome and only returned to Florence after his passing almost another thirty years later. Doors open at 5:30 p.m. Please bring $20 (cash only) per person to pay for entrance at the door.

articles.text: It’s kind of fun trying to be anonymous. Ogden Nash was convinced that it’s kind of fun to be extinct. I’m not sure that I agree with him on that one. But being anonymous is lots of fun. Especially if you are a music critic. You get to eavesdrop on conversations and ask innocent questions pretending that you don’t know very much. I had intended to write an article about being anonymous. That idea changed on Sunday afternoon during the violin recital of Marcio Candido. His violin recital in the Piedmont Center for the Arts was a one-man show devoted entirely to the unaccompanied violin sonatas of J.S. Bach. Candido is a very friendly person and possesses enthusiasm and a love for his art. He expresses these things musically and verbally. The solo sonatas of Johann Sebastian Bach are regarded as the Old Testament of violin music. They are indispensable. Candido began his program with Bach’s monumental Partita No. 2. Modern violinists approach music in general as if music is an antiseptic art. They strive for perfection. In spite of their perfection, their approach lacks the human element. Candido comes from a different school entirely. From the moment he places his bow on the strings of his violin, the music comes to life. No composer in the history of music had more rhythm than Johann Sebastian Bach. His music must dance. It doesn’t need a thump thump thump beat, but it must have a beat that conveys rhythm in a dancing way. When Marcio Candido plays Bach, it comes to life. His concept is expansive. The tone is always beautiful, and the musical lines are always clearly delineated. The tempos are relaxed, but at the same time they are intimate and rhythmic. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington for the fourth time the three of them will perform together. Art historian Michael Stehr presents a spirited, illustrated 50-minute lecture exploring Michelangelo’s work in his hometown of Florence, Italy. At the age of 29, he would put the finishing touches on his David, likely one of the most recognizable sculptures in Western Art. As he moved through his forties, this sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance would continue to yield sculptural masterpieces and explore the art of architecture at San Lorenzo, the parish church of the Medici family. In 1534, he moved to Rome and only returned to Florence after his passing almost another thirty years later. Dick Carter introduced Matthew Hawk, a new participant joining the walk that morning. Announcements done, Dick turned the reins over to Jim Kellogg, who would lead the walk. Jim started by noting that the morning would focus on old and new architecture in the Piedmont City Center. We think of the “old” city center as built from about 1900 to 1920, but many “new” additions have been made, and when done well the two blend together to add to the beauty and value of our city. The first stop was the beautiful courtyard of Piedmont Community Church, where Don Ashburn, PCC associate pastor, met the walkers and talked about the heritage of the church. PCC was formed in 1910 as the first non-denominational church west of the Mississippi. The original goal, which still applies today, was to be a church that reflected the diversity of a Piedmont that was growing and drawing people from all parts of America. Jim then talked about Albert Farr’s 1917 design, with the sanctuary and Guild Hall opening onto the courtyard, each with Spanish Mission style bell towers, the sanctuary with a copper roofed chancel dome, and the two connected by a mission style arched walkway. Additions that were not part of Farr’s original design have added a great deal to what is seen today. The first example is the second level office and administration wing above the arched walkway, designed in 2005 by Piedmont architects Bill and Vicky Kendrick in Spanish Mission style, with detailing that integrates seamlessly with the original building. The walkers took a group photo there. The group then proceeded into Route map the sanctuary, which is Farr’s original Spanish Mission style with open wood roof trusses, stucco walls and Spanish carved wood detailing. Here too, new elements add to what we see today. First is the stunning stained glass leaded window collection on the side walls, designed and built by James Hubbell in 1998 to replace the original windows that were showing their age. The Piedmont walkers take a group photo at Piedmont Community Church. large narthex Psalm 23 window is also new, redesigned in 2017 after the original stained glass began falling out of the lead frames and onto the floor. Something had to be done. The leaded glass work was done by The Hyland Studio in Santa Clara, one of the few remaining stained glass artisans in Northern California. Next is the large projecting bay at the chancel choir loft, under the chancel dome, added in 2005 as part of the Kendricks’ remodel, which also brought three new octagonal chancel windows designed by Hubbell. And last is the church’s grand organ. The church decided in 1957 that a grand organ was needed, and it was built to order by Mathias P. Moller, with pipe ranks up to 32 feet high and installed in a wood sound box behind the chancel screen. Moller immigrated to America from Denmark in 1892, and his shop built organs for the West Point and Naval Academy chapels. This just goes to show that immigrants to America can add significant value to our culture. In due course, however, all good things get old. By 2018 the console keys were sticking, the air bellows were wheezing and the pipes were leaking, and a complete restoration was required, done by Hupalo and Repasky Master Organ Builders in San Francisco. Walkers lined up to poke their heads into the wood sound box on the side of the chancel and see the inner workings of a grand organ. The group was then off down Highland Avenue, pausing at 1900 Oakland Avenue, the Rackcliffe-Coffin House, built in 1899. articles.text: On Monday, September 14, the First Mondays Reading Group met inside the Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. This was actually the second Monday of the month, as the Labor Day holiday had pushed their meeting back a week. The group received an excellent turnout of 24 participants to discuss their August book, Horse, by Geraldine Brooks. Horse is a 2022 historical fiction novel by Australian author Geraldine Brooks. She interlinks three periods with the thoroughbred racehorse Lexington and the enslaved person who groomed him in the 1850s. This is a story of slavery and social justice through the lens of art related to the horse’s celebrated life. The novel takes place in three periods: 1850s pre-Civil War Kentucky, 1950s New York, and 2019 through a painting discovered by Theo, a Nigerian-born Georgetown University graduate student. Brooks blends real history with her fictional story of an enslaved groom named Jarret who nurtured an extraordinarily strong connection with Lexington. This legendary horse won seven of its eight races, was the fastest horse for twenty years, and produced hundreds of race-winning offspring. The painting is rooted in real artwork produced by artists of the time, like itinerant painter Thomas J. Scott. Upon Lexington’s death, the horse’s skeletal remains were rearticulated, displayed for some time by the Smithsonian Museum, stored away for decades, and then rediscovered. Lexington’s importance to racing and breeding was largely forgotten until the 1970s. The novel brings together many different topics: slavery and freedom, the hidden brutality behind the sport of horse racing, the constant pull of greed, the development of the genre of equine art, New York City art galleries, interracial romance, and contemporary police brutality against people of color. Horse was well received by critics and also the reading group. It was noted that Brooks was initially a reporter, and the deep research she did to present Lexington’s history and also the novel’s human characters, with some license taken in historical accuracy, was appreciated. Readers appreciated that the author resurrected a largely lost past. The group valued how Brooks wove the different characters and time periods together to present her social justice message. Readers liked how she blended the actual histories of the book’s characters with her fictionalized enhancements. Readers agreed that the histories of the horse and characters were better than the fictional elements. It was expressed that Brooks seemed to add a romantic component to satisfy her readers. It was noted that the love story might make the book more sellable as a movie where the characters Jarret and Lexington might be more fully developed. Jarret’s powerful commitment to the horse was also noted. He preferred to remain enslaved rather than lose his connection to the horse. Many readers would have preferred Brooks stay with Lexington and the horse’s real history. In fact, one reader only read the chapters dealing with Lexington and Jarret and skipped those dealing with the story’s romantic relationship. It was said that a good writer makes the reader care about a book’s characters, and this might have been a criticism of the book. One topic of discussion was Brooks’ use of the common, contemporary writing technique of jumping back and forth between multiple time periods. While some readers had an issue with it, most readers generally thought Brooks did it well and filled in gaps that increased their understanding of her narrative. Some readers didn’t realize how racist and brutal horse racHorse by Geraldine Brooks ing was during this period, but they did recognize that some elements of it remain today. Brooks brought the racism of today front and center with a shocking murder that connected the fear and discrimination that Jarret and Theo shared over the generations. The murder brought Lexington’s story home to our times. Readers generally liked Horse, but a reader of Brooks’ other works felt it might not be her best book. However, the group agreed they learned a lot from the book and that Horse had provided for a good discussion. That also made it a good book for the First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected Freezing Order by Bill Browder for October, and The Correspondent by Virginia Evans for their November read. After Dick Carter presented three fiction candidates, the readers selected All Creatures Great and Small by James Herriot for their December book. With all their business done, they took a group photo in the circle outside the Community Hall. The readers will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on October 5 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. Among those participating were Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Marj Blackwell, Peggy Shultz, Judy Love, Susie Backer, Rob White, Kristin Howard, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Adrienne Hamlin, Bella Almanzan, Orrel Lanter, Darby Gragg, Melba Yee, Sandy Threlfall, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mary Carter, discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus, Claudia Cate, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Mary Holt and Russell Van Herik, who were there for the first time.

articles.text: On July 25, Beach Play Field in Piedmont was filled with colorful team banners, soccer balls, laughter and plenty of cheering as children and families came together for a special CoachArt Field Day. The event brought together patients from Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland and their siblings for a morning of adapted sports, games and community. Led by CoachArt volunteers and Piedmont teens, and supported by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Field Day gave children an opportunity to play, connect and simply enjoy being kids. CoachArt provides free adaptive lessons in arts, athletics and STEM for children affected by serious illness. Volunteer mentors create safe, encouraging experiences tailored to each child’s needs. For families navigating serious illness, those experiences can help restore moments of childhood that might otherwise be lost. George Saunders, a longtime CoachArt volunteer and Piedmont High School junior, proposed the idea for a Piedmont Field Day and, along with CoachArt National Program Director Erick Rodriguez, brought the event together from the ground up. George and fellow students from Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School, Jonah Cha Foster, Joaquin Fierro, Emmy Hong and Jane Saunders, volunteered their time at the July event, helping organize activities, work with the teams and make the morning welcoming for every participant. The Piedmont Recreation Department was instrumental in making the Field Day possible. Liam Kelly, Recreation Supervisor, helped coordinate the event, provided props and materials for the activities, and issued a permit allowing CoachArt to use Beach Play Field. Participants were given CoachArt T-shirts and divided into teams, each assigned its own color. Before the athletic activities began, children and volunteers worked together to create colorful banners representing their teams. Over snacks and conversation, the teams got to know one another, creating connections before heading out onto the field. When it was time to play, teams rotated through a series of adapted activities, including soccer, Wiffle ball and relay races. Volunteer coaches and student volunteers helped participants take part at their own pace, creating an atmosphere where everyone could contribute and have fun. One CoachArt parent commented, “My family has been wearing their CoachArt T-shirts proudly and has been sharing about the program with family and friends. My daughter feels super supported by the experience.” For the Piedmont students who volunteered, the day offered a chance to give back to their community while helping create an enjoyable experience for participants and their families. Saunders commented, “I am so happy that this idea came to life. It was fun and meaningful to see the Piedmont and CoachArt communities come together for a great day!” The morning wrapped up with more time for the children and volunteers to spend together, along with raffle prizes for participants. CoachArt’s Executive Director, Molly Dirr, said, “The CoachArt families had a great time and enthusiastically shared that they would love to do it again!” Saunders hopes to make the Field Day an annual end-of-summer event in Piedmont and plans to roll out similar field day events in other CoachArt communities throughout the United States. George Saunders, Jonah Cha Foster, Joaquin Fierro, Emmy Hong and Jane Saunders along with CoachArt volunteers and patients from Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland and their families gather for a field day at Beach Play Field. The event brought together patients from Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland and their siblings for a morning of adapted sports, games and community. Led by CoachArt volunteers and Piedmont teens, and supported by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Field Day gave children an opportunity to play, connect and simply enjoy being kids. CoachArt provides free adaptive lessons in arts, athletics and STEM for children affected by serious illness. Volunteer mentors create safe, encouraging experiences tailored to each child’s needs. For families navigating serious illness, those experiences can help restore moments of childhood that might otherwise be lost. George Saunders, a longtime CoachArt volunteer and Piedmont High School junior, proposed the idea for a Piedmont Field Day and, along with CoachArt National Program Director Erick Rodriguez, brought the event together from the ground up. George and fellow students from Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School, Jonah Cha Foster, Joaquin Fierro, Emmy Hong and Jane Saunders, volunteered their time at the July event, helping organize activities, work with the teams and make the morning welcoming for every participant. The Piedmont Recreation Department was instrumental in making the Field Day possible. Liam Kelly, Recreation Supervisor, helped coordinate the event, provided props and materials for the activities, and issued a permit allowing CoachArt to use Beach Play Field. Participants were given CoachArt T-shirts and divided into teams, each assigned its own color. Before the athletic activities began, children and volunteers worked together to create colorful banners representing their teams. Over snacks and conversation, the teams got to know one another, creating connections before heading out onto the field. When it was time to play, teams rotated through a series of adapted activities, including soccer, Wiffle ball and relay races. Volunteer coaches and student volunteers helped participants take part at their own pace, creating an atmosphere where everyone could contribute and have fun. One CoachArt parent commented, “My family has been wearing their CoachArt T-shirts proudly and has been sharing about the program with family and friends. My daughter feels super supported by the experience.” For the Piedmont students who volunteered, the day offered a chance to give back to their community while helping create an enjoyable experience for participants and their families. Saunders commented, “I am so happy that this idea came to life. It was fun and meaningful to see the Piedmont and CoachArt communities come together for a great day!” The morning wrapped up with more time for the children and volunteers to spend together, along with raffle prizes for participants. CoachArt’s Executive Director, Molly Dirr, said, “The CoachArt families had a great time and enthusiastically shared that they would love to do it again!” Saunders hopes to make the Field Day an annual end-of-summer event in Piedmont and plans to roll out similar field day events in other CoachArt communities throughout the United States. George Saunders, Jonah Cha Foster, Joaquin Fierro, Emmy Hong and Jane Saunders along with CoachArt volunteers and patients from Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland and their families gather for a field day at Beach Play Field. articles.text: Many of my most cherished childhood memories came from Scouting. I went all the way through, earning my Arrow of Light and achieving the rank of Eagle Scout, like my dad before me. I grew up in San Diego with a core group of friends whom I met in first grade through Scouting. We camped, explored, learned new skills, and, most importantly, spent time together. Scouting gave us a chance to disconnect from school, sports, and everything else going on, and simply be kids. I’m still friends with many members of this Scouting group today—we have a group chat where we connect nearly daily, and we make a point of getting together at least once a year. Irreplaceable. pages.text: Wednesday, September 23, 2026 23 Adventures in Scouting Why Scouting Matters By Brad Cardon Many of my most cherished childhood memories came from Scouting. I went all the way through, earning my Arrow of Light and achieving the rank of Eagle Scout, like my dad before me. I grew up in San Diego with a core group of friends whom I met in first grade through Scouting. We camped, explored, learned new skills, and, most importantly, spent time together. Scouting gave us a chance to disconnect from school, sports, and everything else going on, and simply be kids. I’m still friends with many members of this Scouting group today—we have a group chat where we connect nearly daily, and we make a point of getting together at least once a year. Irreplaceable. I wanted that same experience for my two boys, now in fifth and second grade. I’m thrilled that they love Cub Scouts. It gives them a chance to get outside, put their feet in the dirt, play with sticks, sleep in a tent, and discover that having fun doesn’t require a screen. My second grader’s favorite experience is camping at Rock City on Mount Diablo. I barely saw him as he was having so much fun with his friends. My fifth grader also loves camping, but his favorite tradition is the Pinewood Derby. We’ve worked together on his car every year in our garage—it’s great father-son time. We’re a big sports family. Between soccer play dates, basketball practices, flag football games, and regular season and travel ball schedules, our calLandry (right) with friends in Muir Woods Landry Cardon at his first Webeloree, Bort Meadow Landry Cardon at the Piedmont Council Pinewood Derby Landry with his dad, Brad, at the Kirby Cove Cub Scout overnighter The Cub Scout Den at the Piedmont Fire Department Cub Scouts hike in Reinhardt Redwood Regional Park Beau Cardon and a friend at the Piedmont Council Pinewood Derby Brad & Marissa Cardon with their boys Landry and Beau hiking in Austria endar gets busy. But I believe kids can—and should—do both. Scouting doesn’t have to compete with sports—it complements it. Scouting isn’t competitive, which is a nice change for kids. Cub Scouts gives kids a place to try something new without worrying about whether they’ll be good at it or even do it correctly. The Cub Scout motto is “Do Your Best,” which says a lot about what Scouting is all about. As a parent and volunteer, I love what Scouting teaches: leadership, citizenship, service, helping others, and appreciation for nature. Yet I also love seeing kids smile and helping them create experiences that they’ll carry with them. I’m especially grateful for the parents who lead our pack. They are creative, dedicated, and committed to making every meeting and event fun. Scouting has a way of bringing out the best in people. For our family, Cub Scouts is one of the few places where the goal is simply to be together, get outside, and have a good time. You don’t have to do everything. You just have to show up, bring a good attitude, and do your best. And sometimes, that’s more than enough. Landry & Beau Cardon at Crater Lake, Oregon

articles.text: A family orders from the Gyro food truck. Families lay out blankets on the park’s lawn after receiving their food from the trucks. Hundreds of Piedmonters flocked to Piedmont Park on Friday, September 18, to enjoy the third Food Truck Friday. From 5 to 8 p.m., residents lined up to try savory foods and listen to music with their friends and family. The event preceded Piedmont High School’s Homecoming, allowing families to grab dinner before heading to the football game. Five food trucks were available on Highland Avenue for attendees to choose from. They included Golden Gate Gyro, Sausage King, El Gran Taco Loco, Crazy Empanadas Truck, and Pineapple Whips. These trucks provided a wide selection of sweet and savory foods, like pineapple drinks, hot dogs, empanadas, burritos, and gyros. From this reporter’s view, the most popular trucks were El Gran Taco Loco and Golden Gate Gyro, with lines extending deep onto the lawn. Piedmonters laid out their blankets for a picnic on the park’s grass after getting their food. Kids ran around the lawn and played at the tot lot nearby. The event gave many the chance to step back and have a nice evening catching up with friends The reporter’s meal of a regular burrito and horchata drink from El Gran Taco Loco. A man surveys the menu from the Sausage King food truck. and family. This reporter sampled the regular burrito and horchata from El Gran Taco Loco. The truck offers three meats for your burritos or tacos: chicken, beef, and pork. I decided to choose the chicken. The burrito came with beans, chicken, rice, and pico de gallo, and two spicy salsas on the side. The burrito was well cooked, and the chicken had that perfect grilled taste. The salsas were the perfect amount of spice to balance out the sweet horchata drink. Overall, I give the meal four out of five stars. The Rec Department will host a movie in the park on September 25, Elio, an animated kids’ movie that follows a young boy’s journey through space with different aliens. The next Food Truck Friday will be on October 16. Families wait in long lines to order their food.

articles.text: Editor, I write to enthusiastically express my support for Nancy Beninati, Tom Ramsey, and Bill Reichle for Piedmont City Council. All three of these candidates are proven leaders in our community. Nancy and I worked closely together as volunteers with the League of Women Voters of Piedmont where she served as President. Her leadership, collaborative spirit, and support of our community are unwavering, not just with the League, but also through serving on multiple Piedmont Commissions. Her professional background as a supervising attorney at the California DOJ and lecturer at UC Berkeley make her exceedingly qualified and ready to work on the issues most important to Piedmont residents. Tom and I have served on the City Council together since December of 2024. He always puts the residents of Piedmont first and has a positive, solution-oriented outlook. He is the epitome of a good public servant and good steward for our city’s funds. Bill is also a longstanding volunteer in Piedmont, supporting our schools that are a cornerstone in our community. His experience as Assistant Vice Chancellor at UC Berkeley makes him highly qualified to make the decisions required of Councilmembers in a way that best serves Piedmont. I urge my fellow Piedmont voters to cast their votes for Nancy, Tom, and Bill for Piedmont City Council. – Lorrel Plimier

articles.text: Editor, I am pleased to endorse Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council. Nancy brings the kind of experience and perspective that would strengthen our City Council. Her public service at the California Department of Justice, combined with her work as a UC Berkeley lecturer in law and public policy, Nancy understands government, policy, and the importance of thoughtful decision-making. Just as importantly, Nancy has been actively involved in the Piedmont community for decades. She has served on the Civil Service Commission, as President of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, and currently as a Recreation Commissioner. She has also volunteered in our schools and youth sports as her high school boys have grown up in Piedmont. Nancy understands what makes Piedmont such a wonderful place to raise a family, and she cares about preserving that sense of community. I look forward to working with Nancy on the City Council. She will bring a thoughtful, collaborative approach, listen to different perspectives, and work with her colleagues to find common ground and get things done for Piedmont. I strongly encourage Piedmont voters to join me in electing Nancy Beninati to the City Council. – Conna McCarthy Vice-Mayor, City of Piedmont

Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) I believe Piedmont’s top infrastructure needs are reflected in the City’s most recent budget: maintaining and improving our streets and sidewalks, upgrading our stormwater and sewer systems, and maintaining and modernizing our public facilities, including parks and recreational facilities. I support the City’s focus on these areas, while also considering public safety, emergency preparedness, and sustainability throughout these projects. I care about the Piedmont community, and with aging infrastructure and ongoing maintenance needs, we have a responsibility to take care of what we have while planning thoughtfully for the future. Places like our Community Hall, pool, parks, and other City facilities are part of what makes Piedmont special. They are where friends and families gather, make memories, and build community, and they should remain vibrant and welcoming. If elected, I would listen to residents, review the City’s capital improvement plans and financial projections, and work with City staff and fellow councilmembers to determine which projects should receive attention first. I would consider condition, public safety, urgency, community impact, available funding, and long-term financial consequences. I want to help take care of the Piedmont we have today while making thoughtful choices about the Piedmont we leave for the next generation. Sunny Bostrom-Flemming In my opinion, the most important infrastructure issues are the ones directly related to safety. At least twice a week, I ride my bike down Oakland Ave on the way to Trader Joe’s, having to dodge cracks in the pavement and potholes big enough to drown a baby chihuahua. Like the city of Alameda, I also recommend a citywide speed limit of 25 miles per hour, and less where posted. The issue of the state mandate requiring 587 new housing units in Piedmont is going to require all of our best effort to provide infrastructure for police, fire, and schools. If the same housing mandate rule applied in Oakland, where they have a current population of 440,000, they will have 80,000 people added that will need housing, education, police, fire, and infrastructure. Any city with this type of situation would have tremendous infrastructure challenges, but I am confident that Piedmont, with its population of men, women, and children of good will and hard work, can meet this challenge. Other stops included 19 Hardwick Avenue, built in 1911, an American Foursquare with two high pitched gable roofs on each side of the front door; 505 Blair Avenue, built in 1940, a perfect example of Monterey style; 110 Monte Avenue, the Hunt House, built in 1907; and, on Park Way, the best Berkeley Arts and Crafts home in Piedmont at 506, built in 1905, facing the 1915 Prairie School house at 503. The next stop was Waldo Avenue, which Jim described as the end of an era for the Piedmont City Center. In its early days Piedmont was thought of as “Queen of the Hills,” with somewhat densely packed elite homes surrounded by pastoral farmland and panoramic vistas. The Waldo property, from Park Way to Blair and from Vernal Avenue (Highland Avenue today) to the backyards of the houses on Bonita Avenue, was part of farmland owned by Walter Blair, and the only parcel of pastureland west of Vernal. Blair’s daughter Florence Blair inherited the property and continued to use it as pastureland until she died in 1925. That was the end of the old pastoral landscape attached to Piedmont’s city center. The parcel was developed as a new neighborhood, Waldo Avenue, and all of the homes were built within a two year period by 1928. The plan made use of consistent front yard setbacks and two story massing that melded varying colors and styles into a very popular neighborhood, one that integrates well into today’s Piedmont City Center. The group continued south on Bonita Avenue past several other notable old homes, then past Havens School, built in 2010 and designed by Piedmont architect Mark Becker in traditional Spanish Mission Revival style. The walk concluded at the observation deck at the north end of the Piedmont Community Swimming Pool, which is available for use by everyone. The group used it as a chance for a brief rest and to admire the spectacular view, greatly appreciated by all. Walking on Wednesdays meets every week at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia Avenues). The program is free and open to all, and new walkers—along with their K-9 best friends—are always welcome. Registration is required. articles.text: Piedmont Police Officer Tyler Petit will have his final shift with the Piedmont Police Department (PPD) today, September 30, as he prepares to transfer to the Brentwood Police Department. Petit has worked for more than eight years keeping the city safe. He served as a department ambassador through many outreach programs, served as a representative on the Police & Fire Pension board, and was Vice President/ Treasurer of the Piedmont Police Officers Association. Petit is leaving Piedmont to serve and protect the community Officer Tyler Petit at the 2023 Coffee Cops and Car Show. Staff Photo

articles.text: Hundreds of Piedmont residents came out this past Sunday, September 27, to enjoy the city’s 28th annual Harvest Festival, with food trucks, farmers’ markets, live music, games, and fun competitions. A crowd favorite was the Watermelon Eating Contest, which drew participants from all age groups. Crowds gathered around to watch kids as young as one and adults eat watermelon as fast as possible. articles.text: Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions. For this year’s race, the Post will send one question every week to the candidates running for City Council until election day. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on Tuesday, September 22, and were asked to reply in 200 words. Week 5 question: Piedmont’s state-approved Housing Element commits the city to plan for 587 new homes by 2031, 257 of them affordable to lower-income households. The largest single project is in Moraga Canyon, where the city is now choosing a developer to build at least 132 units, including at least 60 affordable units, on city-owned land. The next council is expected to approve that developer agreement. What would you need to see in it before voting yes? Tom Ramsey Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com) Before voting “yes” on the developer agreement, I would need to see a clear commitment to the vision our community developed through numerous public workshops, commission reviews, and formal hearings. The Request for Qualifications (RFQ) sets the criteria for selecting a development partner. The chosen developer must demonstrate experience, financial capacity, and the ability to deliver a quality project consistent with the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan (MCSP), including mixed-income housing, infrastructure, and community amenities. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department hosted its eighth annual Car Show on Saturday, September 26, out front of the police station and also along Moraga and Highland Avenues. Event organizer and co-founder Officer Tyler Petit shepherded his last big community outreach event in his Piedmont Police blues, as he will turn in his uniform on Wednesday, September 30. For Petit, this event marked a victory lap; the event he spearheaded along with Sergeant Steve Dewarns in 2018 has quickly turned into a must attend event for local car enthusiasts. The coffee was hot and delicious, getting patrons’ engines revving in the 7 a.m. hour while the chrome was still heating up. Seemingly the entire police force was on hand, with uniformed officers on the street shaking hands and answering questions along with officers in street clothes there to support the community event whether on the clock or not. Staff Photos Hoods were popped and the chrome was polished for the 2026 Coffee, Cops and Cars show on the morning of Saturday, September 26.
articles.title: Coffee, Cops and Cars drives community forward

articles.text: Editor, I’m writing in support of Measure GG. Raising the city’s transfer tax to be more in line with our neighboring cities of Oakland and Berkeley is a reasonable way to raise the funds necessary to fund city services and projects. As a long-serving member and current Chair of the Parks Commission, I successfully advocated for the City of Piedmont to complete a parks master plan. The plan’s conclusions are pretty clear: we’re loving our parks too much, and there is a real need for infrastructure replacements, improvements, and ongoing maintenance to keep our parks welcoming, functional, and sustainable. Park pathways and irrigation systems, in some cases decades old, need priority replacement. Steep slopes in Piedmont and Dracena Parks need erosion mitigation. Costs for all incremental improvements, including ADA upgrades and the replacement of play structures, continue to rise. Measure GG raises badly needed funds, which can help address these needs over time without adding an annual tax burden to city residents. Please join me in supporting Measure GG. –Tom Smegal Chair, Piedmont Parks Commission 3756 Grand Ave., #203, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: (510) 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall Executive Editor: Misha Edel City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jake Lannon Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: As the City Council election approaches, Piedmont Post readers are paying close attention. In a sample of responses from Piedmont Post readers, nearly all, 31 of 33, or 94%, said they plan to vote in November, and 55% said they planned to attend or watch the League of Women Voters candidate forum on Tuesday, Sept. 29. More than 70% of respondents were over 50, a long-tenured and deeply invested local voter base. Readers were asked to pick the three most significant issues facing Piedmont. Five rose to the top: public safety, infrastructure funding, school quality, housing development and city spending. Public safety led the list, cited by 52% of respondents. Readers pointed to pedestrian hazards, traffic enforcement and police staffing. “We do not have enough police service officers. This should be a priority,” one resident wrote. Another described “so many near misses with pedestrians and drivers failing to stop.” Close behind, at 48%, was funding for infrastructure and aging facilities. Residents described potholes, drainage problems, neglected street trees and deferred maintenance across town. “The city has so much deferred maintenance, and we need a source of funding so that it can be addressed,” one resident wrote. School quality ranked third at 45%. School governance is decided in a separate election, but several readers asked council candidates to keep up the long-standing cooperation between the city and the school district on shared facilities. Housing development was named by 42% of readers, driven by state housing mandates and the proposed development in Moraga Canyon. Many were concerned about wildfire evacuation, traffic and the loss of open space in Blair Park. “The Moraga Canyon development will be one of Piedmont’s most consequential land-use decisions in decades,” one resident wrote. Others took a different view: “We need to build more housing to avoid state penalties.” City spending rounded out the top five at 33%, and another 21% chose city and school taxes. Several readers questioned the proposed increase to the real property transfer tax on the November ballot, Measure GG, and asked for more financial transparency. Another asked candidates directly, “How do you control spending while providing the high level of services Piedmont is known for?” With nearly every respondent planning to vote, City Council candidates face an attentive electorate looking for clear, fiscally responsible answers on safety, streets and housing. The Piedmont Post received 33 responses to its online questionnaire Sept. 24-28. Respondents could select up to three issues. articles.text: Editor: The best antidote to screen usage that I can think of is recreation. It is hard to be on a cell phone when you are chasing a soccer ball, blowing bubbles in the pool, or attempting to make a basket. The good news is that we live in a community that prioritizes recreation. Our Piedmont Recreation Department provides all sorts of programming for kids and adults, and helps organize amazing community events like Food Truck Fridays, Movies in the Park, and our beloved Harvest Festival. The not so good news is that we are falling behind on maintaining the very parks, fields, and facilities where these amazing recreational activities take place. Our city employees are working hard with limited funding to prioritize increasingly costly maintenance so that residents can continue to engage in the activities we all enjoy. It is estimated that local Measure GG would provide an additional $1.5 million for the City of Piedmont to help pay for essential services and facilities. Please join me in supporting what we like best about living in Piedmont, please join me in supporting Measure GG. –Chris Hart Piedmont Recreation Commissioner Past President PHS Boosters

articles.text: Piedmonters celebrate New Families Night on the Community Hall patio. New Families Night took over the Community Hall patio Friday night, kicking off a busy weekend of events in and around Piedmont Park. At 5:30 p.m., new residents came to meet other new neighbors and to mingle with school and city elected officials. Dozens of new Piedmonters showed up, affixed a name tag and took the challenge of completing a “meet your neighbors” bingo card by talking to other folks at the get together. Squares on the bingo card included: “went to PHS” and “Is still an A’s fan,” as the ice breaker activity tasked kids and adults with a fun way to meet people. City Communications Officer Echa Schneider worked the swag table giving away new Piedmont-branded apparel and fun toys to those with completed bingo cards. Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen was joined by City Council members Tom Ramsey and Jennifer Long at the event. Their presence showed new residents one of the benefits of living in a small town: accessibility to elected officials. City Council Candidate Adam Hundt was also on hand, getting to know residents and embedding himself in the culture of the city. “It was wonderful to meet families new to Piedmont,” said Hundt. “Great schools, parks and recreation, and a friendly community were mentioned as reasons for moving to Piedmont. Residents commented that given the age of Piedmont homes, replacing outdated electrical wiring with energy efficient systems is an issue that is top of mind. Just yards away, city employees were setting up a large inflatable screen for the movie in the park event. Families brought blankets and sat in front of the screen as barefoot kids ran through the grass while waiting for darkness to fall to view the Disney/Pixar film Elio. On the Piedmont Park bridge another public offering was in full swing, put on by the Scout Chelle Putzer serves lemonade and baked goods at the New Families Night on Friday, September 25. Council. Scout leaders instructed kids to use a bow to shoot padded-arrow at targets floating in mid-air. Attendees of the New Piedmont Families Night enjoyed a full gamut of entertainment options Friday night, showing the best of what Piedmont offers its residents. Movie in the Park night was just a hop, skip and a jump away from the New Families Night. Piedmont Scouts set up an archery target in the park Friday night.

articles.text: She is beauty, she is grace, she is Misha. At 15 years old, this lovely lady knows how to appreciate the finer things: a warm heating pad, a cozy lap, and eating dinner with a friend nearby. While she can be shy when meeting new people, after a few visits, your friends will be her friends, too. Give Misha a comfortable place beside you and plenty of head scratches, and she’ll settle right in. This beautiful Siamese mix loves being brushed, and will happily head-butt you to ask for more attention. She still makes time to bat at her wand toy, too. As a senior, Misha will really sparkle in the care of someone who enjoys making life extra comfortable. Arthritis, early kidney disease, constipation, hearing loss, and some cognitive changes mean her adopter will want to give her a cozy routine that helps Adopt Misha through Cat Town. her feel her best. That includes a monthly arthritis injection, supplements, and a special diet. She’s also eligible for Cat Town’s In It For Life hospice adoption program, which offers lifelong financial support for qualifying veterinary care. Easygoing and wonderfully companionable, Misha is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.

Petit has been awarded eight California Highway Patrol 10851 pins for recovering stolen cars and completed his Master’s degree in April of 2025. Petit aspires to be able to use his degree in the future to promote and get off-street detail and to utilize his customer service skills and management skills to a higher level. In the new department, Petit will have to start by working patrol in his own community, ReQuip is located at 111 Fairmount Avenue in Oakland. Photo Courtesy of PPD Piedmont Police Department officers Tyler Petit (left) and Hugo Diaz deliver Valentine’s cheer to participants in PPD’s You Are Not Alone (YANA) program. and will have to get used to new police protocols in Contra Costa County. His career in law enforcement started here in Piedmont on April 4, 2018. Petit talked about how working in Piedmont has made him a more well-rounded officer. Working for this department has given Petit the knowledge of how to take a case from beginning to end. “Working for Piedmont, I’ve been able to take my cases from step A to Z because we have the time and the training to solve them. We can all be investigators here, write our own warrants, and develop leads through our city’s awesome technology that gives us a trail to follow. This is great experience that not all patrol officers in larger agencies may receive, that’s typically done on the detective level. I’m just so thankful to have learned all I did, and for receiving all of the support from our amazing team of dedicated officers,” he said. On his final day of service, the goodbyes will be hard for everyone, citizens, Petit and his coworkers. Since he made his plans known to the department, word has spread rapidly. Petit has been stopped on the street by acquaintances and even complete strangers wanting to thank him for his service. “The love and support I’ve received from the community members and their kind words just made me feel so appreciative of working for this city. I truly know that I was supported. People liked the kind of officer I am, and that matters most to me,” Petit told the Post. articles.text: Claudia Bustos When we picture science, we often picture expertise. A lab. A credential. A specialized instrument. Someone who knows more than we do. Children absorb that image too. Long before they choose a science class or imagine a career, they are forming ideas about who does science, whose knowledge counts, and whether they can see themselves in it. But science has never been an individual pursuit. Knowledge develops through observation, testing, discussion, disagreement, collaboration, and exchange. And it is shaped by something else too: our values, our lived experiences, and our cultures. At The Lawrence Hall of Science, we call this people-powered science. Expertise takes many forms. A biologist, engineer, farmer, artist, educator, parent, or culture bearer may approach the same question differently. People living in a community may recognize change before it appears in a dataset. They see a creek drying up, a neighborhood getting hotter, or the food available nearby beginning to change. Bring those people together and even the questions can change. For children, that opens up a different relationship with STEM. Science becomes less about being the person who already knows the answer and more about noticing carefully, asking questions, sharing what you know, listening to someone who sees something differently, testing an idea, and changing your thinking. At The Lawrence, we want children to meet the people behind the science. In our lobby, they encounter Auntie Dottie, an Ohlone matriarch sharing knowledge about harvesting acorns rooted in this place across generations. In Future of Food, designer and entrepreneur Mónica Martínez introduces visitors to alternative proteins such as mealworms. These are not side stories. They show children that knowledge comes from people, communities, histories, and experience. And with great science comes great responsibility. Alongside “How does this work?” we ask: Who does this affect? Who is missing? Who gets to help decide? Perhaps that is one of the most important STEM identities we can help a child develop: not simply I can do science, but Families explore The Lawrence’s People-Powered Science lobby, where an exhibit developed with Ohlone youth shares cultural knowledge and shows how science is shaped by people, place, and community. The exhibit highlights Auntie Dottie, a matriarch of the East Bay Chochenyo-speaking Ohlone people, as a community science hero.
articles.title: Who gets to shape science?

articles.text: I have something to contribute. Their questions belong. Their experiences belong. Their curiosity belongs. Science is people powered because science is something we build together. And every child deserves to know there is a place for them in that work. At The Lawrence, we want families to experience that together: asking questions, meeting the people behind the science, and recognizing that their own voices belong in the conversation too. We look forward to welcoming you. The Lawrence Hall of Science is UC Berkeley’s public science center, connecting research, education, and public engagement to help people understand and shape the world around them. From our home in the Bay Area, our work reaches classrooms, educators, families, museums, and communities through exhibitions, programs, K–12 curriculum, professional learning, partnerships, and educational resources used across the country and around the world. articles.text: Piedmont’s Board of Education is asking residents to help with the selection of the next school superintendent. To ensure this is a collaborative and inclusive process, the Board is providing an anonymous online survey and encourages participation. The Piedmont Unified School Board is in the process of conducting a search for the District’s next Superintendent. Leadership Associates, an executive search firm, was selected to advise the Board in this important process. This is an opportunity for students, staff, parents, and community members to provide input on the qualities and priorities they would like to see in our next superintendent. The survey opened September 25 and remains available through October 7 at 4:00 p.m. The survey asks a couple of open response questions such as “What do you see as the major challenges which will confront our new superintendent?” The survey also contains ranked lists of characteristics and qualities desirable for the next superintendent.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. articles.text: Staff Photos Henry Stein scores from a 5-meter penalty shot against Encinal. The Highlanders’ boys’ water polo team got the job done against the visiting Encinal Jets at the Piedmont Pool on Thursday, September 24 in a 14-6 victory. PHS led 12-1 to start the third quarter before rotating out its usual starters, which is a testament to their quality with the Jets entering the match with an 8-1 record. “Encinal’s program is on the up and rising with really good coaching and a lot of club players. So, I’m really proud of the way we executed what we’ve been working on the last couple of weeks,” coach Rik Krumins said. Piedmont has now passed the midway point of its season, holding a 6-6 overall record with seven matches left in its regular season. It was a strong defensive display for the Highlanders on Thursday night against Encinal. It’s something coach Krumins has been looking to instill in his group this season. “We’ve been working on lane defense, counter attack, and knowing when to get to our spots. It really comes out of our defense; we had a game plan to get in the lanes, be aggressive, and be ball hawks. That’s something we’ve talked about all season long,” Krumins said. “Our defense has gotten a lot better; we were a little all over the place on defense or know when to drop. We’ve progressed a ton and have become a lot better. We still need to work on our shot blocking, but other than that, we’re going to be ready to go for WACC and NCS,” sophomore goalie Dylan Jerez mentioned. In water polo, solid defense turns into offensive output. Junior Henry Stein is at the head of that, turning counter attacks into goals. Goalie Dylan Jerez gets his arm on a ball for a save against Encinal. “It starts with the defense. We’re getting the steals, and my goal is to counter out of that and lead our offense down the pool. I’m supposed to be the first one down the pool and being like a quarterback to see what’s there,” Stein said. Match Recap It was a dominant first quarter with Piedmont leading 5-0 through the opening seven minutes. Stein opened the scoring after 52 seconds, then Jack Dahling scored two minutes later when cleaning up his own shot that rebounded off the post. After that, Stein scored after drawing a 5-meter penalty shot with 3:14 to go, and then scored again on an assist from Raffi Banin with 1:58 remaining. Graham Smith then assisted Rylan Patty with 29 seconds left. Encinal scored its first goal 40 seconds into the second quarter, but Piedmont added two more goals in the second to give themselves a 7-1 lead at halftime. They scored via Patty with 4:20 on the clock, and then Jerez hurled a long assist to Stein one minute later. PHS poured on five more unanswered goals in the third quarter to take a commanding 12-1 lead. After falling 5-2 to Marin Academy on Wednesday, September 23, the squad turned around to beat Western Alameda County Conference rivals Bishop O’Dowd 4-3 for a critical league win. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split its last pair of matches against Western Alameda County Conference competition, beating Encinal 3-0 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Tuesday, September 22 but losing 3-1 at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland the following day. The pair of results brings PHS’ record to 12-8 overall and 1-2 in league. Their overall win total officially marks the program’s most wins since 2017 when the team went 16-8 and got a No. 7 seed in the North Coast Section playoffs. It was a strong couple of matches for junior outside hitter Maika Ting who had 17 kills against Encinal and 16 kills vs. O’Dowd. 3-0 over Encinal Piedmont swept the Jets by scores of 25-21, 25-20, 25-14. Both teams traded points in the first set with six total lead changes. Encinal held a 20-19 lead, but PHS finished with the final five of seven points, including two kills by Maika Ting, an ace by Mia Bechtel, a block by Charlotte Bailey, and a set-clinching kill by Izara Dando. In the second set, PHS took a 3-2 lead and never relinquished their advantage, extending the lead to 10-2 with three kills by Ting, two aces by Bechtel, and individual kills by Dando and Bailey. Encinal cut the deficit to 19-17, but Piedmont closed out with six of the final nine points. During that stretch, Lucia Dorsey logged two kills and two blocks, while Nora Trombi and Dando also scored from spikes. After both sides traded points Staff Photos Maika Ting had 17 kills against Encinal and 16 kills vs. Bishop O’Dowd. to a 4-4 deadlock, Piedmont scored seven of eight points to take an 11-5 lead. Encinal cut it to 11-9, but PHS ran their lead up to 19-11, and closed out with six of the final nine points – once again. Final stats: Fiona Olsen had two kills. Ting had 17 kills, one block and five digs. Bailey had three kills, one block and four digs. Dando had six kills. Sofia Meyer had six kills and one block. Nora Trombi had one kill, six digs and seven assists. Olivia Stevens had three kills, one ace and 14 digs. Dorsey had six kills, two blocks and one dig. Allyson Huynh had two aces, 19 digs and six assists. Corina Vora had two aces, 14 digs and 14 assists. Hazel Schaeffer had two digs. Bechtel had three aces, three digs and eight assists. Sarina Hill had three digs and one assist. Final stats: Olsen had two kills, one block and two digs. Ting had 16 kills, one block and four digs. Bailey had four kills and two blocks. Huynh recorded two aces, 21 digs and five assists. Vora recorded 10 digs and 22 assists. Dando had three kills. Meyer recorded seven kills and six digs. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s Naiya Alexander (left) and Agatha Filha Gama (right) celebrate Nea Mafi’s (#1) touchdown. Piedmont High’s flag football team claimed a come-from-behind 18-6 win over Mt. Eden on Thursday, September 24 at Witter Field. The Highlanders scored all three of their touchdowns in the fourth quarter after trailing 6-0 in the first quarter. “There was no reason for us to be scoreless going into the fourth quarter. Our team needed some time to get it together, but we didn’t collapse, and that’s a win itself,” coach Beth Black said. Piedmont got its first touchdown on an interception returned for a touchdown by Kate Tong with 9:31 left in the fourth. Mt. Eden’s offense relied on stretch runs toward the sidelines, and running back passes from those plays. In the fourth quarter, the Highlanders adjusted, leading to the defense reading it as it happened. “I was playing outside. They were repeating the same play a lot and were sending their blockers out wide. I figured out if I step around their blockers, I could grab it. We definitely watched and learned,” Tong said of the play. Mafi scored a near 40-yard touchdown run with 4:15 left in the game, dodging multiple defenders on her way to the end zone. “We called snake and I knew I wanted the ball. I knew I had to leave the game knowing I did well on both offense and defense. I got the ball, saw my blocks, and kept running until the whistle,” Mafi said. It’s worth noting that Piedmont was credited with a controversial 25-12 loss to Mt. Eden earlier in the season on September 1, where the Monarchs’ varsity squad mistakenly played PHS’ junior varsity team. That result means Piedmont still holds a 6-7 overall and 5-3 against Western Alameda County Conference competition. PHS is disputing the result, but still hasn’t gotten a decision from league officials. “The loss is still there, there hasn’t been a ruling, and they still have that point on us. That stings a lot. I’ve written to the league and we still don’t know what the ruling will be,” Black said. Game Recap Mt. Eden scored the game’s first touchdown with 4:30 remainKate Tong breaks into the end zone after making an interception for a touchdown. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s flag football team claimed a come-from-behind 18-6 win over Mt. Eden on Thursday, September 24 at Witter Field. The Highlanders scored all three of their touchdowns in the fourth quarter after trailing 6-0 in the first quarter. “There was no reason for us to be scoreless going into the fourth quarter. Our team needed some time to get it together, but we didn’t collapse, and that’s a win itself,” coach Beth Black said. Piedmont got its first touchdown on an interception returned for a touchdown by Kate Tong with 9:31 left in the fourth. Mt. Eden’s offense relied on stretch runs toward the sidelines, and running back passes from those plays. In the fourth quarter, the Highlanders adjusted, leading to the defense reading it as it happened. “I was playing outside. They were repeating the same play a lot and were sending their blockers out wide. I figured out if I step around their blockers, I could grab it. We definitely watched and learned,” Tong said of the play. Mafi scored a near 40-yard touchdown run with 4:15 left in the game, dodging multiple defenders on her way to the end zone. “We called snake and I knew I wanted the ball. I knew I had to leave the game knowing I did well on both offense and defense. I got the ball, saw my blocks, and kept running until the whistle,” Mafi said. It’s worth noting that Piedmont was credited with a controversial 25-12 loss to Mt. Eden earlier in the season on September 1, where the Monarchs’ varsity squad mistakenly played PHS’ junior varsity team. That result means Piedmont still holds a 6-7 overall and 5-3 against Western Alameda County Conference competition. PHS is disputing the result, but still hasn’t gotten a decision from league officials. “The loss is still there, there hasn’t been a ruling, and they still have that point on us. That stings a lot. I’ve written to the league and we still don’t know what the ruling will be,” Black said. Game Recap Mt. articles.text: Diego Hurwitz had five catches for 102 yards against Moreau. Piedmont High’s football team suffered a 31-17 loss to Moreau Catholic in Hayward on Friday, September 25. The result brings the Highlanders’ record to 1-4 as they enter a bye week. Despite the loss, it was a strong offensive day for three players with more than 100 yards each as they returned from injuries. Senior running back Rehan Mumtaz logged 128 rushing yards on 18 carries, while junior running back Vaha Mafi made an outstanding season debut with 111 rushing yards and one touchdown on 10 carries. Senior receiver Diego Hurwitz had five receptions for 102 yards, and junior receiver Mason Gray had five receptions for 55 yards and a touchdown. Piedmont will return from their bye week to play their first Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division game against Arroyo on Friday, October 9. Game Recap Piedmont scored with a 24-yard field goal on its first drive of the game, a nine-play, 74-yard series. It started with a 19-yard carry by Mumtaz on a reverse, followed by a 12-yard run by Mumtaz. They converted a 3rd-and-3 with a 25-yard catch and run by Hurwitz to the 11, but PHS couldn’t convert a 3rd-and-6 at the seven, leading to a field goal by Emanuelson. PHS forced a punt on Moreau’s ensuing possession and drove 78 yards to the Mariners’ 15, but stalled out on a pass to the end zone on 4th-and-15. The home side responded with a five-play, 85-yard touchdown drive that concluded with a 44-yard catch and run up the middle to go up 7-3 midway through the second quarter, which remained the score at halftime. In the second, Piedmont got down to the Moreau 15, but couldn’t push the ball further, turning over on 4th-and-17 at the 22. They forced a punt and got to the Mariners’ 17 in the late minutes, but missed on a 34-yard field goal in the final seconds. The Mariners poured it on in the third quarter with 17 more points to take a commanding 24-3 lead into the fourth, and then scored on a touchdown series after recovering an onside kick to make it 31-3. Mafi got Piedmont back on the Staff Photos board in the fourth quarter with a 58-yard touchdown carry up the gut, where he broke two tackles before making his way down the field. Piedmont’s final touchdown came on a 10-play, 78-yard drive. It started with a 20-yard carry by Mumtaz, while Emanuelson converted a 4th-and-3 at the Moreau 40 with a five-yard scramble. On 2nd-and-6 at the Mariners’ 18, Emanuelson found Gray on a crossing route for the touchdown. Final stats: Emanuelson completed 14 of 33 passes for 195 yards and one touchdown. Mumtaz had 128 rushing yards on 18 carries. Mafi had 111 yards on 10 carries and one touchdown. Hurwitz had five receptions for 102 yards. Gray had five receptions for 55 yards and a touchdown. articles.text: The Piedmont Highlander JV football team traveled to Hayward on Friday, September 25 looking to secure its third consecutive win as it faced the Moreau Catholic Mariners. PHS got the job done, claiming a narrow 21-15 victory. Moreau Catholic opened the scoring after starting its first possession at its own 40-yard line. The Mariners moved downfield and connected on a pass over the middle for a touchdown before adding the extra point to take a 7-0 lead. However, the early score did not hurt the Highlanders’ spirits. Fierro returned the following kickoff to Piedmont’s 40-yard line, and a combination of short passes and runs moved the Highlanders into Moreau territory. Quarterback Gio López then connected with Fierro on a 30-yard pass near the goal line, but Moreau forced and recovered a fumble on the next play. Halfway through the second quarter, Diego Garcia jumped a quick out route at the 37-yard line and returned the interception for a touchdown. It marked the second consecutive game in which Piedmont opened its scoring with a pick-six. Ben Gerber added the extra point to tie the game at 7-7. Piedmont’s defense then forced a punt on fourth-and-28 after a key sack from Hildreth pushed Moreau back to its own eight-yard line. Hildreth returned the punt to the Mariners’ seven, and after Joe Logwood gained four yards, Hildreth ran in the touchdown. Piedmont converted the two-point attempt to take a 15-7 lead into halftime. Will Dietrick opened the second half with a 51-yard kickoff return to the Moreau 34. Piedmont drove to the 11-yard line before another forced fumble gave the Mariners possession. Moreau capitalized on the turnover, using a combination of short passes and runs to move downfield before a 30-yard reception set up the tying score. The Mariners then converted the two-point attempt to make it 15-15. Dietrick answered with another strong return, and Piedmont again moved into Moreau territory, but the Mariners’ defense held and forced a turnover on downs. Piedmont’s defense responded with key stops of its own, including a pass breakup from Lev Kuluva on a deep fade. Heading into the fourth quarter, Moreau had the ball near its own 40-yard line. A sack from Havea helped force fourth-and-10, where Piedmont’s defense came up with another crucial stop. Just two plays later, Dietrick broke free for a 60-yard touchdown, giving Piedmont a 21-15 lead. The extra point was unsuccessful, leaving the Highlanders’ defense with a six-point lead to protect. Moreau made one final push, driving as far as Piedmont’s 45-yard line before Gael Fierro intercepted a pass to end the threat. After Piedmont picked up the first down it needed, Hildreth took a knee to seal the Highlanders’ third consecutive victory, 21-15. Piedmont now enters a bye week before its first league game. NEXT UP The Highlanders (3-2 overall) will look to continue their threegame winning streak when they host Arroyo at Witter Field at 4:00 p.m. on Friday, October 9. one-point conversion. PHS’ defense then forced a punt on Mt. Eden’s next drive. After Edie Elmquist hit Agatha Filha Gama for a big gain to midfield, that’s when Mafi broke her 40-yard touchdown run to give her side a 12-6 lead with 4:15 remaining after another missed conversion. The Highlanders then gained possession at the Monarchs’ 16 after they turned over on downs. On 2nd-and-goal at the 10, Tong scored again with a run down the left side for Piedmont’s final touchdown.
