articles.text: San Francisco Opera is presenting Scottish composer Thea Musgrave’s Mary, Queen of Scots at the War Memorial Opera House, bringing the 1977 opera back to San Francisco in a new production by director and designer Stewart Laing. “I am thrilled to have my opera Mary, Queen of Scots return to San Francisco Opera this fall,” Musgrave said in a press release. “I have always felt it to be the cornerstone of my operatic repertoire. It is also very close to me personally as I am a woman, a Scot and lived for several years in Paris.” The production, which opened September 20, is a co-production with English National Opera. Italian conductor Clelia Cafiero is making her San Francisco Opera debut leading the San Francisco Opera Orchestra, with soprano Heidi Stober in the title role. Musgrave’s opera centers on the young queen’s struggle to maintain power in Scotland. Three men in Mary’s life, including her half-brother James Stewart, second husband Lord Darnley and future third husband the Earl of Bothwell, each seek to influence or control her reign. The opera combines scenes of political unrest and court intrigue with more intimate moments, including Mary singing a lullaby to her infant son, the future King James I. Musgrave’s opera premiered at the Edinburgh International Festival in 1977. Its U.S. premiere followed in 1978, and Musgrave herself conducted the West Coast premiere at San Francisco Opera’s Spring Opera Theater in 1979. Laing’s production, first presented by English National Opera in 2025, places the story in a contemporary setting and highlights sectarian violence in modern Scotland. D.M. Wood and Mimi Jordan Sherin are the lighting designers, and Colm Seery is the choreographer. Stober returns to the role after performing Mary at London’s Coliseum in 2025. British baritone Thomas Mole makes his American debut as James Stewart, while San Francisco Opera Adler Fellow tenor Thomas Kinch portrays Bothwell. Christopher Sokolowski makes his company debut as Lord Darnley. Baritone Hadleigh Adams portrays the musician and secretary to the queen, David Riccio; bass David Soar is Cardinal Beaton; current Adler Fellow baritone Olivier Zerouali is the Earl of Morton; tenor Chance JonasO’Toole is the Earl of Ruthven; bass-baritone Philip Skinner is Lord Gordon; and Mary’s four eponymous ladies-in-waiting are performed by Adler Fellows Sadie Cheslak (Mary Seton), Sofia Gotch (Mary Beaton), Mary Hoskins (Mary Livingston) and Alexa Frankian (Mary Fleming). Mary, Queen of Scots continues through October 4 at the War Memorial Opera House. For tickets and more information, visit sfopera.com.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera presents Mary, Queen of Scots now through Oct. 4

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will turn its rooftop sculpture garden into a Korean-pop dance party Thursday, October 15, featuring live performances. “Rooftop Radio: K-pop” will take place from 5:30 to 9 p.m. in the sculpture garden on the museum’s fifth floor. K-pop, short for Korean popular music, encompasses a range of musical styles but is known internationally for elaborate choreography and highly visual performances. The genre has become a major part of American pop culture, with groups such as BTS and BLACKPINK reaching the U.S. mainstream through chart success, sold-out concerts and appearances on American television. SFMOMA’s event will feature sets by Bay Area DJs CAZU, AyumiPlease and Peter Lo, along with performances by local K-pop cover groups Groobeu, K-Pop-Up, Homeground Dance and ECLIPSE. articles.text: Alonzo King LINES Ballet has launched its 2026-27 national tour, bringing four works by San Francisco choreographer Alonzo King to audiences across the country, with San Francisco performances scheduled in November. The tour features LEGACY, King’s recent collaboration with jazz bassist, vocalist and composer esperanza spalding; Ode to Alice Coltrane, a tribute to the composer, pianist and spiritual leader; Ma Mère l’Oye (Mother Goose), set to Maurice Ravel’s score; and Deep River, King’s collaboration with Grammy Award-winning vocalist Lisa Fischer and jazz pianist and composer Jason Moran. The company has several San Francisco performances scheduled this season, including a November 19 through 21 collaboration with the San Francisco Symphony at Davies Symphony Hall. The program will feature world premieres of two ballets choreographed by King to Claude Debussy’s Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune and Aaron Copland’s Appalachian Spring. James Gaffigan will conduct the Symphony. “For more than four decades, touring has been an essential part of the life of LINES Ballet,” King, the company’s founder and artistic director, said in a press release. “Dance is a language that transcends geography and speaks directly to our shared humanity. Every community we visit brings a different energy and perspective to the work. That exchange between artists and audiences is an essential part of why we tour.” Visit www.linesballet.org to purchase tickets. Courtesy of Alonzo King LINES Ballet The tour will showcase four signature works from Alonzo King’s repertoire.

pages.text: 16 Wednesday, September 30, 2026 Arts & Entertainment San Francisco Opera presents Mary, Queen of Scots now through Oct. 4 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Opera is presenting Scottish composer Thea Musgrave’s Mary, Queen of Scots at the War Memorial Opera House, bringing the 1977 opera back to San Francisco in a new production by director and designer Stewart Laing. “I am thrilled to have my opera Mary, Queen of Scots return to San Francisco Opera this fall,” Musgrave said in a press release. “I have always felt it to be the cornerstone of my operatic repertoire. It is also very close to me personally as I am a woman, a Scot and lived for several years in Paris.” The production, which opened September 20, is a co-production with English National Opera. Italian conductor Clelia Cafiero is making her San Francisco Opera debut leading the San Francisco Opera Orchestra, with soprano Heidi Stober in the title role. Musgrave’s opera centers on the young queen’s struggle to maintain power in Scotland. Three men in Mary’s life, including her half-brother James Stewart, second husband Lord Darnley and future third husband the Earl of Bothwell, each seek to influence or control her reign. The opera combines scenes of political unrest and court intrigue with more intimate moments, including Mary singing a lullaby to her infant son, the future King James I. Musgrave’s opera premiered at the Edinburgh International Festival in 1977. Its U.S. premiere followed in 1978, and Musgrave herself conducted the West Coast premiere at San Francisco Opera’s Spring Opera Theater in 1979. Laing’s production, first presented by English National Opera in 2025, places the story in a contemporary setting and highlights sectarian violence in modern Scotland. D.M. Wood and Mimi Jordan Sherin are the lighting designers, and Colm Seery is the choreographer. Stober returns to the role after performing Mary at London’s Coliseum in 2025. British baritone Thomas Mole makes his American debut as James Stewart, while San Francisco Opera Adler Fellow tenor Thomas Kinch portrays Bothwell. Christopher Sokolowski makes his company debut as Lord Darnley. Baritone Hadleigh Adams portrays the musician and secretary to the queen, David Riccio; bass David Soar is Cardinal Beaton; current Adler Fellow baritone Olivier Zerouali is the Earl of Morton; tenor Chance JonasO’Toole is the Earl of Ruthven; bass-baritone Philip Skinner is Lord Gordon; and Mary’s four eponymous ladies-in-waiting are performed by Adler Fellows Sadie Cheslak (Mary Seton), Sofia Gotch (Mary Beaton), Mary Hoskins (Mary Livingston) and Alexa Frankian (Mary Fleming). Mary, Queen of Scots continues through October 4 at the War Memorial Opera House. For tickets and more information, visit sfopera.com. articles.text: September 26 - November 1 Oakland Art Association gallery show Oakland Art Association presents Hopes and Dreams — a curated show that encompasses everyone’s most precious and intimate desires for the future. It can be a dream vacation, a dream come true, a dream for the future of the world or just your part of it. Hope knows no bounds, hope for change, for healing, a brighter future, or for world peace. OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties whose mission is to encourage artistic endeavor in the community, support public school art education, and arrange show venues for our members’ artworks. Free and open to all! For more information, see www.oaklandart. org. Gallery is open and staffed Saturdays and Sundays from 11 am to 2 pm. Saturday, October 3, 7:00 p.m. Mads Tolling with Kenny Washington Two-time GRAMMY Award-winning Danish jazz violinist Mads Tolling returns to PCA with prolific pianist John R. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington. It will be the fourth time the three have performed together. The trio will perform their own music as well as that of composers Chick Corea, Ornette Coleman, and the group Toto, along with songs from the American Songbook, including the Temptations, Carole King, and jazz greats like Thelonious Monk and George Gershwin. Advance tickets are recommended, and are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/jazzviolin; doors open at 6:30 p.m. Tickets are selling rapidly and may well sell out! Friday, October 9, 6:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art History Lecture A Friday night Extravaganza! Art historian Michael Stehr presents a spirited, illustrated 50-minute lecture exploring Michelangelo’s work in his home town of Florence, Italy. At the age of 29, he would put the finishing touches on his David, likely one of the most recognizable sculptures in Western art. As he moved through his forties, this sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance would continue to yield sculptural masterpieces and explore the art of architecture at San Lorenzo, the parish church of the Medici family. In 1534, he moved to Rome and only returned to Florence after his passing almost another thirty years later. Doors open at 5:30 p.m. Please bring $20 (cash only) per person to pay for entrance at the door. Saturday, October 10, 7:00 p.m. Virginia Tichenor’s Ragtime Quartet Concert This quartet features ragtime pianist Virginia Tichenor with a stellar line-up of musicians performing ragtime and traditional jazz music. The quartet includes Virginia, of course, Ryan Calloway, clarinet, banjo and vocals; Marty Eggers, tuba, and Robert Young, cornet. Virginia Tichenor is an Oakland-based pianist, originally from St. Louis, MO, the daughter of the late Trebor Tichenor, a noted scholar, pianist and collector of ragtime music. Virginia plays solo piano locally in the Bay Area and is also a traditional jazz pianist, working currently with her husband, Marty Eggers, who also plays with the Zenith, Silver Bell, and Barrelhouse Jazz Bands. Advance tickets are highly recommended for this show, and available now at https://www.ticketsignup.io/ Ragtime. Sunday, October 11, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Mark Williams, and Albert Brooks – will pay tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which fifty or more have become American standards. Van Heusen, although not as well-known as some other American popular music composers, gave us jazz standards such as: Like Someone in Love (1944) and Polka Dots and Moonbeams (1940). He wrote popular music mainly for film and stage. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of an afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. articles.text: Good things often come in groups of three. If you are into literature, it’s the Three Musketeers. If you are into religion, it’s the Holy Trinity. For me, it is memories, menus, and music. My wife and I arrived in the Swiss city of Geneva, a very beautiful and clean city on the shores of Lake Geneva with its stupendous water fountain. Being in Geneva brought back some memories. During the opening festivities of the Los Angeles Music Center the USC Orchestra was invited to participate. At that time, I was the orchestra’s associate concertmaster, seated prominently at the front of the orchestra near the audience. Our soloist for that occasion was the noted American tenor Brian Sullivan. During the rehearsal, Sullivan took his place standing next to me and facing the audience. I was very impressed by his voice and stage presence. During the middle of the aria, he turned around and sang directly to me. I have never heard anything so beautiful in all my life from a singer. Sullivan took me under his wing and helped direct my musical career. He also gave me excellent advice. A few years after this the news media announced the death of Brian Sullivan. His body was discovered in Lake Geneva. It was never determined if he died because of an accident or perhaps by suicide. His voice and personality remain vivid in my memory. Simply stated, his was the greatest voice I ever heard in person. If you are into religion, it’s the Holy Trinity. For me, it is memories, menus, and music. During the opening festivities of the Los Angeles Music Center the USC Orchestra was invited to participate. At that time, I was the orchestra’s associate concertmaster, seated prominently at the front of the orchestra near the audience. Our soloist for that occasion was the noted American tenor Brian Sullivan. During the rehearsal, Sullivan took his place standing next to me and facing the audience. I was very impressed by his voice and stage presence. During the middle of the aria, he turned around and sang directly to me. I have never heard anything so beautiful in all my life from a singer. Sullivan took me under his wing and helped direct my musical career. He also gave me excellent advice. The 3 M’s A few years after this the news media announced the death of Brian Sullivan. His body was discovered in Lake Geneva. It was never determined if he died because of an accident or perhaps by suicide. His voice and personality remain vivid in my memory. Simply stated, his was the greatest voice I ever heard in person. As Rocky Marciano once said: “The bigger they are, the nicer they are.” After Geneva, my wife and I took the train to Northern Italy, where we stayed in the home of our friends Tiziano and Rafaela Micci. Mrs. Micci has a very successful political career. She was the mayor of the city of Orino. Mr. Micci is able to see humor in almost anything. He is a gourmet of high status and knows the history of just about every recipe. One of his friends is the noted Italian chef Sergio Borzetti. Tiziano prepared a special dinner for us which featured the northern Italian specialty of polenta. In the United States polenta is known as grits. It is also the national dish of Romania. You can prepare polenta in two different ways. I always cooked the corn grits over a high heat. Tiziano prefers to cook The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet polenta very slowly. In preparation, it takes an hour at low heat, and he stirs it every five minutes. Polenta lends itself to a variety of presentations. It is marvelous by itself or served as a side dish with vegetables or meats of any kind. We enjoyed the polenta as a side dish and it was served with a slow cooked beef roast, accompanied by a slightly sweet vegetarian sauce. The polenta was topped with Gorgonzola cheese or Taleggio cheese. It is advisable not to cook the polenta with olive oil or Parmesan cheese. When you prepare polenta, use your imagination. It is so adaptable that you can use practically any side dish. Success is guaranteed. Three of us attended a concert in an old church very near Orino. It was impressive to see that the church was filled to overflowing with an audience of perhaps more than 300 people in attendance. Andrew Jolliffe is the impresario of a very successful concert season. It is obvious that he has a very efficient staff to assist him. This particular concert featured the first trumpet of the La Scala Orchestra, Francesco Tamiati, and the excellent local organist, Margherita Gianola Mascioni. We arrived early and were fortunate to hear maestro Tamiati warming up. It was thrilling to hear his agile technique, articulation, and fine tone quality. The program began with the famous Trumpet Voluntary composed by Jeremiah Clarke. As the program progressed, the artists took turns in performance. I enjoyed the playing of both; however, I wished that this famous trumpet player took the opportunity to really show off his abilities. This criticism is minor when you consider the quality of the concert. After the concert, impresario Jolliffe gathered his staff, the two featured musicians and the former mayor of the city of Orino for a photograph. Seeking information for my article, I spoke with the impresario. He is a very gracious Englishman, who resides locally in Italy. He said that he would be very happy to engage me as a violin soloist for his festival next year. It turns out that my European pianist lives just a few minutes away from the concert hall. How convenient is that? I thought it over and I am convinced that I have a perfect program for his audience. The line from The Godfather movie came back to me: “Make him an offer he can’t refuse.” I think that I should not refuse his offer. A memorable Italian dinner featuring classic polenta and slow cooked beef. It was delicious and quite easy to prepare. articles.text: When people think about the legacy they want to leave, their thoughts may turn to family, an alma mater, a hospital or another large institution. Stagebridge hopes to add another possibility: local arts organizations. Founded in 1978, Stagebridge is the longest-running performing arts organization for older adults. As it approaches its 50th anniversary, the Oakland nonprofit is thinking about its own future and that of the East Bay arts community. This fall, Stagebridge will bring together local and national arts organizations and community partners, including Women’s Foundation California, Oakland Interfaith Gospel Choir and Faith in Action, among others. Stagebridge’s Legacy Event will explore how lifetime and planned gifts can sustain the arts while connecting organizations, supporters and advisors to share knowledge about legacy giving. For Stagebridge board member Tracy Gary, a nationally known philanthropic and legacy advisor, the opportunity includes broadening how people think about legacy. Universities and hospitals are often top of mind in long-term charitable planning, she says, while smaller organizations that enrich their communities can be overlooked. Stagebridge knows firsthand what a legacy gift can make Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet Oakland Ballet’s Luna Mexicana is showing at Paramount Theatre next month. Oakland Ballet Company performs Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Dia de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on October 30 and November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission, and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza . Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Tickets are available online now. articles.text: possible. Like many arts nonprofits, it weathered uncertainty following the COVID shutdown. Today, Stagebridge is rebuilding and growing, thanks in part to a generous legacy gift and bequest that has helped expand programming, develop partnerships and strengthen its arts and legacy education. The Legacy Event will feature performances by Brenda Marie Turner, Terrence Kelly and Brian Young, along with personal stories, a panel of people who have made or are considering legacy gifts, and advisors who can answer questions. Participating organizations will introduce their work and share resources. “We all love the arts, and we want to create more of a partnership and network,” Gary said. “This is the first of our partnership events.” The goal extends beyond giving to one organization: to build a stronger network of East Bay arts groups and broaden the conversation about sustaining the community’s cultural life. A founding partner of Unleashing Generosity, Gary has helped start more than 27 nonprofits, served on 32 boards and authored Inspired Philanthropy. Her forthcoming book, Redesigning Nonprofits: Catalysts for a Stronger Democracy, explores ways to strengthen the nonprofit sector and will be available at the Legacy Event. For those ready to take a next step, Gary suggests speaking with a financial advisor or using a free will-planning tool such as FreeWill, then having an attorney review the documents. “The arts are saving us right now,” Gary said. “Think about the organizations that have brought joy to your life. Think about the impact you want your legacy to have.” Find out more at Stagebridge. org/donate. ARTIST & ART HISTORIAN

For those ready to take a next step, Gary suggests speaking with a financial advisor or using a free will-planning tool such as FreeWill, then having an attorney review the documents. “The arts are saving us right now,” Gary said. “Think about the organizations that have brought joy to your life. Think about the impact you want your legacy to have.” Find out more at Stagebridge. org/donate. By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Ballet Company performs Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Dia de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on October 30 and November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission, and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza . Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Tickets are available online now. Visit https://oaklandballet. org to purchase tickets. articles.text: On Wednesday, September 23, the Piedmont Seniors group celebrated their 30th anniversary at the Community Hall. Group members and city officials came together to celebrate this significant milestone with cake, food, and welcoming conversations. The event began with members signing in at a table outside and enjoying tea and coffee while chatting before the festivities began. Around the room were scrapbooks with old newspaper clippings referencing the group and photos of outings. Some of the scrapbooks dated back to the founding of Piedmont Seniors and how it came to be. The first speaker was Piedmont historian Gail Lombardi, who spoke about Piedmont’s beginnings in 1907 and showed photos of what the city looked like. After Lombardi’s presentation, attendees were treated to lunch from Ann’s Catering, which served chicken sandwiches and salads along with other items tailored to guests’ liking. After lunch a special Piedmont Seniors cake was cut and handed out to each table for everyone to enjoy. The lunch gave everyone a chance to speak with city officials, including Fire Chief Dave Piedmont Seniors 30th anniversary cake Brannigan, Police Captain Chris Monahan, Police Officer Tyler Petit, City Administrator Rosana Bayon Moore, Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, Recreation Supervisor Paula Cooper-Tipton, and Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen. After lunch, Program Coordinator Janet Epstein offered a few words in honor of the group’s 30th anniversary. “It’s really hard to come up here and believe that I’ve been doing this since I was 10. It’s been 30 years since the beginning of the Piedmont Seniors in 1996,” said Epstein. She mentioned some of the 300 excursions the group has been on and honored the long-standing members in attendance. After her speech, she welcomed former Recreation Director Mark Delventhal to the stage after honoring him for his decision to help form Piedmont Seniors 30 years ago. Mark Delventhal gives a speech on how happy he is to see Piedmont Seniors thriving. their excursions. The crowd gives an ovation for all the speakers at the 30th celebration. This program has always held a real special place in my heart, and it’s hard to believe that it’s been 30 years,” said Delventhal. “I think one of the reasons this program is so special to me is it changes lives. It creates connection. It provides an additional community and support system for people, and a very important part of their lives. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors took a recent excursion, crossing the Bay Bridge for two private group tours, one each of the San Francisco City Hall and the historic James R. Browning United States Federal Building Courthouse. San Francisco City Hall – known as the “People’s Palace” – is the magnificent Beaux-Arts seat of government for the City and County of San Francisco. Reopened in 1915 after the catastrophic destruction of its predecessor in the 1906 earthquake, its iconic dome stands 307 feet tall, making it 42 feet higher than the U.S. Capitol dome! The building has witnessed profound historical moments, including the 1978 assassinations of Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk, and hosted California’s first same-sex marriages in 2004. Speaking of marriages, the City Hall is a very popular venue for weddings, using its elaborate staircase as a backdrop. Several notable public figures and celebrities have been married at San Francisco City Hall, including Marilyn Monroe and Joe DiMaggio, Rosie O’Donnell and Kelli Carpenter, etc. On the morning of the Piedmont Seniors’ visit to City Hall there were several weddings taking place, as well as a couple of quinceañeras. After the City Hall tour the Piedmont Seniors then headed to Max’s Opera Café, an upscale restaurant located in the heart of San Francisco’s Civic Center, which offers classic American fare with an old-school feel and upbeat atmosphere. After lunch the Piedmont Seniors then continued their tour in San Francisco by visiting the James R. Browning United States Courthouse, where they got an in-depth guided tour from John O. Tulloch, retired former Piedmont city clerk and former assistant city administrator. This courthouse has been described as the second most beautiful public building in the United States and was described by Sunset Magazine shortly after its 1905 opening as “A Post Office That’s a Palace.” Today, this historic courthouse is the headquarters of the United States Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. Built in the Beaux-Arts/American Renaissance style, builders used the finest materials and craftsmen to make the building an ode to Greek and Roman architecture. From stained glass skylights to marble columns, with Tiffany glass mosaics to redwood libraries, hand-carved sculptures to hand-tiled floors, the Browning Courthouse is an architectural masterpiece. One of the true highlights of the visit to this building was a visit to Courtroom One, a most elaborate interior space. Originally designed as a trial court and renovated in the 1960s for use by the Court of Appeals, it features marble Corinthian columns and classical symbols of cast-plaster caryatids and cupids. Three ceramic tile mosaics adorn the arched panels. The bench includes Venetian glass motifs, while the wall behind features a decorative design from many colors of marble. It also has marble and plaster representations of 28 different varieties of California fruits and vegetables. All in all, it was a fun-filled, very informative day for the Piedmont Seniors. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov or phone (510) 420-3070. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors recently took an excursion to Calistoga to tour Castello di Amorosa, an authentically built, 14th century replica Tuscan castle-style winery, nestled in the hills in the heart of the Napa Valley. On the way to the tour, the Piedmont Seniors made a short stop along the way to visit the historic Oakville Grocery, a wine country landmark since 1881. Adjacent to the grocery is the Oakville Wine Merchant, a 150-year-old Victorian house which not only is a museum but is also the setting for wine tastings. Then it was off to visit Castello di Amorosa. Castello di Amorosa is renowned for its world-class wines made by a fourth-generation winemaking family that has been crafting fine wine for over 130 years. After decades of researching and studying medieval castles throughout Europe, Dario Sattui began his 15-year building project in 1993. Today, experts consider the Castello an architectural masterpiece as it transports visitors to medieval Italy. The 141,000 square-foot Castello features: 107 rooms (each one of While on their way to Calistoga, the Piedmont Seniors took a brief rest stop at the historic Oakville Grocery. This grocery is considered the oldest one in the state of California. Pictured are: Yorkman Lowe (left), Sue Getreuer, Greg Jurin, Lilly Guardia-LeBar, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, and Judy Wong. One of the highlights of the Piedmont Seniors’ tour was a visit to the winery’s Great Hall. With its handpainted Italian frescoes, and 500-year-old Umbrian fireplace, the Great Hall is the castle’s most prestigious and most sought-after room for special events. It’s one of the only rooms in the Castle with glass windows. The walls were hand painted by brothers Fabio and Elio Sanzogni, and it took them more than 18 months to complete the art. Each fresco was inspired by Tuscan medieval paintings. Pictured for the Piedmont Seniors are: Kelly Hope (left), Andre Brown, Greg Jurin, Sandra Ponce, Judy Wong, Gloria Wilmer, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Jan Yager, Jim Ayotte, Sue Getreuer, Yorkman Lowe, Kristi Yager, and Lilly Guardia-LeBar. During their winery tour, the Piedmont Seniors gathered in the Grand Barrel Room, located three levels below ground. It is 12,000-square-feet and has 14-foot tall ceilings and 40 cross-vaults with ribbing. The brick is hundreds of years old and imported from Europe. pages.text: Wednesday, September 30, 2026 21 Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I know the new iPhones came out, and I have an iPhone 13 and I’d like to update it. The two that I’m the most interested in are the folding phone, or the bigger iPhone Pro. Can you give me an idea of what the differences are? –Sal, Oakland Dear Sal: Yes, it’s that time of year when Apple releases the new iPhone models. Apple has been talking about making a foldable phone for years, and this year, they finally announce the iPhone Duo. The two models that you mentioned; the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the iPhone Duo, really cater to different needs. You can order an iPhone 18 Pro Max or (smaller) 18 Pro now, and in many cases, you can just walk into one of the Apple stores and get one. They have several of the models in stock depending on how much storage you need or what color you want. There will be a non-Pro version of the iPhone 18 probably early next year. As far as the iPhone Duo, you can pre-order that starting on October 16 with availability starting on October 23. Let’s compare the two. First, the iPhone Duo is going to be quite a bit more expensive than the Pro Max starting at around $2000 for 256 GB in storage all the way up to $3200 for 2TB of storage. Compare that to the iPhone 18 Pro Max which starts at $1300 for 256 GB up to $2500 for 2TB. (The smaller 18 Pro costs between $1200 and $2400). The new Duo is made of premium titanium, while the iPhone models are still made with aluminum, which can tend to scratch easily. Since you mentioned that you’re interested in the bigger iPhone Pro Max, the screen size is 6.9 inches. Not quite pocket size, but if you have a thin case, you can fit it in your back pocket. I have the 18 Pro Max, and even with my wallet case I can stick it in my back jeans pocket. It’s bulky, and I can’t really sit down with it in my pocket, but I’m used to that size as I have had the max size since it was available. As in previous models, iPhone 18 Pro is smaller, with a 6.3 inch display. It’s the dual display of the Duo that really makes the biggest difference to user experience. The Duo has a 5.4 inch front display closed and 7.6 inch inner display open. Folded open, it’s like an iPad mini, with more working space than any of the other models. It gives you the opportunity to have more than one app on your screen at a time, with the ability to drag things from one to the other. Also, Apple has claimed that users will be able to use an Apple Pencil on not only the big display but on the front display also. That could be a game changer for creatives that don’t want to carry their laptop around but want the ability to quickly send sketches to clients and friends. While the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max still use Face ID, the Duo uses touch ID on the side button. And folded open, the Duo is quite thin, but thicker than the 18 Pro Max when closed. The big new feature on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is the triple camera set up with variable aperture. Unlike previous iPhones, this one allows you to choose the aperture when taking a shot. While the Duo is no slouch with a 48MP dual fusion camera system, the Pro models blow it out of the water when it comes to photo specs. This is why I decided to get the 18 Pro Max. The iPhone 18 Pro Max has up to 45 hours of video playback, and if you use the Duo closed, it almost matches that at 44 hours. But why would you keep that screen closed if you are watching a video? With the Duo’s inner display, it’s only 31 hours of video playback. These numbers are deceiving because often it depends on what other apps or processes are running on the phone. I have found Apple’s claims of battery life not to be particularly precise, on phones, watches, and laptops. So, who is the iPhone Duo best suited for? If you’re a person who likes to have that newest thing, and don’t mind paying a premium, and you don’t need all of the camera features, then it’s for you. If you want the features of an iPad and iPhone and one device, then it might be worth paying the premium cost for this new iPhone Duo. articles.text: An autumn walk through Piedmont turned into a literary treasure hunt last Wednesday, showing how a shared love of reading can bring a community together step by step. While last Wednesday was the warmest day of the week, weather was no obstacle for our Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. A turnout of 51 walkers and six K-9 companions met at the Exedra to embark on our weekly outing on this crisp first full day of fall. Since July, different participants have taken turns leading the weekly walks. This rotation has highlighted the varied interests and creativity of our members. Last week’s route was designed by June Yee, who invited us to visit four little sidewalk book libraries scattered along a 2.3-mile loop through Piedmont’s scenic neighborhood streets. Walkers were encouraged to bring books to swap or donate. Lois Price, who is currently building an ADU and looking to downsize her personal library, arrived with a generous bag of volumes to distribute along the way. Before setting off, June offered a brief background on the sidewalk library movement. These small, weather-resistant boxes allow neighbors to take or leave books freely. Though informal book sharing has historical roots in older public reading initiatives, today’s widespread sidewalk library phenomenon is remarkably recent. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, September 30, 2026 Exedra Plaza, 972 Magnolia Ave, Piedmon Features CA 94611 to Exedra Plaza, 972 Magnolia A WEDNESDAY WALKERS - MAIN Walking on Wednesday WEDNESDAY WALKERS - MAIN Little libraries, big connections on Wednesday Walk By Dick Carter An autumn walk through Piedmont turned into a literary treasure hunt last Wednesday, showing how a shared love of reading can bring a community together step by step. While last Wednesday was the warmest day of the week, weather was no obstacle for our Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. A turnout of 51 walkers and six K-9 companions met at the Exedra to embark on our weekly outing on this crisp first full day of fall. Since July, different participants have taken turns leading the weekly walks. This rotation has highlighted the varied interests and creativity of our members. Last week’s route was designed by June Yee, who invited us to visit four little sidewalk book libraries scattered along a 2.3-mile loop through Piedmont’s scenic neighborhood streets. Walkers were encouraged to bring books to swap or donate. Lois Price, who is currently building an ADU and looking to downsize her personal library, arrived with a generous bag of volumes to distribute along the way. Before setting off, June offered a brief background on the sidewalk library movement. These small, weather-resistant boxes allow neighbors to take or leave books freely. Though informal book sharing has historical roots in older public reading initiatives, today’s widespread sidewalk library phenomenon is remarkably recent. During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, broad efforts emerged to widen book access regardless of income. Philanthropist Andrew Carnegie used his fortune to fund thousands of free public libraries across English-speaking countries. Several local landmarks, such as Oakland’s Temescal Branch, originated as Carnegie libraries. The pioneers of today’s micro-library movement often cite Carnegie’s vision as a primary inspiration. Map of route M 200 ft · 200 ft June Yee talking to walkers about Sidewalk Libraries Walkers searching for books Sign for LittleFreeLibrary.org European precursors also paved the way. In Germany, artist-designed public bookcases began appearing in the 1990s. By 2002, German designer Trixy Royeck developed dedicated outdoor book exchanges. These early installations shifted reading away from formal institutions, establishing the informal, anonymous book swaps we see today. The modern Little Free Library movement was sparked in 2009 by Todd Bol of Hudson, Wisconsin. Bol built a small wooden structure styled like a one-room schoolhouse, placed it on a post in his front yard, and filled it with books as a tribute to his mother, a passionate 469 ft schoolteacher. The idea quickly captured public imagination. Partnering with educator Rick 292 ft Brooks, Bol began promoting the concept nationwide. Their original goal was to surpass the 2,509 Carnegie libraries in existence—a milestone achieved by August 2012, when their initiative formally incorporated as a non-profit organization. The movement’s growth since has been remarkable. By 2016, over 50,000 registered libraries spanned all 50 states and 70 countries. articles.text: One of the pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month and offers movies in a comfortable setting with lively discussion afterwards. The Grand Budapest Hotel, written and directed by Wes Anderson and released to critical acclaim in 2014, is a comedy-drama displaying a wide range of cinematic effects to tell the story of an aging Eastern European hotel through a narrator cast as a writer visiting the hotel in its final days. In the opening scenes, the writer shares his belief that vivid thoughts and memories can’t help but be shared. He begins to learn about the hotel in an interview with the current owner. We are visually transported back in time through the clever use of miniatures in long-distance scenes that are barely noticeable, and varying aspect ratios. They used 1.37:1 for the 1930s, 2.35:1 for the 1960s, and 1.85:1 for the 1980s. Colors in various shades set the mood for the time period being filmed, with unusually rich detailed scenes require the viewer’s full concentration to follow the storyline. Many scenes are perfectly symmetrical, creating visual pairings that emphasize the dialogue taking place between characters. The principal character in this story is the hotel concierge, M. Gustave H., played to perfection by Ralph Fiennes. He reflects on his history with the hotel through whimsical satire, stylized pretension, and nostalgia to alter our perspective from our own current reality. F. Murray Abraham, as Mr. Moustafa, plays the current hotel owner, and is represented in flashbacks as the Lobby Boy, an immigrant fleeing political turmoil before being employed by M. Gustave H. The storyline is linear and a straightforward portrayal of a wealthy dowager’s 20-year affair with the Concierge and the conflicts arising from her desire to leave her estate to him if her death is caused by murder. The dowager’s lawyer, played by Jeff Goldblum, is the center of the controversy involving a forged will fabricated by the dowager’s son, Dimitri, whose role in the dowager’s death leads to suspicion of murder. When the Concierge and Lobby Boy visit the dowager’s estate for a reading of the will, Dimitri conspires to accuse them of her murder and has them arrested and thrown in prison. Their escape from prison, aided by Lobby Boy’s girlfriend, Agatha, and their confrontation with Dimitri unfold in a well-choreographed sequence that reflects the quirky disposition of the dowager’s estate, which includes ownership of the Grand Budapest Hotel. Tragedy arrives in the final scenes with the deaths of the Concierge and Agatha, leaving the Lobby Boy as the surviving owner. The Grand Budapest Hotel will be shown on Thursday, October 8 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Ave. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free to anyone 18 and over. Our next movie is A Few Good Men, a 1992 drama to be shown on November 12 at 1 p.m. The Grand Budapest Hotel, written and directed by Wes Anderson

articles.text: One of the most well-known types of service dogs is the mobility assistance dog. Organizations such as Canine Companions and Guide Dogs for the Blind are well known for training these amazing dogs, who can dramatically improve the quality of life for their handlers. But very few people understand the vast array of tasks these dogs are able to perform. Fewer still realize that people may qualify for mobility assistance based on their own health-related needs. A well-known area of mobility assistance service dog training is balance and stability tasks. Counterbalance is where the dog provides physical support by walking with steady tension on a rigid harness handle, gently helping to guide the owner should there be a disturbance in their gait or balance. This can be used while walking on flat surfaces, but may be especially helpful when steadying a handler on stairs or while walking uphill. Mobility assistance dogs may also be trained to provide balance support as the handler moves from a seated to a standing position, or vice versa. In this case, the dog acts as a steadying point of contact or counterweight as the handler raises or lowers their body. Although they are not as well known, retrieval and delivery tasks make up an important area of mobility assistance training. Dogs who are able to pick up dropped items may save their owners a great deal of discomfort or improve their safety. Fetching specific items such as a phone, water bottle, or even medication can be extremely important. Many mobility assistance dogs carry items such as medication or water bottles inside specialized vest pockets, but dogs can also be trained to carry specific lightweight items in their mouths for short distances. Finally, certain independence-related tasks help handlers navigate the world more safely. Door and drawer operation means that a dog is trained to pull open doors, drawers, or cabinets using attached fabric pulls, and to close them again with a nose or paw. Dogs may also be trained to press buttons, such as those for automatic doors or light switches. Some may even be trained to pull a manual wheelchair short distances over flat surfaces or provide mild forward momentum on a gentle incline using a specialized harness. This can be essen-

articles.text: engagement process: properly vetted plans for traffic improvements and pedestrian safety; wildfire-resilient design; safe emergency evacuation routes; and a financially feasible project that meets state housing obligations while integrating affordable and market-rate housing. As a licensed architect with seven years on the Planning Commission working on Piedmont’s Design Guidelines, and four years on City Council, I understand the technical and financial challenges of development. I know our obligation to meet state housing requirements while making sure city-owned land serves Piedmont’s broader community needs. I will evaluate the proposed partner against the RFQ criteria, the Specific Plan, our fiscal realities, and community commitments. I will vote yes only if the agreement is specific, financially credible, and aligns with the MCSP. Sunny Bostrom-Fleming Several years ago, I placed an offer to purchase a home on Moraga Ave. The offer was accepted, subject to inspections, and they turned out positive. Then, two days before closing escrow, the house started to slide. Inside, the marble counters in the kitchen separated from the back wall. The hillside-facing walls separated from the hardwood floors. An independent engineer did an inspection and said this whole area is a mudslide area, and the proposed soccer field stadium will not work in this area. I decided to run for City Council to make sure the word got out about the dangers of the soccer project and the mudslides. Finally, just before the final council vote to approve the soccer field on Moraga Ave, there was a mudslide, closing Moraga Ave for 2 days, as I had predicted. We need massive community input to ensure that if this area is developed, the city aligns our history and our vision for the future, keeping our citizens, our children, our pets, and wildlife safe. Bill Reichle (ReichleforPiedmont.com) The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is part of the Housing Element mandated by the State of California for all cities. A few cities resisted their housing mandates and exposed themselves to litigation, fines, and penalties, including the loss of control over zoning decisions. One consequence of non-compliance is the state-imposed “Builder’s Remedy,” which allows developers to choose where and what to build without resident input. I am grateful to our city leaders for their determination to keep Piedmont in compliance. The Specific Plan is a comprehensive vision developed with city staff leadership and considerable public input. The plan envisions design, landscaping, traffic circulation, pedestrian safety, wildfire mitigation, storm drainage, geological studies, financing, and other details. The plan is available for review on Piedmont’s Planning & Building Department website. The Specific Plan was used to issue Requests for Interest to prospective developers. If one or more developers express interest in this project, proposals and qualifications would be evaluated for adherence to the plan. I am interested in ensuring a developer’s financial viability and track record in delivering similar projects. My focus would be on public safety, traffic circulation, emergency evacuation, pedestrian and bicycle safety, and wildfire mitigation. Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) I support creating new and affordable housing. Throughout my career at the Attorney General’s Office, I advocated for equitable, accessible, and affordable housing. Where you live impacts so many aspects of your life — where you work and buy food, public safety, transportation, your friends and neighbors, and your schools. At the same time, Piedmont is required to plan for hundreds of new homes in a city with little undeveloped land. Meeting that state housing obligation will require thoughtful planning and difficult choices. Any development needs to reflect both our housing obligations and the needs of the Piedmont community.

articles.text: Editor: It gives me great pleasure to highly recommend Adam Hundt for the Piedmont City Council. Adam is a leader who understands the issues impacting our daily quality of life: safety, community spaces, and preserving our green environments. As a father with young children, he also recognizes long-term challenges, particularly the climate crisis. Adam knows every community must contribute to robust climate action by accelerating home and vehicle electrification and using public facilities for clean energy. These actions will boost our quality of life, improve property values, and secure a better future. The city understands the climate work ahead. In 2025, the Planning Department created the Award for Sustainable Home Design and Construction. I was honored to be one of the inaugural winners for fully electrifying our home. However, there is much more to do. Adam will invigorate Piedmont’s climate plan to help us realize these goals. Please visit Adam’s webpage (AdamHundt.com) and invest in Piedmont’s future by giving him your vote. –James Glauber, MD, MPH

I encourage Piedmont voters to vote for Nancy. –Jeremy Bowers Retired Piedmont Police Chief Why I am voting for Adam Hundt Editor: It gives me great pleasure to highly recommend Adam Hundt for the Piedmont City Council. Adam is a leader who understands the issues impacting our daily quality of life: safety, community spaces, and preserving our green environments. As a father with young children, he also recognizes long-term challenges, particularly the climate crisis. Adam knows every community must contribute to robust climate action by accelerating home and vehicle electrification and using public facilities for clean energy. These actions will boost our quality of life, improve property values, and secure a better future. The city understands the climate work ahead. In 2025, the Planning Department created the Award for Sustainable Home Design and Construction. I was honored to be one of the inaugural winners for fully electrifying our home. However, there is much more to do. Adam will invigorate Piedmont’s climate plan to help us realize these goals. Please visit Adam’s webpage (AdamHundt.com) and invest in Piedmont’s future by giving him your vote. –James Glauber, MD, MPH In support of Bill Reichle Piedmont Post, I’m writing in support of Bill Reichle for City Council. I had the privilege of serving on the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) board with Bill. He is thoughtful, kind, and genuinely dedicated to making Piedmont a better place. He has demonstrated his commitment to Piedmont by volunteering in many capacities and he always leaves organizations, and people, better than he found them. His experience working for UC Berkeley would bring valuable perspective to the City, and I believe he would do a great job listening to the concerns of Piedmont residents and thinking through the issues. His priorities are clear and sensible — public safety, fiscal discipline, and community engagement. We would be fortunate to have Bill representing us on the City Council, and I hope you will join me in voting for him. Sincerely, –Christine Wente von Metzsch Strong boost for Nancy Beninati Editor: I am writing to support Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council. I joined the Piedmont Police Department in 2014 and had the honor of serving as Piedmont’s Police Chief from 2016 until my retirement in 2025. I worked with Nancy on racial and identity profiling and police reform. As a Supervising Deputy Attorney General at the California Department of Justice, Nancy has extensive experience in law enforcement and public safety. I found her to be smart, thoughtful, and collaborative, and she was always willing to share her expertise and help our Police Department. In 2020, Nancy and I presented together at a Piedmont community forum on police reform. She also joined me as my guest at a meeting of the Alameda County Police Chiefs, where she presented on racial and In support of Bill Reichle Editor: We are writing in full support of Bill Reichle’s candidacy for Piedmont City Council. As close neighbors, we have known Bill and his wife Julie for about 25 years. Bill is an extremely friendly, approachable person and a very good listener. He is a very honest, trustworthy person, and these qualities are what we look for in a candidate. His experience as a former Assistant Vice Chancellor at UC Berkeley demonstrates that he is a leader. As a candidate for City Council, he is already hard at work finding out the issues that are facing Piedmont. If he is elected to City Council, we know that Bill will take his job very seriously. He will be a champion for public safety, fiscal prudence, and community engagement. Bill is a great neighbor, and he will make an outstanding Piedmont City Council member. Come election day, we will definitely vote for Bill Reichle! With our strong support, –Wayne Leong, MD and Suzanna Chan, PharmD Candidates Q&A Continued from page 1 engagement process: properly vetted plans for traffic improvements and pedestrian safety; wildfire-resilient design; safe emergency evacuation routes; and a financially feasible project that meets state housing obligations while integrating affordable and market-rate housing. As a licensed architect with seven years on the Planning Commission working on Piedmont’s Design Guidelines, and four years on City Council, I understand the technical and financial challenges of development. I know our obligation to meet state housing requirements while making sure city-owned land serves Piedmont’s broader community needs. I will evaluate the proposed partner against the RFQ criteria, the Specific Plan, our fiscal realities, and community commitments. I will vote yes only if the agreement is specific, financially credible, and aligns with the MCSP. Sunny Bostrom-Fleming Several years ago, I placed an offer to purchase a home on Moraga Ave. The offer was accepted, subject to inspections, and they turned out positive. Then, two days before closing escrow, the house started to slide. Inside, the marble counters in the kitchen separated from the back wall. The hillside-facing walls separated from the hardwood floors. An independent engineer did an inspection and said this whole area is a mudslide area, and the proposed soccer field stadium will not work in this area. I decided to run for City Council to make sure the word got out about the dangers of the soccer project and the mudslides. Finally, just before the final council vote to approve the soccer field on Moraga Ave, there was a mudslide, closing Moraga Ave for 2 days, as I had predicted. We need massive community input to ensure that if this area is developed, the city aligns our history and our vision for the future, keeping our citizens, our children, our pets, and wildlife safe. Bill Reichle (ReichleforPiedmont.com) The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is part of the Housing Element mandated by the State of California for all cities. A few cities resisted their housing mandates and exposed themselves to litigation, fines, and penalties, including the loss of control over zoning decisions. One consequence of non-compliance is the state-imposed “Builder’s Remedy,” which allows developers to choose where and what to build without resident input. I am grateful to our city leaders for their determination to keep Piedmont in compliance. The Specific Plan is a comprehensive vision developed with city staff leadership and considerable public input. The plan envisions design, landscaping, traffic circulation, pedestrian safety, wildfire mitigation, storm drainage, geological studies, financing, and other details. The plan is available for review on Piedmont’s Planning & Building Department website. The Specific Plan was used to issue Requests for Interest to prospective developers. If one or more developers express interest in this project, proposals and qualifications would be evaluated for adherence to the plan. I am interested in ensuring a developer’s financial viability and track record in delivering similar projects. My focus would be on public safety, traffic circulation, emergency evacuation, pedestrian and bicycle safety, and wildfire mitigation. Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) I support creating new and affordable housing. Throughout my career at the Attorney General’s Office, I advocated for equitable, accessible, and affordable housing. Where you live impacts so many aspects of your life — where you work and buy food, public safety, transportation, your friends and neighbors, and your schools. At the same time, Piedmont is required to plan for hundreds of new homes in a city with little undeveloped land. Meeting that state housing obligation will require thoughtful planning and difficult choices. Any development needs to reflect both our housing obligations and the needs of the Piedmont community. Candidate Score Card Before I could support a project, I would want to know that it delivers the required affordable housing, is financially and legally sound, and enhances the community. I would want clear commitments regarding infrastructure, traffic and parking, public safety, environmental and wildfire impacts, construction impacts, and preservation of open space where feasible. Most importantly, I would want a transparent process, clear performance requirements, and meaningful accountability if the developer does not meet its commitments. We should approach our housing obligations thoughtfully and realistically, given Piedmont’s limited land and the need to carefully consider how new development will affect our community. Adam Hundt (adamhundt.com) Piedmont can benefit from new housing; it’ll add to the tax base, increase diversity and enrollment in schools, and hopefully allow those who work in our schools, police, and fire departments to live in Piedmont. Such development must comply with state law and local building code. Planning should incorporate Piedmont residents’ feedback. To be approved, a developer must meet specifications outlined in the City’s Moraga Canyon Specific Plan (MCSP), which accounts for impact to utilities, roads and pedestrian/bike pathways, stormwater drainage systems, and landscape. If elected to City Council, I will examine planning for AC Transit service and road traffic, especially given the use of Moraga Avenue as an escape route in an emergency evacuation. I will work to ensure noise levels are controlled in compliance with wildfire safety protocols, and to preserve Coaches Field and the Corporation Yard. I will appropriately plan from a financial perspective. The MCSP notes that a “fiscal analysis found that the estimated annual, ongoing impact of the MCSP on the City’s General Fund was neutral to slightly positive.” Given taxes from housing development, revenues cover increased costs related to safety and facilities. That said, I will seek feedback from residents regarding funding options for housing development. articles.text: Piedmont’s annual Harvest Festival has featured an Edibles Contest every year since its inception. The name embodies the festival’s larger celebration. This year, the Harvest Festival celebrated 28 years of Piedmont-grown produce. The competition is held in the Community Hall, where the judges evaluated the submissions and determined their rankings. This year, a total of 109 entries were submitted for the Edibles Contest. The Bill Drum Award, for the winner with the most blue ribbons, was awarded to the Slatoff family. Named after the co-founder of the Harvest Festival, the award is sponsored by Ace Garden Center. The Sweepstakes Award went to the Slatoff Family for entering items in the most categories. The Slatoffs received a $75 gift certificate from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. Blue Ribbon Award winners each received $5 gift certificates to Village Market. The Susan Hill Award for Best Youth Entry was awarded to fouryear-old Blaire Davis. The reward was a $30 gift certificate. The city thanks Edibles Contest volunteers Lilla Wells, Alex Slatoff, Carolyn George, and Susan Hill. articles.text: On September 24, Piedmont Police announced a significant update in a case that led to the arrest of multiple suspects and the seizure of illegally possessed items. In August, Sergeant Kristina Foster conducted a traffic stop that led to the discovery of two firearms concealed inside the vehicle’s engine compartment and the arrest of a suspect. Sgt. Foster continued to follow up on the investigation with members of the police department, leading to the arrest and a search warrant at the suspect’s residence. The department worked with the Oakland Police Department and California Highway Patrol Air Unit to safely execute the search warrant at the suspect’s residence, where they seized guns, ammunition, and weapons. The suspect was taken into custody and booked at Santa Rita Jail without incident. “This case is a great example of the work that continues long after an initial arrest, following leads, developing information, and working collaboratively with our law enforcement partners to keep our communities safe,” said the Piedmont Police Department in a statement released on their Facebook page. articles.text: Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions. For this year’s race, the Post will send one question per week to the candidates running for City Council until Election Day. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on Tuesday, September 27, and were asked to reply in 200 words. Week 6 question: The police and fire departments are highly regarded amongst the public. According to the fire department’s union, they are asking for health benefits and retention pay to help recruitment and retention efforts. Would you, as a councilmember, support funding the union’s requests? If so, how would you fund these increased benefits? Bill Reichle (ReichleforPiedmont.com) Piedmont residents I speak with consistently place a high value on public safety. Ensuring the police and fire departments have the personnel, training, and equipment they need — when they need them — will always be my top priority. That is why I support local Measure GG on November’s ballot. Living in a high-cost metropolitan area with a competitive employment market creates inflationary pressure on the city budget, which limits management and personnel options. Measure GG is a well-thought-out solution to raise revenue that will stay here in Piedmont to fund essential services, including public safety.

articles.text: Editor: We seek your assistance in making sure that Piedmont Firefighters are accorded salaries and health benefits in keeping with the fact that they are our Piedmont citizens’ extended family in terms of their dedication to our health and safety. We moved to Piedmont in 1993 and raised our two children here. We have experienced the intelligence, caring and decision-making of our Piedmont Firefighters. Had we not personally benefited from the firefighters’ kindness and skill, we would still feel tremendous gratitude to them for being here just in case. We were very distressed to read the article in the September 23 Piedmont Post indicating that negotiations between the firefighters and the city are at a standstill. We carefully read the firefighters’ concerns about the necessity of 1) having pay increases to encourage longevity, and 2) having retirement benefits to cover firefighters’ medical care for the period between retirement and Social Security eligibility. We share the firefighters’ underlying concern about inadequate staffing which requires excessive overtime to keep us safe. As residents and taxpayers, we support the firefighters’ demands. Piedmont prides itself on being a city that is at the forefront of good decision-making. Piedmont needs to step up to support the firefighters and to inform its citizens what efforts and finances are required to do so. We rely on Piedmont Firefighters for our lives and the lives of our children. Is there anything more important? The firefighters’ knowledge, skills, courage and work ethic should be celebrated and honored by accepting their demands. We are both retired attorneys; Joe represented injured workers and clients denied social security disability; I practiced civil rights law. As residents of Piedmont, we find the city’s response puzzling and extraordinarily short-sighted (using overtime instead of properly hiring, making the very hiring process discouraging by not providing the enticement of raises after certain years of service are reached, by not meeting the basic human need of health insurance until Social Security eligibility is reached). We look forward to hearing from you. –Susan Goldsmith and Joseph Waxman
articles.title: City needs to fix hiring procedure at Fire Dept.

articles.text: Editor, We are writing to Piedmont voters to urge a YES vote on Measure GG. Our families planted roots in Piedmont more than 100 years ago. We have made our home here because Piedmont offers a unique combination of small-town ambiance with strong public safety, outstanding public schools and excellent quality of life amenities such as beautiful parks, strong recreation programs and lovely public spaces. We believe the financial experts who are telling us we soon will have a shortfall in revenues to pay for existing city services, facilities and infrastructure. The cuts that will come if that happens, most likely starting with “quality of life” expenses, threaten the things we hold most dear about Piedmont. We believe the small increase in the real estate transfer tax proposed by Measure GG is the most painless method of dealing with the threat. It is only imposed at a time when property is being sold—a time when funds are most likely to be available to make a payment. Your YES vote on Measure GG will help preserve the Piedmont that has kept our families here for so long. –Fran Bishopric Wolfe and Cameron Wolfe, Jr.
articles.title: Yes on Measure GG

articles.text: Editor, My family moved to Piedmont for the schools AND for the public safety. Having a local police and fire department won’t protect everyone from all crimes and accidents, but knowing that our professional first responders have the ability to respond in 5 minutes or less is very reassuring. These services are paid for by tax dollars which are allocated annually by our elected leaders, supported by volunteer financial experts, and professional city staff. The entire process is public and the proposed and approved budgets are posted on the City’s web site at https://piedmont. ca.gov. The budget reflects our community’s priorities of fiscal responsibility and public safety. This is reflected in the fact that the vast majority of operating expenditures go to the police, fire, and public works departments. When people ask me what Measure GG will support, I tell them it will support what our community values. It will support all the things that make Piedmont a safe place to live and raise our families. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure GG. –Kim Hunter Retired Alameda County Senior Deputy District Attorney
articles.title: Support Measure GG: Support our community

articles.text: Dear Editor, When I was young, Piedmont Recreation Department programs were instrumental in my development and helped form the person I am today. When I was fortunate enough to serve as Piedmont’s Recreation Director and later as City Administrator, I gained insight into the ongoing cost of the many services provided by the City of Piedmont to the community. From streets to parks, sidewalks to police cars, fire apparatus to building maintenance, the costs to provide essential services to Piedmont have continued to rise. Piedmont is one of a small number of California cities whose revenues are primarily property based. This funding structure severely limits options for increased revenues needed to keep Piedmont from falling further behind. Measure GG is a reasonable way to provide additional and ongoing funds to support city services, while not placing an ongoing burden on property owners. If approved, Measure GG will bring Piedmont’s transfer tax more in line with our surrounding communities and provide approximately $1.5 million in additional revenue to support essential services and city infrastructure. Piedmonters understand the value of ongoing investment, especially in community services and assets. Supporting Measure GG is a way to keep up and keep Piedmont moving forward for years to come. Sincerely, Sara Lillevand Retired City Administrator
articles.title: Keep Piedmont moving forward with Measure GG

articles.text: Editor, As Piedmont residents since 2012 and parents of two Piedmont Middle School students, we offer our enthusiastic support for Adam Hundt’s candidacy for Piedmont City Council. In a close-knit city like Piedmont, effective leadership requires a deep understanding of our community’s values and priorities, along with a rigorous, forward-looking approach to our unique challenges. Adam embodies these qualities. He has a natural curiosity and is already hard at work listening to and learning from other residents and city leaders. His educational background in business, engineering, and public policy gives him sharp problem-solving skills and a collaborative style, while his professional experience in operations and supply chain management provides the analytical discipline needed to tackle Piedmont’s longterm infrastructure challenges. As a father of two young children, Adam has his finger on the pulse of the issues facing local families and demonstrates a genuine drive to ensure Piedmont remains a welcoming place for residents of all ages. His platform strikes the right balance for our city’s future, placing emphasis on energy-efficient home upgrades, improved sustainability, and mitigating community risks from wildfires and other natural threats. Adam will bring a fresh perspective, analytical approach, and creative problem-solving to Piedmont’s city governance. We’re excited to support his candidacy and encourage you to join us in voting for Adam Hundt for City Council. Sincerely, Erin and Andrew Schultz
articles.title: Join us in supporting Adam Hundt

articles.text: Editor, Having served eight years on the Piedmont City Council, including two years as mayor, I understand deeply that the true measure of public service is not the popularity of every individual decision; it is whether the institution is stronger, more accountable, and better prepared for the future when one’s service concludes. That is why I am again supporting Dr. Cindi Reiss for the Peralta Community College District Board. When I endorsed Cindi in 2022, I noted her educational and accreditation experience, devotion to the common good, attention to detail, intellect and vision. I also recognized her willingness to challenge entrenched interests in pursuit of sound fiscal management. When she ran for the Board in 2018, Peralta faced serious financial instability, accreditation concerns, leadership turnover, board conflict, board micromanagement of chancellors and possible state-takeover of the district. Cindi Reiss has fulfilled those promises. Today, Peralta is financially and institutionally stronger. Its four colleges are fully accredited. Stable executive leadership, stronger financial practices, greater transparency, and more disciplined longrange planning have replaced years of instability. Recent credit ratings reflect increased confidence in the District’s governance and financial direction, while a 2025 bond-refunding transaction saved taxpayers $13.7 million. These gains did not happen by accident. Cindi helped foster a Board culture focused on its proper responsibilities: setting policy, safeguarding public resources, requiring accountability, and supporting strong professional leadership without micromanaging it. She has also demonstrated the courage to make difficult decisions when the district’s long-term interests required them. But recovery is not completion. Peralta must now carry its Transformation Plan from vision into implementation. That means reducing fragmentation, coordinating programs and services, strengthening pathways for students, and building a fiscal structure capable of sustaining the colleges well beyond the tenure of any trustee or administrator. As Piedmont residents, we have a direct stake in Peralta’s future, in its strength and success. Whether it’s through our many Piedmont high school students that have participated in dual enrollment with Peralta by taking Calculus III: Partial Differentiation, Discrete Mathematics, Linear Algebra or business management classes; adults that have taken art and language classes, or through the thousands of students that Peralta’s colleges serve in Alameda County, Piedmont benefits from a strong Peralta Community College system. When Peralta helps students earn degrees, certificates or transfer to universities, and build economically secure lives, the benefits extend well beyond its campuses. A strong Peralta means a stronger regional workforce, greater economic mobility, responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars, and a healthier and more stable East Bay. Our support of Peralta’s colleges is an investment in the regional institutions and quality of life on which Piedmont itself depends. I urge my fellow Piedmonters to reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta Community College District Trustee, Area 5, on November 3. Best, Teddy Gray King
articles.title: Reelect Dr. Cindi Reiss as Peralta Community College District Trustee, Area 5

We believe the small increase in the real estate transfer tax proposed by Measure GG is the most painless method of dealing with the threat. It is only imposed at a time when property is being sold—a time when funds are most likely to be available to make a payment.
