articles.text: Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen will deliver Piedmont’s 2026 State of the City address on Thursday, October 15, at 5:30 p.m. in Community Hall. The evening is a chance to come together as a community to celebrate Piedmont, reflect on recent accomplishments, learn about work underway now, and look at the challenges ahead. Andersen’s address will look across city government at the projects, priorities, and challenges shaping the city’s work today. As she approaches the end of her term after nine years on the City Council, she’ll also reflect on how her perspective has changed after seeing firsthand what it takes to deliver the services, projects, and programs residents rely on. “After nine years on the City Council, I have a deep appreciation for what it takes to make this city work,” said Mayor Andersen. “We have much to celebrate, but we also have real challenges in front of us. I hope people will come spend the evening with us and leave with a stronger sense of where Piedmont stands today.” Come to hear what’s happening – and stay for the conversation. For residents who want to understand what the city is working on and where Piedmont is headed, the event offers a chance to hear directly from the Mayor and get a broader view of the work happening across the city. A reception with light refreshments will follow the address, with an opportunity to connect with Councilmembers, city staff, and neighbors. Community members planning to attend are encouraged to RSVP at piedmont.ca.gov/SOTC-RSVP. All are welcome, and sharing with your networks is appreciated!
articles.title: Community invited to Mayor Andersen’s State of the City address on Oct. 15

articles.text: On November 3, Piedmont voters will elect representatives to fill three seats on the Piedmont City Council and to federal, state, county, and special district offices. The ballot also includes a proposed increase to the City’s Real Estate Transfer Tax and 14 statewide ballot measures. All registered Alameda County voters will receive a vote-by-mail ballot. The Registrar of Voters began mailing voter information guides on September 24 and will begin mailing ballots starting Monday, October 5. Sign up for the Registrar of Voters’ Track My Ballot tool to get notified when your ballot is mailed, received, and counted. The last day to register to vote for the November 3 election is Monday, October 19. If you’re already registered, check your registration status before October 19 to confirm that your information is correct. You’ll need to re-register if you have moved, changed your name, or wish to change your political party preference. Voter registration forms are available at the City Clerk’s Office and from the Registrar of Voters. You can also register to vote online at registertovote. ca.gov. In Piedmont, ballot drop boxes are near the mailboxes at Highland Way and Mountain Avenue and are available 24 hours a day. The Alameda County Sheriff’s Office picks up ballots from the drop boxes and returns them to the Registrar of Voters daily. The last pickup will be at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3. The Registrar of Voters is hosting a series of pop-up events throughout Alameda County where voters can hand their ballot directly to ROV staff. More information on the location of the pop-up events can be found online at: https://acvote.alamedacountyca.gov/dropstop. If you mail your ballot through the post office, it must be postmarked by November 3 and received by November 10. Whether submitting your ballot by mail or a secure drop box, remember to sign the back of your return envelope – otherwise your vote will not be counted! Alameda County voters can vote in person at any of 100 Vote Centers across the county. In Piedmont, the Veterans Memorial Building at 401 Highland Avenue will serve as a Vote Center. All vote centers will be open: • Saturday, October 31 – Monday, November 2: 9 a.m. - 5 p.m. • Tuesday, November 3: 7 a.m. - 8 p.m. A smaller subset of vote centers will be open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. for 11 days before the election, starting on October 24. The closest 11-day vote center to Piedmont is in Oakland at Parks Chapel AME Church, 476 34th Street. If you have any questions regarding your voter registration, ballot status, or voting locations, contact the Alameda County Registrar of Voters at (510) 272- 6933.
articles.title: Voting information for the November 3 Election

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is asking community members to complete a brief disaster preparedness survey by October 30. The survey will measure changes since 2024 and help guide future preparedness efforts. Preparedness knowledge and actions have changed since the city’s first community survey in 2024. This survey will help the city understand how prepared the community is for earthquakes, wildfires, and other disasters. The survey should take about 5-7 minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ DisasterSurvey. The city’s 2024 survey showed that many respondents recognized disaster risk but had not taken some basic preparedness steps. Among respondents: • 73% were registered for AC Alert • 22% had a current household emergency communication plan • 34% had a current two-week emergency water supply • 27% felt confident or very confident in their knowledge of how to prepare for disasters This year’s survey revisits many of these measures and includes new questions about how the city’s preparedness efforts have developed. This includes earthquake safety and steps that residents can take to minimize wildfire risks at home. The survey will ask where people turn for information during an emergency, what gets in the way of becoming better prepared, and what kinds of resources would be most useful. Since the 2024 survey, Piedmont Fire has expanded preparedness outreach and community engagement, including: • Updating Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan with extensive community participation • Increasing education about wildfire home hardening and defensible space, including a series of presentations to community groups • Conducting a practical wildfire evacuation exercise in the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood and creating an at-home evacuation exercise available to all households • Continuing year-round outreach on emergency alerts, evacuation readiness, and household preparedness The survey data will help the city evaluate where the work is having an impact and what gaps remain. It will also establish a stronger baseline for earthquake preparedness as Piedmont Fire looks to expand outreach in this area. Results will help guide future communications, educational resources, exercises, and community programs. Complete the survey by October 30 at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. For resources and information about preparing for disasters, visit piedmont.ca.gov/Disaster.
articles.title: Fire Dept. seeks community input on disaster preparedness

articles.text: At the September 22 City Council meeting, the Council voted to award the Moraga Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project contract to Terocons Inc. for $785,533. The project will install safety improvements as recommended in the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan. Construction is expected to begin in early October along Moraga Avenue between Ramona Avenue and Red Rock Avenue. The project will install bulbouts and high-visibility crosswalk striping at the intersection of Ramona and Moraga. The intersection of Monticello & Moraga will receive a landscaped pedestrian refuge island and high-visibility crosswalk striping. The last intersection, Mesa & Moraga, will receive a bulb-out, flashing beacons, and a repositioned crosswalk for improved visibility. Interim Public Works Director Rich Cunningham presented the project to the City Council, detailing some of the changes the project will make. “The intersection between Moraga and Monticello, which you have to walk 120 feet across that intersection to cross it, was not safe, and so we’ve put a traffic island there. Part of that traffic island is set aside for landscape, and we’re bringing water across the street from the cemetery planted area via a pipe that will be installed before paving the Moraga Avenue section. The design also includes preservation of the bike lane,” said Cunningham. The city will fund the project through an Alameda County Transportation Commission (ACTC) grant, which awarded the city $748,000 for design and construction. The ACTC funds transportation improvements throughout Alameda County that facilitate safe, efficient, and accessible travel for all types of transportation. The City’s 2021 Safer Streets Plan identified the Mesa/Moraga intersection as the highest-priority location for citywide pedestrian safety enhancements, prioritizing intersections based on proximity to a school, location on an arterial street, and inclusion on a bike/bus route. Moraga Avenue is one of the few arterial roadways within the City of Piedmont eligible for regional transportation funding. “There’s been almost uniform support across the community. We got a lot of nice emails, proactive people up and down Moraga who are all for it,” said Cunningham. The contract agreement with Terocons Inc. is for 16 weeks to complete the work.
articles.title: City Council awards $785,000 contract for Moraga Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project

articles.text: On Monday, October 5, Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee announced that Children’s Fairyland has secured a $5,000,000 allocation from the state of California to close out phase one of its capital investment in the park. The funds are designed to facilitate the initial stages of restoration and revitalization. “It’s really a storybook that comes to life. Regardless of how old you are or young you are, my family can attest to the fact, this is a dream come true,” said Lee. Children’s Fairyland CEO Kymberly Miller elucidated the details of the funding, $3,000,000 will be designated to the park’s capital investment to make “sure we are taking care of this physical space for 76 more years.” The remaining two million will go to the park’s general operations. The funds come from the state’s budget which has allocated $14 million for Oakland community organizations, small businesses, public safety, and transitional housing. Other Oakland institutions receiving state funding include: Juntos Fruitvale Cultural Arts Center, Samuel Merritt University’s human trafficking prevention initiative, commercial corridors across Oakland, the city’s Department of Violence Prevention and The Holland transitional housing facility. “For 76 years, Fairyland has given Oakland’s children a place to imagine what’s possible. I still remember bringing my sons here, and today we’re making sure the next generation gets that same magic. This $5 million is a proud victory for Oakland because every dollar we put into community spaces comes back to us in the children they raise,” said Lee. Children’s Fairyland has been a vital part of Oakland’s culture since opening in 1950. As the park that pioneered children’s entertainment in this country, Fairyland forever changed the landscape of “family fun” as it is known today. Children’s Fairyland is ten acres of green space on the shores of Lake Merritt, designed for outdoor play and low-tech, high-touch hands-on learning. It is a rare and increasingly precious resource for children. The $5 million allocation will fund numerous initiatives within Fairyland’s strategic capital investment plan, including essential infrastructure and facility upgrades. Miller describes the funding as foundational, rather than final. “This funding is a launchpad, not a landing place. We have much more work to do to create the Fairyland of tomorrow. We’re deeply grateful to Governor Newsom, Mayor Lee, and our State of California partners for recognizing what Fairyland means to this community, to Oakland, and to the entire Bay Area. We are laying the groundwork for Fairyland’s financial sustainability so we can continue to be a safe and inclusive environment for playing and learning, where children build critical literacy skills and grow both socially and emotionally,” said Miller. The state funding is a commitment to ensure the 76-year-old iconic and beloved Oakland destination remains a safe, vibrant, and accessible oasis for generations to come. It also signals a broader shift underway at Fairyland. As an organization upheld and supported by its community, admissions, memberships, and the generosity of donors of all kinds, Children’s Fairyland is now adding the kind of institutional support it needs to fuel the next phase of its modernization. Learn more at Fairyland.org.
articles.title: Barbara Lee announces $5,000,000 in state funding for Fairyland

articles.text: Mocha is a 6-year-old Siamese mix who knows how to make herself at home. Although she’s guarded in new situations, when she’s relaxed, you might find her snoozing in a lap or accepting belly rubs. When she wants to play, you’ll love watching her pounce after her favorite wand toys, zoom through her tunnel, and tackle her tiny toy caterpillar. That playful streak can occasionally get ahead of her manners: Mocha can switch quickly from cuddling to play mode, and may grab or swat at nearby hands. So she’ll do well with an adopter who has enough experience with cats to notice when to preemptively redirect her energy. She prefers to be the only cat in her kingdom, and takes daily anxiety medication to help her feel her best. Give her the boundaries she craves, and the playtime she adores, and you’ll have a clever, affectionate companion who greets you at the door with little meows, rubs against your legs, and sleeps on your chest. Her foster sums her up simply: “She’s such a beautiful, sweet girl.” Mocha is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org to ask about meeting her!
articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

articles.text: On Wednesday, September 30, Piedmont High School held its annual Consent Assembly for seniors and freshmen. The assembly, organized by acting teacher Kim Taylor, junior Stella Joseph, and senior Ben Ramakrishnan, involved current PHS students reading real stories from anonymous PHS graduates about their experiences involving sexual assault and consent. “The purpose of the Consent Assembly is to bring awareness and educate people about how to stay safe and how to prevent these stories from happening again,” junior Ida Marshall said. Marshall was one of 16 students who read stories. Although Marshall is enrolled in acting, students do not need to take acting to present in the assembly. A goal of the assembly is for people from across the school to be involved. “I think it went well. All of the other story readers were really talented and I thought we made the stories sound really real. I heard stories about people being affected by it,” Marshall said. PHS also has a lunch club, Piedmont for Consent (P4C), that focuses on spreading awareness about consent. According to P4C co-president junior Sophia Puckett, the club’s goal is to make sure everyone feels comfortable about consent and their personal boundaries. Puckett said that club events this year include giving presentations about what consent is at elementary schools in Piedmont, along with partnering with an elective class at Piedmont Middle School. “The middle school has a new class that’s going to help us lead presentations for the elementary school. It’s called LEAD,” Puckett said. “It’s an elective class, and it focuses on consent next semester.” P4C co-president junior Lucy Shoop said that they are working on a middle school assembly as well. “We’re working on a script that the middle schoolers are going to use in the new elective. Basically, we’re going to help them teach,” Shoop said. The Consent Assembly happened to coincide with the reopening of a 2024 sexual assault case at Cornell University, which sparked conversations across the PHS campus. Puckett said that Piedmont for Consent held an open conversation at lunch for students to share their thoughts about the case. “I think with the Cornell case, a lot of the stories and conversations can be triggering for a lot of people, and we want to make sure people have a place they can come if they need something,” Puckett said. Although Piedmont for Consent is not directly affiliated with the Consent Assembly, Puckett said that their goals very much align. “The assembly is a great way that we are getting the message of consent culture out to Piedmont and other Bay Area schools,” said Puckett. The Consent Assembly takes place once a year, and Marshall said she hopes to continue her involvement. “I really enjoyed doing it. I thought it was a really meaningful and valuable experience, and I hope I’m able to do it next year,” Marshall said. “I think bringing awareness to this stuff is not talked about enough and that’s why it’s really important.” Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: PHS holds annual Consent Assembly

articles.text: There are lots of signs that fall is arriving in the Bay Area. The days are getting shorter. Leaves are beginning to change. And in my family, we start looking for spiders. Every year around this time, my kids and I search Golden Gate Park for shamrock orbweavers. They’re hard to miss once you know what you’re looking for: often in wait for prey at the center of giant, wheel-shaped webs— where their family name “orbweaver” comes from—these spiders’ large abdomens range in color from pale cream to bright orange, and their long legs are striped with light and dark colors. It’s no wonder local birds often notice them before we do! I know for some of you, I’ve already lost you. Spiders make plenty of people uncomfortable. But I’ve always loved them, and over the years my kids and I have made a tradition of getting closer rather than backing away. We find a few orbweavers each fall in the park and think of them as our “pets” for the season, returning regularly to watch them spin webs, grow, and change. By the time we encounter these adult orbweavers at their biggest and most spectacular, they’re nearing the end of their lives. They’ve reproduced and left behind egg sacs containing the beginnings of another generation. And eventually, the spiders we’ve been watching disappear. There is something both beautiful and sad about witnessing the cycle. The natural world gives us countless opportunities to notice cycles of change. Flowers bloom and die. Leaves fall and return. Insects emerge and disappear. A spider reaches the end of its life, but leaves behind hundreds of eggs that will begin the cycle again. This fall, I encourage you to look for opportunities to notice life changing around you, including the parts that may feel strange, uncomfortable, or even a little scary. Ask questions. Look closer. Come back tomorrow. You might be surprised by what captures your curiosity.
articles.title: The season of the spider

articles.text: Dress Best for Less, Piedmont’s longtime resale shop, has pledged $100,000 to the Piedmont Education Foundation’s 2026 Giving Campaign, continuing a relationship with Piedmont schools that has spanned more than four decades. “Dress Best for Less is thrilled to kick off the start of the 2026 Giving Campaign with our $100,000 pledge,” said DBFL President Nagisa Yamamoto. “Our long relationship with PEF has continued to be strong, and we are honored to support the #1 unified school district in Northern California.” Founded in 1982, Dress Best for Less has contributed more than $1 million to Piedmont schools and neighboring communities over the past 44 years. The organization’s annual support of PEF has become a longstanding tradition and reflects its broader commitment to the Piedmont community. “We are incredibly grateful for this generous contribution and for DBFL’s longstanding commitment to our schools,” said PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. “Their continued support helps provide the teachers, staff and programs that make a difference for Piedmont students every day.” The $100,000 pledge comes as PEF launches its 2026 Giving Campaign, which raises funds to help bridge the gap between public funding and the cost of providing Piedmont students with the educational experience the community expects. The community can also celebrate with Dress Best for Less on Friday, October 16, when the shop sponsors the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Movie in the Park, featuring a showing of Wonka. DBFL will have a selection of Halloween costumes available for families who are still searching for the perfect costume. Located on Piedmont Avenue next to Piedmont Grocery, Dress Best for Less sells affordable vintage and gently used clothing, accessories and home décor. The resale shop also promotes sustainability by giving pre-loved items a second life and keeping usable goods out of the landfill. To learn more, visit dressbestforless.org. To make a donation to this year’s Giving Campaign, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/ donate.
articles.title: Dress Best for Less grants $100,000 to Piedmont schools

articles.text: After years of colleges moving away from requiring standardized testing, the admissions process is shifting once again. As more universities reinstate SAT or ACT requirements, high school students are reconsidering the role tests, like the PSAT, play in their college preparation. During COVID-19, many universities stopped requiring test scores as part of their application process, shifting to test-optional or test-blind. As testing gains popularity, many students view the PSAT as their first step of the college application process. “I took the PSAT to get a baseline of what my score was without studying, so that I could compare it to my preACT score to see which one I was better at,” junior Chiara Silvio said. Students often take these exams in their sophomore year of high school, so they can know which test they want to take and are most confident in junior year. “I wanted to see which one I was better at so junior year I can really focus on studying,” sophomore Naomi Jerez said. Although the PSAT has become increasingly popular, some students are choosing to use other resources to determine which direction they want to go in. “I did not take the PSAT; I didn’t sign up for it because I plan to take the online ones at home,” junior Kyla Williams said. “I was also going to take the SAT in December, January, and another one in March.” As top schools switch to being test-required, it affects students differently depending on their educational experiences and future goals. “A lot of people study for it, and it’s not actually accurate, it’s more about the tools you have available to you than how well you’d naturally do,” Silvio said. While preparation plays a large role in a student’s success when taking a standardized test, each student nationwide is taking the same test. This uniformity provides colleges with a baseline to help determine a student’s admission. “Giving your grades or just your transcript only shows in comparison to your school,” Williams said. “For the SAT, it’s an overall evaluation that doesn’t solely compare to your surroundings.” With the increase in resources available to students, standardized tests help colleges determine how a student truly performs. “Nowadays you can get good grades by taking online classes, and get into a good school,” Jerez said. “With a standardized test, everyone’s taking the same thing, so it’s easier to compare scores objectively.” Taking the PSAT and preACT is not a required step for the real SAT or ACT, and can take multiple hours depending on testing location. PreACT exams were conducted in the PHS STEAM building on Saturday, October 3, starting at 8:45 a.m. and lasting for two hours and 45 minutes. “The test was really draining, and it was a lot harder than I thought it was going to be,” Silvio said. However, many students say the benefits outweigh the effort required. “I’ll be able to know which format I like better and I’ll also get an idea of the test taking environment,” Jerez said. Along with prepping students for the SAT, taking the PSAT offers students a series of other benefits to support their college applications. “You can sign up for National Merit, because it helps you qualify if you take the PSAT,” Williams said. For the class of 2026, many universities have announced their switch from test optional to test required. Cornell University, Yale University, Columbia University and Princeton University are some of many that have announced their change. Many schools have also announced changes to their requirements that won’t take effect for a few more years. The University of California schools (UC Berkeley, UCSB, UCLA, etc.) are still test-free for the fall 2027 admission, and are reviewing whether or not to bring back testing for future applicants, according to the University of California. Ayla Blanford is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern with the Piedmont Post.

To take or not to take: that is the PSAT and preACT question By Ayla Blanford After years of colleges moving away from requiring standardized testing, the admissions process is shifting once again. As more universities reinstate SAT or ACT requirements, high school students are reconsidering the role tests, like the PSAT, play in their college preparation. During COVID-19, many universities stopped requiring test scores as part of their application process, shifting to test-optional or test-blind. As testing gains popularity, many students view the PSAT as their first step of the college application process. “I took the PSAT to get a baseline of what my score was without studying, so that I could compare it to my preACT score to see which one I was better at,” junior Chiara Silvio said. Students often take these exams in their sophomore year of high school, so they can know which test they want to take and are most confident in junior year. “I wanted to see which one I was better at so junior year I can really focus on studying,” sophomore Naomi Jerez said. Although the PSAT has become increasingly popular, some students are choosing to use other resources to determine which direction they want to go in. “I did not take the PSAT; I didn’t sign up for it because I plan to take the online ones at home,” junior Kyla Williams said. “I was also going to take the SAT in December, January, and another one in March.” As top schools switch to being test-required, it affects students differently depending on their educational experiences and future goals. “A lot of people study for it, and it’s not actually accurate, it’s more about the tools you have available to you than how well you’d naturally do,” Silvio said. While preparation plays a large role in a student’s success when taking a standardized test, each student nationwide is taking the same test. This uniformity provides colleges with a baseline to help determine a student’s admission. “Giving your grades or just your transcript only shows in comparison to your school,” Williams said. “For the SAT, it’s an overall evaluation that doesn’t solely compare to your surroundings.” With the increase in resources available to students, standardized tests help colleges determine how a student truly performs. “Nowadays you can get good grades by taking online classes, and get into a good school,” Jerez said. “With a standardized test, everyone’s taking the same thing, so it’s easier to compare scores objectively.” Taking the PSAT and preACT is not a required step for the real SAT or ACT, and can take multiple hours depending on testing location. PreACT exams were conducted in the PHS STEAM building on Saturday, October 3, starting at 8:45 a.m. and lasting for two hours and 45 minutes. “The test was really draining, and it was a lot harder than I thought it was going to be,” Silvio said. However, many students say the benefits outweigh the effort required. “I’ll be able to know which format I like better and I’ll also get an idea of the test taking environment,” Jerez said. Along with prepping students for the SAT, taking the PSAT offers students a series of other benefits to support their college applications. “You can sign up for National Merit, because it helps you qualify if you take the PSAT,” Williams said. For the class of 2026, many universities have announced their switch from test optional to test required. Cornell University, Yale University, Columbia University and Princeton University are some of many that have announced their change. Many schools have also announced changes to their requirements that won’t take effect for a few more years. The University of California schools (UC Berkeley, UCSB, UCLA, etc.) are still test-free for the fall 2027 admission, and are reviewing whether or not to bring back testing for future applicants, according to the University of California. Ayla Blanford is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern with the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Every year, Harvest Festival scarecrows are constructed by Piedmont students to be auctioned off in Piedmont Park during the event to fund the schools. The Havens TK pumpkin and 3rd-grade turkey scarecrows both started as giant balloons coated with several layers of Piedmont Post paper strips and wood glue before coming to life at the festival. Normally, each grade at the three elementary school makes its own scarecrow, but this year some grades combined forces and others did not participate. Those that were on display were fantastic. The Havens creators of two of the seven scarecrows shared their process with the Post. “Due to drying time, we could only apply a couple of layers per day, working over several weekends alongside some late-night prep work. My kids, Simone and Sloane, did a lot of the initial papier-mâché work before our scheduled class work parties,” said parent Holen Brady. Brady shared that the main challenge was applying enough coats to dry thoroughly before the balloon lost air. One scarecrow had to be scrapped when a balloon deflated and distorted the shape. These two Havens scarecrows required three separate work parties, with 20 families in total participating. “The kids really enjoyed the papier-mâché and painting, but the highlight for them is seeing their final product displayed at the Harvest Festival and knowing they helped create it,” added Brady. These scarecrows are not heavy, but their size makes transporting them tricky. The Fedor and Moravy Havens families put on their trucker hats and transported the giant turkey and pumpkin scarecrows to the park and then to the auction winners’ homes. This labor of love supports the schools while championing the arts, and the efforts of all scarecrow makers kept a beautiful Piedmont tradition alive.
articles.title: Bringing Harvest Festival scarecrows to life

articles.text: If spiders still feel like too much of a stretch, perhaps monarch butterflies are more your speed. On October 24, join us for We All Journey (https://www. exploratorium.edu/visit/calendar/ we-all-journey), a special daytime event at the Exploratorium exploring another remarkable cycle of life: the monarch’s transformation from caterpillar to butterfly and its annual migration to Mexico, where its arrival often coincides with Día de Muertos. Through art and hands-on activities, families can explore how cultures find meaning in the natural cycles of life, change, and renewal. Whether it’s a spider or a butterfly, there’s a lot to learn when we take the time to look closely. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life.

articles.text: On Saturday, September 26, Girl Scout Troop 32605 gathered books for their book drive. More than 800 books were donated by the troop to Bananas, a local nonprofit in Oakland that serves low-income families. The troop of 12 Girl Scouts advertised for over a month about collecting lightly used books for kids age 0 to 8. The troop’s collection of 800 books from Piedmont and Oakland residents surpassed the amount they collected last year by 200 books. Completing the book drive helped the troop earn their Literacy Badge. Troop 32605 is a co-op troop led by parents Katy Bradford and Lauren Freeman this year. The troop puts its focus on community outreach and volunteerism, and different parents lead the monthly events. The troop’s next community service project will collect warm clothes to give to the homeless this winter.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team claimed a big 3-0 sweep of Castro Valley on Thursday, October 1 at Binks Rawlings Gym, improving their record to 14-8 with five matches left in the regular season. The victory marked the school’s first win over the Trojans since 2018, a testament to the program’s progress over the last two years. “Castro Valley may have been undermanned, but we didn’t blink or let off. We had strong play in all three sets, and that’s what we want. The girls stayed really focused,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. This year’s volleyball team is already among the school’s best in the last decade based its record. Their 14 wins is the most since 2017 when the team went 16-8. Other top teams in school history include 2013 when they went 19-11, the 2012 team (18- 15), 2009 (22-9), and 2008’s alltime best team that went 24-6 and reached the D4 North Coast Section Championship. Piedmont hasn’t won an NCS game since 2015, making that the goal of this year’s team. “We’re making steady progress. There’s a lot we still want to work on, so we just want to keep doing our best to improve. I think we’re playing our best right now. We have moments where we lock in against our top competition, so we want to see that all the time,” Glass said. “Year after year, the Piedmont program is strengthening more and more. In this game, we came out with a bunch of energy every single set. We just played our own game,” junior middle hitter Lucia Dorsey mentioned. Against Castro Valley, PHS was without starting outside hitters Fiona Olsen and Sofia Meyer. It led to big games by Dorsey with 10 kills, Nora Trombi with seven kills, and Olivia Stevens with five. Glass called Dorsey’s performance her best of the season. “Where a lot of the power came from was from Corina [Vora’s] sets. She encouraged some of our plays between me and Maika [Ting]. My chemistry with the setters is becoming super strong,” Dorsey said. Match Recap Piedmont won by scores of 25-21, 25-17, 25-17 over the visiting Trojans. In the first set, Piedmont trailed 4-2 before scoring four straight points to take a 6-4 advantage and never relinquished the lead. Both teams traded points with PHS holding an 18-14 lead, then scored on three straight kills by Izara Dando, and two by Trombi. Castro Valley closed the gap to 23-20, but Piedmont scored two of the final three points with kills by Trombi and Dorsey. PHS opened to a 5-1 lead in the second set, but CV battled back to take a 6-5 lead. The Highlanders regained the lead at 7-6 and maintained their advantage from then on. After that, Piedmont scored seven of nine points to take a commanding 14-9 lead and extended to 21-13. They finished with four of the closing eight points to win 25-17. Castro Valley started with a 4-2 lead in the third set, but Piedmont took control with a run nine straight points with two kills by Maika Ting. CV inched closer to 12-7 but PHS scored three straight with kills by Ting and a block by Dorsey Final stats: Ting had 13 kills and 11 digs. Charlotte Bailey had three kills, two blocks and one dig. Dando had three kills and seven digs. Trombi had seven kills and two digs. Stevens had five kills, two aces, and 14 digs. Dorsey had 10 kills, one ace, and one block.. Allyson Huynh had 16 digs and four assists. Corina Vora had two aces, nine digs and 25 assists. Hazel Schaeffer had 11 digs. Mia Bechtel had one ace, four digs and seven assists. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont visited Alameda on Tuesday, October 6. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (14-8 overall, 3-2 league) hosts league rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 8 at 6:30 p.m.

articles.text: We have now rolled through the first month of school. With our first Athlete of the Month of the new school year, we’re awarding Maika Ting of girls’ volleyball and Henry Stein of boys’ water polo our two Athletes of the Month for September. Honorable mentions go to Maddy Huynh of girls’ tennis and Dylan Jerez of boys’ water polo. MAIKA TING Maika Ting earns Athlete of the Month for September after leading the girls’ volleyball team in kills in every match this season. Some of her best performances include 24 kills and six aces in a 3-2 loss to Salesian on September 3, 13 kills and three aces in a 3-1 win over San Leandro on September 8, 17 kills in a 3-0 win over Encinal on September 22, and 16 kills in a 3-1 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on September 23. HENRY STEIN Henry Stein earns Athlete of the Month for September for filling the stat sheet in multiple categories for the boys’ water polo team. Some of his best games include nine goals, one assist, and two steals in a 12-11 loss to San Marin on September 19, five goals and three assists in a 9-8 loss to Clayton Valley on September 18, five goals and two assists in an 11-8 victory over Marin Catholic on September 18, and four goals, an assist, and three steals in a 14-6 win over Encinal on September 24.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team suffered two losses on the road over the past week, bringing their overall record to 6-8 overall and 1-2 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. The Highlanders suffered a 17-10 loss at Acalanes on Thursday, October 1 and fell narrowly 13-12 at league foes Berkeley on Tuesday, September 29. “We’re getting game experience against bigger and faster players. The goal is to get game experience against better players so we can get more aggressive,” coach Rik Krumins said. Both of Piedmont’s losses to Berkeley this season have come by just one goal after falling to the Yellowjackets 10-0 back on September 4. The result means Piedmont is currently tie for fourth-place in league with Castro Valley and Encinal ahead of the league tournament on October 27. The Highlanders dominated Encinal 15-6 on September 24, and have two matches remaining against Castro Valley. 17-10 to Acalanes The Dons, notably, achieved the No. 13 seed in last year’s Division 1 North Coast Section bracket, while the Highlanders were No. 1 in the Division 2 ladder. Acalanes had a strong first half to lead 12-5 going into halftime. The Dons pulled ahead even further in the third with four goals to Piedmont’s three, making it 16-8. PHS added two more goals in the fourth quarter and allowed one. Final score-line and first-quarter goals was unfortunately not provided. Final stats: Rylan Patty led with three goals. Henry Stein had two goals, three assists, and a steal. Henry Van Den Bos had two goals and an assist. Graham Smith had one goal, one assist, and a steal. Walker Wilson had a goal and a steal. Jack Dahling had an individual goal. Oliver Hurwitz had two steals, Mara Pasani had one steal, while Leo Maltz had one assist. Goalie Dylan Jerez had eight saves and eight steals. 13-12 to Berkeley Both teams were tied 3-3 through the first quarter and 6-6 going into halftime. The Yellowjackets scored four goals and only conceded two in the third quarter to take a 10-8 advantage going into the fourth. PHS scored four goals in the final going, but Berkeley’s three goals was enough to put them above. Final stats: Patty led with eight goals and one steal. Stein had two goals, six assists, and five steals. Oliver Hurwitz had one goal and one steal. Van Den Bos scored an individual goal. Jerez had eight saves and two steals. Tuesday vs. Castro Valley Piedmont hosted Castro Valley for a league match on Tuesday, October 6. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-8 overall, 1-2 league) play in the Monterey Tournament on Friday and Saturday, October 9-10. They face Pacific Grove on Friday at 1:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Point Pinole Regional Park in Richmond for their first Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season on Wednesday, September 30. The boys’ team finished fifth of nine schools, while the girls were fifth of eight. “There were a lot of things to be encouraged about in these results. We had strong performances at the front of both teams, some very impressive performances from our younger runners, and, most importantly, quite a few runners making significant improvements. We still have plenty of work ahead of us, but it is great to see the training beginning to show up in the race results as we head into October,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Senior running Alex Schleuning led things for the boys’ team, finishing seventh of 88 runners with a time of 16:26.1 on the three-mile course. It was the first time for the team to be led by a runner other than junior Dresden Schulte-Sasse in four events this season. Schulte-Sasse, meanwhile, was close behind Schleuning in 10th, clocking a 16:32.2. “Alex Schleuning led Piedmont with a great race. Dresden Schulte-Sasse was right behind him 10th overall. Dresden improved by an impressive 53 seconds from his previous 17:25 on the same course,” Zirkelbach said. Next in for Piedmont was sophomore Dylan Wallway finishing 17th in 17:12.1, while rounding out their best-five was freshman Cormac Ross in 40th in 18:19.1 and sophomore Blake Riif behind him in 41st, 18:29.4. “Freshman Cormac Ross continued his strong first season, running 18:19 as our fourth Varsity runner. Blake Riiff also continued his significant improvement this season, taking 37 seconds off his previous three-mile time,” Zirkelbach said. As for the girls’ team, they continue to work without star runners like Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, and Kelsey Coleman. Junior Viviane Oesterer placed 14th of 68 runners, clocking a time of 20:19.1, and has now led the Highlanders in three of its four events this season. “On the girls’ side, Viviane Oesterer led Piedmont with a strong run. She improved her previous time on this course by 13 seconds,” Zirkelbach said. Behind Oesterer was senior Cora Brozowski Schrader finishing 18th in 20:45.1, junior Nikita Gorelik in 27th in 21:00, sophomore Camille Hauser in 34th in 21:19.8, while senior Annie Thornton rounded out their best five times in 46th, 22:56.5. “Viviane was followed by Cora Brozowski Schrader, Nikita Gorelik, and Camille Hauser. Our first four girls were separated by exactly one minute, which is great to see as this group continues to develop. One of the biggest improvements of the meet came from Annie Thornton, who ran nearly two full minutes faster than her previous time on the course,” Zirkelbach said. NEXT UP Piedmont competes in the 47th annual Asics Clovis Invitational at Woodward Park on Friday and Saturday, October 9-10. The boys’ varsity team runs at 7:40 a.m. on Friday, while the girls compete at 10:00 a.m. the same day.
articles.title: Piedmont competes in first league meet of season

articles.text: It was a big night for the flag football team when hosting American on Thursday, October 1, The Highlanders beat the visiting Eagles by a one-sided 53-6 score. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 7-8 overall and 6-4 against Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division competition. With four games left in the regular season, Piedmont needs one win to assure a .500 league record going into the WACC tournament on October 20. “To be honest, I have not even spoke about NCS yet to the team. We’ve talked about our record in league and what we want to accomplish in the league, so our focus has been that. What I did talk to them about tonight is getting to the line, being intense, getting out quickly, and being prepared at the line. That intensity takes us into the rest of the season,” coach Beth Black said. One player who has emerged as a defensive leader is Nea Mafi as the team’s new starting safety. She’s filling big shoes left by Class of 2026 starter Dahlia Osman, who finished her high school career with 24 interceptions. Mafi is often acting as the defense’s signal caller, communicating with her other defensive teammates before the snap. She had an interception returned for a touchdown against American. “She is a leader when she’s on the field and on the sideline. She’s constantly watching the game, and that’s helping her improve,” Black said of Mafi. “I’m the safety and the last line of defense. It’s important to keep up communication because I see what the game from a different angle at safety. In the beginning of the season, I wasn’t as communicative. I didn’t know exactly how to get my voice out, but I’ve gotten more and more comfortable with the team, so I slowly started to learn it’s okay to be loud,” Mafi said. Game Recap After American punted on its opening possession, Piedmont scored on its very first offensive play on a short pass to Naiya Alexander that turned into a 50-yard catch and run. The receiver weaved her way around three defenders to doge tackles on the play, sprinting to the end zone. PHS converted a one-point try on a pass from Edie Elmquist to Sydney Latvala to give them a 7-0 lead with 4:52 left in the first quarter. With American pushed back to their own five, Piedmont’s next score was an interception returned for a touchdown by Nea Mafi with 2:59 left. Elmquist completed a pass to Alexander for the onepoint conversion, making it 14-0. PHS scored again with 1:22 left in the first. This time, Elquist found Latvala on a 15-yard pass, making it 20-0 after a missed extra point. American answered with its only touchdown with 7:01 remaining in the second quarter. The Highlanders scored on its ensuing possession on a 10-play, 66-yard drive. They converted a 4th-and-3 in the process at the Eagles’ 23 with an eight-yard run by Mafi and capped off with a nine-yard quarterback keeper by Elmquist. They converted another one-point try on a pass to Latvala, now 27-6 with 2:30 left. They scored again with 8:36 left in the third quarter on a sixplay, 66-yard series. This time, Skye Prata Baack made a nice catch on a near 10-yard pass by Elmquist for the score, making it 33-6 after a missed conversion. Piedmont’s final three touchdowns were not recorded due to an overlap in sports schedules. Details were not provided, but two scores were logged by Zoya Shulze and one by Latvala.
articles.title: Flag football team dominates American 53-6

articles.text: Spooky season has arrived with Halloween right around the corner. What better time to awaken some spooky history of around the area, including your very own town? Here’s a look into a batch of locations with rumors of a spooky past. Tyson Lake, Piedmont Tyson Lake is a small reservoir located between private residences between La Salle and Sotelo Avenues, tucked quietly behind the Hampton Field. The location is not public property, but is the only body of water in Piedmont a few locals are known to reel out some carp. On July 20, 1951, the Oakland Tribune published that the Alameda County coroner’s jury today recommended that Tyson Lake, an unused reservoir here, be either drained or properly fenced to prevent further accidents following the drowning of 17-year old James Richards four days earlier. But near a year to the day of the first accident, a second victim on July 10 drowned in Tyson; 19-year old Donald Stracner after swimming with two other companions. World War 2 Navy diver John Haubner, who was a former Piedmont Police Officer, was called on to retrieve Stacner’s body. “As search for the body continued, Police Chief William Pflaum said he will “definitely recommend that some action be taken to alleviate this menace to life.” He said that in view of the fact there have been two drownings in the lake within a year, “something must be done’,” wrote the Oakland Tribune, via HistoryofPiedmont.com. Later on August 8 of 1952, the City of Piedmont sought out to determine the owner of Tyson Lake following the drowning of Stracner. City Council urged the 20 home owners surrounding the lake to erect a fence Tyson Lake now sits quant and quietly behind the lush homes of Sotelo and La Salle. Hayward Plunge, Hayward Allegedly, a swimming instructor back in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps pitter pattering, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in all-white garb from head-to-toe during the day as a teenager. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to continue the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in the process through the hills of Green Belt Park. Black Diamond Mines, Antioch The Black Diamond Mines is a location of the White Witch or Wailing Witch, per urban legend. The story goes that a nanny was expelled from town in the 1870s for practicing witchcraft, only to turn up dead in the mines under suspicious circumstances. Other legend says a nanny, named Mary, was executed after being accused of witchcraft when all of the children under her watch died of illnesses. Niles Canyon, Fremont The Niles Canyon ghost is an urban legend about young woman who died in a horse carriage accident over 100 years ago, said to have occurred specifically on February 28 when horses were spooked by two oncoming automobiles—throwing her from the carried. Legend has it a vanishing hitchhiker walks the road on that day every year, looking to hitch a ride to San Francisco Moss Beach Distillery, Moss Beach Grab a bite, a drink, a spectacular view, and a haunting story at the Moss Beach Distillery slightly past El Granada and Half Moon Bay. The “Blue Lady” is a story from over 70 years ago, where a young woman had an affair with a handsome piano player at the restaurant, falling in love with him. The lady in blue was said to have been murdered by her betrayed fiancé while walking on the beach below the restaurant. Redwood Road Preschool, Oakland Hills This one is very peculiar. Slightly past the intersection of Pinehurst and Redwood Road, there is a former preschool with a gruesome history. Legend has it, a knife wielding murder in the early 80s slayed an entire class of preschoolers on the grounds. Other reports from the Gasden Times indicated a man, Alan Robert Baer, was shot by police on the preschool property in 1981. All that is left of the school is the foundation and a lone swing set, while people have reported paranormal experiences of children’s laughter, voices, and swings in full-motion as if the school yard was bustling.
articles.title: Jaunts for a haunted Halloween

articles.text: Festival Opera’s Salon Series continues October 25 with Mad Scenes, a concert featuring sopranos Aura Veruni and Lila Khazoum and pianist Daniel Lockert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The 4 p.m. performance will feature scenes from operas including Mozart’s Idomeneo and The Magic Flute, Verdi’s Macbeth, Donizetti’s Anna Bolena and Lucia di Lammermoor, and Ambroise Thomas’ Hamlet. The program will explore the darker and more theatrical side of opera, with costumes by designer Marina Polakoff and props incorporated into the performance to help tell the stories. The concert is scheduled just before Halloween and will highlight the macabre and unhinged elements of opera. Audience members are invited to attend in costume. Veruni and Khazoum are both acclaimed sopranos who will perform the featured scenes with Lockert accompanying on piano. The concert is part of Festival Opera’s three-concert Salon Series, which is presented at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series concludes November 22 with baritone Efraín Solís, making his Festival Opera debut, accompanied by San Francisco Opera pianist Marika Yasuda. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is at 801 Magnolia Ave. in Piedmont. Tickets for the October 25 concert are $40. Visit festivalopera.org/salon-series to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Festival Opera presents Mad Scenes at PCA on Oct. 25

articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 15. Now in its 15th year, the threenight festival brings illuminated art installations to the gardens surrounding Lake Merritt. The event has drawn more than 12,000 visitors since its launch in 2012. This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays throughout the gardens, along with live entertainment, an art market, children’s activities and food and beverage vendors. Additional activities include a costume contest for children and adults, an artist awards program and a kids zone. The festival’s food court will feature local food trucks and vendors, along with beer and wine gardens. Proceeds from ticket sales benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a nonprofit volunteer organization formed in 2004. The organization works with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization and programming of the gardens at Lakeside Park. The seven-acre collection of themed gardens includes the Bonsai Garden, Sensory Garden, Toddler Garden and Urban Edible Garden, among others. FGLM volunteers provide maintenance assistance as the city’s gardening staff has been reduced over time. The Autumn Lights Festival is the organization’s largest annual fundraiser. Tickets and additional information are available through the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt at https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/about/.
articles.title: Autumn Lights Festival returns to Lake Merritt Oct. 15

articles.text: Filoli’s “Nightfall Halloween” event is underway at the historic Woodside estate, with more than 53,000 tickets sold across its fall programs following a sold-out opening weekend. “Nightfall” runs now through November 1 and is open from 5:30 to 10 p.m. The Halloween event features more than 1,000 illuminated jack-o’-lanterns, more than 200 scarecrows, character actors, food trucks and Halloween-themed attractions throughout Filoli’s historic house and gardens. New this year is a Witches’ Village in the redwoods, featuring a 20-foot witches’ cauldron, woven wicker witches, live banjo music and haunted railway conductors. The new Haunted Railway includes more than 1,000 feet of track through the redwoods, with miniature houses and other handcrafted elements along the route. Nightfall is in its third year as a large-scale Halloween event at Filoli. The event had sold more than 32,000 tickets before the end of summer, according to Filoli. A Nightfall Champagne Lounge is also offered at 5:30, 7 and 8:30 p.m. The 60-minute experience in Filoli’s Historic Ballroom includes three pours from a champagne flight and admission to Nightfall. Filoli said the Champagne Lounge also provides admission on some nights when general admission tickets have sold out. During the day, Filoli is hosting Autumn Days through November 1 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The daytime program includes a pumpkin patch, fall decorations, harvest games, seasonal food and drinks, and photo opportunities. Tickets and information are available at www.filoli.org.
articles.title: Filoli’s “Nightfall Halloween” event runs through Nov. 1

New this year is a Witches’ Village in the redwoods, featuring a 20-foot witches’ cauldron, woven wicker witches, live banjo music and haunted railway conductors. Nightfall is in its third year as a large-scale Halloween event at Filoli. The event had sold more than 32,000 tickets before the end of summer, according to Filoli. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Peter Pan Goes Wrong, a comedy about an amateur theater company attempting to stage Peter Pan while a series of mishaps threatens to derail the production. Written by Henry Lewis, Henry Shields and Jonathan Sayer, the play follows the fictional Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society as its members take on J.M. Barrie’s classic story. The production features flying rigs, sword fights and a crocodile, along with forgotten lines, malfunctioning scenery and rivalries that spill onto the stage. The play is by the creators of The Play That Goes Wrong, which similarly follows a fictional theater troupe whose production goes increasingly awry. Peter Pan Goes Wrong premiered in London in 2013 before later moving to the West End and Broadway. Susi Damilano directs the San Francisco production. The cast includes Greg Ayers, Joe Ayers, Maggie Mason, Christian McCooey, Ezra Reaves, Renee Rogoff, Patrick Russell, Sophie Schulman, Terrance Austin Smith, Jomar Tagatac and Phaedra Tillery-Boughton, among others. The production runs through November 28 at San Francisco Playhouse, 450 Post St. in San Francisco’s Union Square neighborhood. Performances are Tuesday through Sunday, with evening and matinee performances on select days. The show runs approximately two hours and five minutes, including a 15-minute intermission, and is recommended for ages 8 and older. Tickets and information for Peter Pan Goes Wrong and additional shows and musicals are available at sfplayhouse.org/.
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents Peter Pan Goes Wrong

articles.text: Music at Kohl Mansion will open its 44th season on October 18, with a performance by the Escher String Quartet, an internationally recognized chamber ensemble based in New York City. The Escher String Quartet features Adam Barnett-Hart and Bryan Lee on violin, Pierre Lapointe on viola and Brook Speltz on cello. Formed in 2005 and named for Dutch graphic artist M.C. Escher, the quartet is known for performances combining technical precision, interpretive depth and a distinctive ensemble sound. The program will feature three works from the string quartet repertoire: Haydn’s Quartet in G major, Op. 76, No. 1; Shostakovich’s Quartet No. 3 in F major, Op. 73; and Brahms’ Quartet in A minor, Op. 51, No. 2. The Escher String Quartet serves as Artists of the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center and has performed at venues and festivals including Wigmore Hall in London, the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., and the Auditorium du Louvre in Paris. The ensemble has received several honors, including an Avery Fisher Career Grant and Lincoln Center’s Martin E. Segal Award. Its recording projects have included the complete string quartets of composers Alexander Zemlinsky and Felix Mendelssohn. The concert will begin at 7 p.m. at Kohl Mansion, 2750 Adeline Drive in Burlingame. A pre-concert talk by Stanford cellist and educator Christopher Costanza will begin at 6 p.m., followed by a complimentary glass of wine and dessert after the performance at 9 p.m. Music at Kohl Mansion’s 2026- 27 season includes eight performances through May 2, 2027, featuring chamber music ensembles and artists from the United States and Europe. Performances take place in the historic Kohl Mansion, also known as The Oaks, which was built in 1914 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. Tickets and season subscriptions are available at www.musicatkohl.org.
articles.title: Music at Kohl Mansion opens 44th season with Escher String Quartet

articles.text: San Francisco Opera hosts a costume collection sale in Burlingame October 17 and 18, offering shoppers the chance to purchase theatrical garments and accessories from decades of productions at the War Memorial Opera House. The two-day sale will take place at the company’s Scene Shop in Burlingame, with items ranging from Victorian dresses and Edwardian ensembles to 1920s fashions, military uniforms, capes and fantasy costumes. The collection includes pieces from productions such as Luisa Miller, Un Ballo in Maschera, Idomeneo, Fidelio and Don Giovanni. Prices will range from $5 to $525, with premium items priced higher. Stage props and other opera merchandise will also be available. The sale offers opportunities for collectors, performers and others seeking distinctive clothing for Halloween, Renaissance fairs, theatrical productions and masquerades. San Francisco Opera periodically holds costume sales to make room for new productions. Proceeds from admission fees and sales will support the company. The public sale will run from 9:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. both days, with the last entry at 4:30 p.m. Timed-entry tickets are required and include two hours of shopping. Admission ranges from $5 to $25, depending on the day and time.
articles.title: SF Opera hosts two-day costume sale in Burlingame

articles.text: What does it mean to find your voice—and a place to belong? The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) will explore that question at its 2026 Benefit Concert & Auction, “The Sound of Home,” at 6 p.m. on Saturday, October 10, at the DoubleTree by Hilton Berkeley Marina. The evening will celebrate extraordinary young singers and the community of families, educators, alumni, volunteers, accompanists, and supporters who make their musical journey possible. Led by award-winning Artistic Director Eric Tuan, the evening will feature performances by PEBCC singers, including the Ensemble Choir, along with two special guest soloists: alumna Kate Offer, a classical singer and conductor, and PEBCC singer Naomi Walker, who recently received the 1st Prize Solo Competition award at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival. For Tuan, a world-class choral education is about far more than learning to sing. “Choral music is one of the most powerful ways for young people to build connections with each other and the world around them,” says Tuan. “Our singers learn to listen to each other, to share their voices in a way that empowers the whole team, and to explore different cultures and perspectives through the universal language of music. As our alumni remind us, those experiences last for a lifetime.” At the heart of PEBCC’s mission is the belief that every young person should have the opportunity to experience that journey, regardless of financial circumstances. Financial assistance is central to the organization’s commitment to building a community where every singer belongs. The benefit concert supports that mission while celebrating the full circle of community surrounding the choir. “Our singers are part of a community much bigger than themselves,” says Tuan. “The transformative experiences singers experience wouldn’t be possible without the alumni who come back to teach and volunteer, the families who support them through the program, and the supporters who give so generously of their time, talent, and treasure to ensure every singer finds a home at PEBCC.” Tickets are available at piedmontchoirs.org. PEBCC’s Online Silent Auction opened Saturday, October 3, at 9:00 a.m. and closes Sunday, October 11, at 11:00 p.m. The 2026 Benefit Concert & Auction is made possible through the generous support of Bell Investment Advisors, Commercial Bank of California, and Anonymous Foundation. Sponsorship helps PEBCC provide transformative musical experiences and keep many choir and festival events free and accessible, enriching the cultural life of the Bay Area. To learn about becoming a Benefit Sponsor, contact Natalie Titone at ntitone@ piedmontchoirs.org.
articles.title: PEBCC celebrates “The Sound of Home” at 2026 benefit concert & auction

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest youth orchestra and the second-oldest in the United States, announces its landmark 90th Anniversary Season, celebrating nine decades of guiding young musicians toward excellence through orchestral music, education, and community. The 2026–27 anniversary season will feature four concerts spanning music from across centuries and cultures. Founded in Berkeley in 1936 by conductor Jessica Marcelli, when women conductors were exceedingly rare, YPSO enters its 90th season following a successful concert tour of Finland and Sweden in June 2026. From its Berkeley roots, the orchestra has grown to bring together young musicians from across the San Francisco Bay Area. Today, under Music Director and Conductor David Ramadanoff, YPSO continues a tradition of challenging young musicians with great orchestral repertoire while fostering accomplishment, community, and a lifelong passion for music. “I’m very proud to be part of an organization that has been providing young people the opportunity to play great music for 90 seasons,” Ramadanoff said. “During my 38 years as Music Director, it has been exciting and heartwarming to help this orchestra develop into an outstanding ensemble capable of playing the wonderful and challenging music we have programmed this season.” The season starts with the fall concert on Saturday, November 7, 2026, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. YPSO will open its 90th season with Shostakovich’s Festival Overture, Debussy’s Nocturnes, and Brahms’ Symphony No. 1. The winter concert will take place on Saturday, February 20, 2027, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. The winter concert features Tchaikovsky’s Romeo and Juliet Fantasy-Overture, Gabriela Lena Frank’s Three Latin American Dances, and other works, including music by Ralph Vaughan Williams. The spring concert is on Saturday, May 1, 2027, at 7:30 p.m., at First Church Berkeley. They’ll play Verdi’s Overture to La forza del destino, Dvořák’s Symphony No. 6, and additional repertoire. The season culminates on Sunday, June 6, 2027, at 3 p.m. (venue TBA) with a special 90th Anniversary Pops Concert, bringing together current YPSO musicians with alumni from across generations of the orchestra’s history. Former YPSO musicians will be invited to return, reconnect, and play alongside the next generation, celebrating the lasting community YPSO has built over nine decades. The program is expected to feature Arturo Márquez’s Danzón No. 2 and a festive selection of audience favorites from stage and screen, creating a joyful celebration of YPSO’s past, present, and future. The 2026–27 season honors YPSO’s 90-year legacy by bringing together generations of musicians through the music and community that continue to connect them. Enjoy all four concerts of YPSO’s 90th Anniversary Season and save with a season package. Season packages are on sale now. The season package price for General is $70, and Premium is $100. Single Tickets for General are $25, and Premium are $35. Students are free, and registration is required. Premium tickets include an early seating benefit. Box office & concert information is available at ypsomusic.org/ events.
articles.title: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra announces 90th anniversary

articles.text: Ongoing through November 1 Oakland Art Association gallery show Oakland Art Association presents Hopes and Dreams — a curated show that encompasses everyone’s most precious and intimate desires for the future. It can be a dream vacation, a dream come true, a dream for the future of the world or just your part of it. Hope knows no bounds: hope for change, for healing, a brighter future, or for world peace. OAA is a nonprofit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties whose mission is to encourage artistic endeavor in the community, support public school art education, and arrange show venues for our members’ artworks. Free and open to all! For more information, see www.oaklandart.org. Gallery is open and staffed Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday, October 9, 6:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art History Lecture A Friday night Extravaganza! Art historian Michael Stehr presents a spirited, illustrated 50-minute lecture exploring Michelangelo’s work in his hometown of Florence, Italy. At the age of 29, he would put the finishing touches on his David, likely one of the most recognizable sculptures in Western Art. As he moved through his forties, this sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance would continue to yield sculptural masterpieces and explore the art of architecture at San Lorenzo, the parish church of the Medici family. In 1534, he moved to Rome and only returned to Florence after his passing almost another thirty years later. Doors open at 5:30 p.m. $20 (cash only). Saturday, October 10, 7:00 p.m. Virginia Tichenor’s Ragtime Quartet Concert This quartet features ragtime pianist Virginia Tichenor with a stellar line-up of musicians performing ragtime and traditional jazz music. The quartet includes Virginia, of course; Ryan Calloway, clarinet, banjo and vocals; Marty Eggers, tuba; and Robert Young, cornet. Virginia Tichenor is an Oakland-based pianist, originally from St. Louis, MO, the daughter of the late Trebor Tichenor, a noted scholar, pianist and collector of ragtime music. Virginia plays solo piano locally in the Bay Area and is also a traditional jazz pianist, working currently with her husband, Marty Eggers, who also plays with the Zenith, Silver Bell, and Barrelhouse Jazz Bands. Advance tickets are highly recommended for this show, and available now at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Ragtime. Sunday, October 11, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Mark Williams, and Albert Brooks – will pay tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1,000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which 50 or more have become American standards. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of an afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Tickets $25 + fee at https://www.ticketsignup.io/JVH, or $30 at the door. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Friday, October 16, 7:00 p.m. String, Skin, & Breath Band Concert String, Skin, & Breath creates contemporary chamber music rooted in global traditions, blending ancient musical languages with modern expression. Drawing from Latin and North African modes, Ethio-jazz, desert blues, and global folk traditions, the ensemble weaves hypnotic rhythms, spacious improvisation, and rich acoustic textures into immersive performances that feel both timeless and new. The group exists to create a space for spontaneous, deep-listening musical conversation across cultures—stripping music down to its most elemental ingredients, honoring rhythm, vibration, and breath as the shared language beneath every tradition. The intention is to craft unrepeatable performances that move fluidly between meditative stillness and intricate rhythmic interplay, guided by trust and collective intuition rather than rigid arrangement— treating music-making itself as an act of human connection and cross-cultural dialogue. The band includes Uzbek-American cellist Misha Khalikulov, Latin-Grammy-nominated multi-instrumentalist Daniel Riera, percussionist/educator Aaron Kierbel, and Tunisian qanun virtuoso Arslen Metouii. Tickets available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/SSB. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org
articles.title: Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts

articles.text: Braving another warm day on Sept. 30, the last day of the month, 50 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group and five of their canine companions gathered at the Exedra excited to see if Nace Avenue really is nice. Leading our walk and tour was Pat Keller, a long-time Piedmont resident and Wednesday walker. Having lived on Nace Avenue for years, Pat was well qualified to relate the history of the area and provide information about some of the homes. We began the walk heading in the direction of Dracena Park. As we walked through the park on our way to Nace, Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup noted that there are now four great horned owls in residence. Nace is a tiny street with 27 houses. One unusual feature of Nace is that it’s L-shaped, making a 90-degree turn toward the middle. The street was named after Frank C. Havens’ secretary, John Nace. At the time, it was common to name streets after the people who were involved in developing the city. Nace is now a popular street for young families, with approximately 28 kids on it. The first house we visited was 22 Nace. It was built in 1906 for $2,820. We were fortunate enough to encounter one of the owners, KT, who graciously invited us to come into her magnificent backyard. It’s a breathtaking and fun little surprise when you enter the rear. The first thing you notice is the immensity of the outdoor living space with beautiful views of Piedmont. In addition there was a hot tub surrounded by redwood decking, a wooden, round-shaped sauna with a cold plunge adjacent, and an outdoor shower. To top things off, an inviting outdoor cabana with sofas tempted some of the walkers to sit and relax. Leaving 22 Nace, we walked down the street to 42 Nace, which has an uncommon flat roof. Pat explained to the group that a fire in the 1950s destroyed the original pitched roof which was then replaced by the flat roof. Continuing just next door, we visited 46 Nace, the present residence of Dave and Kathy Yam. Known as the “Gibson house,” it was built in 1910 by the Fenton family of ice cream fame. The original house had lath and plaster walls and the beams were first generation old-growth redwood. The Smith family moved in around 1912 and the home remained in the family until 1991 (79 years!). It is reported that they planted the large Catalpa tree out front, which is now a Piedmont Heritage Tree. However, a neighbor, Mrs. Gibson, claimed to have grown up at 46 Nace and her father planted the tree. Winnifred inherited the house and married Orrin Smith sometime between 1940 and 1950. They had no children, but all of the family celebrations were held at the house. Orrin was a wood shop teacher at McClymonds High School in Oakland and had a great workshop in the basement. The shelves and drawers for storing hardware were built by his students as a shop project. Orrin and Winnifred remodeled the house extensively both inside and outside, excavating a basement and using the surplus soil to level the backyard. Next, they dug out the front and built a garage. In 1976, Winnifred started the “Nace is Nice” block party to celebrate the Fourth of July. The current owner, Kathy, inherited the block party tradition and revived it in the 1990s. When Winnifred passed away, her sister Barbara became the executor of the estate. Barbara was the mother of one of Kathy Yam’s best friends. At the time, Kathy and her husband Dave were looking for a home to buy since their daughter Amy was about to begin kindergarten. Fortunately for Dave and Kathy, Barbara agreed to sell the house in time for Amy’s schooling. Since moving in, Dave and Kathy have extensively remodeled the house: adding a deck to the back, building a second story, re-shingling, constructing interior stairs to the basement, and assembling a new roof for the garage. In 2021, the house received the Design Award in the Excellence in Architecturally Consistent Design Category from the City. The added garage was the winner of the City’s Excellence in Integrated Garage Design in 2024. Dave provided the group with ink-on-linen drawings of the original house plans, as well as two photo albums of the 1950 remodel. Crossing the street to our final stop, we ended our tour at 35 Nace, the home of Greg and Pat Keller. Walkers were directed into a lushly landscaped backyard. Beneath a slatted roof arbor, a table of ice cold water, chocolate chip cookies and chocolate cake were waiting. Enough sustenance to fuel the walkers on their uphill hike back to their Exedra start. All the walkers agreed, Nace is really nice!!! For further reading, “Queen of the Hills: The Story of Piedmont, A California City” by Evelyn Craig Pattiani mentions on page 92 a Mabel Nace. Walking on Wednesday meets weekly at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra. The program is free and open to the public. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
articles.title: Wednesday Walkers discover that “Nace is Nice!”
