articles.text: High in the French Alps, where vineyards cling to steep slopes beneath snow-capped peaks, the wines of Savoie are gaining attention for their distinctive character and sense of place. For generations, Savoie’s vineyards have been closely tied to the region’s mountain communities. Today, a new generation of winemakers is bringing renewed energy to an area once known primarily to French locals and Alpine holidaymakers. The result is a collection of wines that can be remarkably fresh, mineral-driven and unlike those produced in France’s better-known regions. White wines dominate Savoie’s production, with the Jacquère grape playing a central role. Light-bodied and crisp, Jacquère produces wines with lively acidity and subtle floral and citrus notes, making them natural companions to local mountain cuisine. Altesse, another important white grape, produces the more structured and aromatic wines known as Roussette de Savoie. My favorite wine is Chignin-Bergeron, which is made from the Rhone Valley’s Roussanne grape. The region also has its own red specialties. Mondeuse, a traditional local grape, creates deeply colored wines with bright acidity, peppery spice and dark-fruit flavors. Gamay and Pinot Noir are also planted, adding further variety to the region’s offerings. Savoie’s geography is central to its identity. Vineyards are scattered across valleys and foothills, often at considerable elevations. The cool Alpine climate allows grapes to ripen slowly while retaining the acidity that gives the wines their characteristic freshness. That freshness is particularly well suited to Savoie’s traditional foods: fondue, raclette, tartiflette and other rich mountain dishes. The wines cut through the richness of the cheese and potatoes, creating a pairing that reflects the region itself. As interest in distinctive, terroir-driven wines continues to grow, Savoie is increasingly finding a place on the international wine map. Its bottles offer something increasingly sought after by modern wine drinkers: wines with a strong sense of origin, tradition and landscape. Philippe Viallet: a family name in Savoie wine At the foot of Mont Granier in France’s Alpine Savoie region, the name Philippe Viallet has become closely associated with the area’s distinctive wines. The family wine story began in 1966, when Marcel and Yvonne Viallet acquired a small vineyard in Apremont. Their sons, Pierre and Philippe, later continued the family business, with Philippe helping to develop it into both a wine producer and wine merchant. The Viallet range reflects the diversity of Savoie’s mountain vineyards. Among its bestknown wines is Apremont, made from the Jacquère grape. It is a light, crisp and refreshing white wine with bright acidity. Another important wine is Chignin-Bergeron, made from the Roussanne grape and generally fuller and more aromatic, with flavors of ripe fruit and flowers. Roussette de Savoie, made from the Altesse grape, offers another distinctive style, while the winery’s red wines include Mondeuse, one of Savoie’s traditional varieties, as well as Pinot Noir and Gamay. The winery also produces Crémant de Savoie, a sparkling wine, along with rosé wines. Philippe Viallet’s wines offer a taste of the Alpine landscape. Fresh, lively and closely connected to local grape varieties, they demonstrate why Savoie is attracting growing interest from wine drinkers looking for wines with a strong sense of place and a character of their own. • NV Viallet Crémant de Savoie A sparkling wine made in the style of Champagne, this is light and refreshing, dry and crisp with tiny bubbles. At $13 a bottle it is an incredible bargain. • 2024 G.G. Bouvet Roussette de Savoie This is another of the Viallet labels and Roussette is their name for the Altesse grape. It is a charming white wine, clean and crisp with floral notes of honeysuckle and orange blossoms. On the palate it shows peach and apricot flavors. Perfect aperitif. • 2024 Vialet ChigninBergeron Chignin-Bergeron is the name in Savoie for the Roussanne grape from the Rhone Valley. It is my favorite of the Savoie wines. Richer and fuller and round in the mouth with good weight and structure. Flavors of melons and pears and a long lingering finish. Excellent effort. • 2023 Clos de la Galeze Mondeuse Mondeuse is related to the Syrah grape and makes the best red wines in the Savoie. It is medium-bodied with flavors of cherries and currants and moderate tannins. It has ample acid and should drink well for five years.
articles.title: Savoie: France’s Alpine wines

articles.text: The world of competitive dog sports can be one of the most exciting for canine enthusiasts. There is the opportunity to meet fellow dog lovers, win awards for your pup, and spend quality time with them. Unfortunately, fewer and fewer new people are joining. Let’s examine a couple of reasons that may explain this, and hopefully drive current professionals in the American Kennel Club (AKC) world to make some changes. Not everything is the fault of individuals, but of our infrastructure. Simply put, money is an issue. With the costs of operating training clubs and events going up just like the cost of living, many people are being priced out of dog shows. To enter a dog in AKC conformation, the majority of shows cost around $37 a day. To compete in a four-day show, that’s well over $100, not counting the cost of travel and food. Even newer sports, such as Fast CAT, demonstrate significant costs on their entry forms. In California, pre-entry for Fast CAT, which allows two runs per dog per day, costs between $28 and $35 per run. Considering this sport is entirely based on participation, the unfortunate truth is that people are now paying for their titles rather than needing to demonstrate excellence with their dog. For young people who may have bachelor’s-degree-level jobs, these prohibitively high entry fees make it impossible for them to get their foot in the door. Lack of new exhibitors is a big concern, not just because it means dog shows are slowly becoming an event only for the wealthy, but because fewer competitors means fewer championship points and majors. The AKC point system is based on winning against a certain number of dogs, and with more competitors aging out than entering the sport, it will become markedly harder for individuals to achieve championship titles with their dogs. Now let’s talk about attitude. Many people coming from pet backgrounds assume that all dog people are enthusiastic and kind. Unfortunately, this is not always so within the dog show world. Many new participants at dog shows report feeling unwelcome and unsupported. Although there is no clear reason for this, the idea of people simply being competitive does not fully explain it. The high costs of entry, plus feeling excluded by veterans in the sport, unfortunately lead many new exhibitors to quit before they’ve really started. This means that it is up to the old-timers in dog sports to open their hearts to new competitors, and for new competitors to set the tone in the sport as welcoming going forward. Perhaps the American Kennel Club should consider the long-term results of pricing out exhibitors with these high entry fees. Only time will tell if dog enthusiasts are able to commit to these necessary changes. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510-507- 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.
articles.title: The price of the prize: Why AKC dog sports are slowly dying

articles.text: J. Ronald (Ron) Pengilly passed peacefully on September 28, 2026. Ron was born on May 5, 1934 to Joseph and Lillian Pengilly in Montebello, CA where he was raised. He leaves behind his beloved wife of 67 years, Margaret Ann (Margy) Pengilly, his daughter, Kathryn Ann Pengilly, son James W. Pengilly and seven grandchildren. Ron was a straight A student throughout high school and college. He attended UCLA where he was a member of the Phi Beta Kappa academic honorary society and the Phi Gamma Delta fraternity while participating in student government. Boalt Law School (now named UC Berkeley Law) came next. While at Boalt he won the state Moot Court championship. During his law school years, he worked as a “hasher” at the Kappa Alpha Theta sorority where he met his future wife, Margy. They were married in 1959 after they both graduated. articles.text: A new Oakland nonprofit, ReQuip, is giving gently used medical equipment and supplies a second life, while making those resources available free of charge to people throughout the community. The organization was created to address two needs at once: improving access to essential medical equipment and keeping usable medical resources out of the landfill. ReQuip collects, sanitizes and redistributes gently used medical equipment and supplies to individuals who need them. Community members can donate items they no longer need, while people who need equipment for themselves or a family member, are welcome to access the available resources at no cost. It is a place to donate and a resource for anyone who needs these items. ReQuip accepts a wide range of gently used medical equipment and supplies, including four-wheeled walkers, wheelchairs, continence supplies, bandages, wound care products, braces, shower seats, and other usable medical resources. Information about ReQuip, what can and cannot be accepted, and the mission statement, is available on the website, ReQuipoakland.org. And of course, it would be lovely to have you come volunteer. The organization was founded on the belief that medical equipment that is no longer of use to one person, can tremendously benefit the next person, while reducing waste, and strengthening community health and independence. ReQuip will open its doors October 13, and will be open every Tuesday from 10:00 a.m. - 2:00p.m. ReQuip is located in the Oakland Peace Center, 111 Fairmount Avenue at 29th Street. (Look for the blue-wall patio on the right). ReQuipoakland.org

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, October 7, 2026 The price of the prize: Why AKC dog sports are slowly dying Coral the Great Dane poses for the judge, her handler hoping for a win after paying high entry fees. By Sierra Berrick The world of competitive dog sports can be one of the most exciting for canine enthusiasts. There is the opportunity to meet fellow dog lovers, win awards for your pup, and spend quality time with them. Unfortunately, fewer and fewer new people are joining. Let’s examine a couple of reasons that may explain this, and hopefully drive current professionals in the American Kennel Club (AKC) world to make some changes. Not everything is the fault of individuals, but of our infrastructure. Simply put, money is an issue. With the costs of operating training clubs and events going up just like the cost of living, many people are being priced out of dog shows. To enter a dog in AKC conformation, the majority of shows cost around $37 a day. To compete in a four-day show, that’s well over $100, not counting the cost of travel and food. Even newer sports, such as Fast CAT, demonstrate significant costs on their entry forms. In California, pre-entry for Fast CAT, which allows two runs per dog per day, costs between $28 and $35 per run. Considering this sport is entirely based on participation, the unfortunate truth is that people are now paying for their titles rather than needing to demonstrate excellence with their dog. For young people who may have bachelor’s-degree-level jobs, these prohibitively high entry fees make it impossible for them to get their foot in the door. Lack of new exhibitors is a big concern, not just because it means dog shows are slowly becoming an event only for the wealthy, but because fewer competitors means fewer championship points and majors. The AKC point system is based on winning against a certain number of dogs, and with more competitors aging out than entering the sport, it will become markedly harder for individuals to achieve championship titles with their dogs. Now let’s talk about attitude. Many people coming from pet backgrounds assume that all dog people are enthusiastic and kind. Unfortunately, this is not always so within the dog show world. Many new participants at dog shows report feeling unwelcome and unsupported. Although there is no clear reason for this, the idea of people simply being competitive does not fully explain it. The high costs of entry, plus feeling excluded by veterans in the sport, unfortunately lead many new exhibitors to quit before they’ve really started. This means that it is up to the old-timers in dog sports to open their hearts to new competitors, and for new competitors to set the tone in the sport as welcoming going forward. Perhaps the American Kennel Club should consider the long-term results of pricing out exhibitors with these high entry fees. Only time will tell if dog enthusiasts are able to commit to these necessary changes. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: Part 2 in a series It all started with the water. It smelled awful, but it made his old joints feel better. In the mid- 1850s, old Isaac Holmes dragged a bathtub down the ravine to the mineral springs on the side of the hill. Soaking in the mineral water helped to ease his rheumatism. When he died, the mineral springs were forgotten. In the 1860s, these mineral springs (said to contain sulphur, magnesia, iodine and iron) were re-discovered in the ravine behind today’s Exedra, the current location of Bushy Dell Creek. Drinking or soaking in mineral water was believed to have great curative powers. These mineral springs were similar to the popular mineral waters in Calistoga, and they were only three miles from downtown Oakland. Investors quickly saw an opportunity to develop the springs and build a hotel to accommodate visitors who came to “take the waters.” They selected the name “Piedmont,” meaning “foot of the hills,” thus securing the name of Piedmont to our locale. The investors formed the Piedmont Land Company to buy 350 acres around the ravine, build the hotel and sell any adjoining land not needed for the hotel purposes as residential lots. In 1871, the Piedmont Springs Hotel opened near today’s Exedra as a first-class resort. The photo of the hotel shows only the northern portion of the building, which had two wings and was twice the size of the building as shown. The hotel had a wide veranda, 20 first-class bedrooms and two suites, five dining rooms, telegraph service, and a Grand Saloon (for men only) with an elegant mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove. The ladies’ entrance allowed women to enter the hotel, avoid the saloon and proceed directly to the main dining room with its crystal chandelier, linen tablecloths and fine china. The hotel quickly became a popular destination and drew visitors who passed a pleasant Sunday at Piedmont Springs, strolling the meandering paths to the mineral springs and enjoying an excellent lunch or dinner. The dining rooms served fresh meat from nearby ranches, milk and butter from Blair’s Dairy, and fresh fruit and vegetables from its gardens. The hotel also offered fine wine and liquor for those who did not care for mineral water. Fashionable San Franciscans would come for a week to escape the summer fog. Many hotel guests enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to buy land and build their homes here. The hotel thrived until 1892, when a spark from a faulty chimney started a fire on the roof. Hotel guests watched helplessly as the hotel burned to the ground before firefighters could arrive from downtown Oakland. The site would not be empty for long... but that’s another story. The mineral springs are still in Piedmont Park, but they were capped in the 1950s because the sulphur fumes offended many residents. The historical marker at the Veterans’ Building gives the location of the springs. To learn more about Piedmont’s history, see the Piedmont Historical Society website: Piedmonthistorical.org. Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on March 28, 2018.

Previously, at the City of Ontario, Tam oversaw a $690 million five-year Capital Improvement Program and led major initiatives including implementing an agency-wide asset management program. Her municipal career also includes service with the cities of Monterey Park and Long Beach. Tam joins Piedmont at an important moment. The City has substantial needs across aging infrastructure and facilities. Meeting those needs will require careful prioritization, strategic use of local dollars, and maximizing opportunities to leverage outside resources. Tam cites Piedmont’s engaged community as a major factor in her decision, saying “I was drawn to Piedmont because it is a closeknit community where people care deeply about their city and are involved in how it moves forward. My approach is centered on communication and collaboration – listening to residents, working across departments, and identifying and solving problems early.” “I look forward to working with my colleagues and the community to preserve what makes Piedmont special while continuing to elevate the infrastructure and services residents rely on every day,” Tam said. Tam holds a Master of Public Administration from the University of Southern California and a bachelor’s degree in Criminology, Law and Society from the University of California, Irvine. The City engaged Bob Murray & Associates to conduct the recruitment following the departure of former Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Rich Cunningham has served as Interim Public Works Director in Piedmont since former director Daniel Gonzales departed, The salary for the Public Works Director is $237,029. This position includes reimbursement for professional development, a monthly auto allowance, and standard benefits associated with management team. These benefits include bereavement leave, personal leave, vacation leave, sick leave, and recognized holidays.

articles.text: Editor, We proudly support the candidacy of Bill Reichle for City Council. As Piedmont residents for nearly 50 years, we’ve always been grateful for the dedicated service of our elected public officials — the people who step up to run for challenging offices, and the people with the integrity and the competence so critically needed to get important community work done, and done right. Bill Reichle has our enthusiastic support because he represents the finest example of one of those step-up people: Motivated by nothing more than a wish to give back to his community, he accepts no outside donations and is self-funding his campaign. Just as important, he brings to his candidacy a rare set of critical skills for the Council post — an even and generous personality, and an unequaled career background in administrative management. No surprise, then, that Reichle’s candidacy has been endorsed not only by Piedmont’s current mayor, but by eight former mayors, as well. Beyond all that, Bill Reichle has developed a thoughtfully progressive program that emphasizes Public Safety, Fiscal Discipline, and Community Engagement. We urge you to check it out in detail at ReichleforPiedmont.com. Tim and Marian Nelson 237 Scenic Avenue

articles.text: Editor, I am writing to endorse Adam Hundt for Piedmont City Council. I first met Adam while assisting him with his home search in Piedmont. During that process, I quickly came to appreciate his gentle, thoughtful manner and the respectful way he communicated his priorities, traits that I believe are essential for local leadership. Adam is an exceptional candidate whose unique, highly relevant perspective makes him a strong asset for our city. His impressive academic background includes a bachelor’s degree from Brown, an MBA, a master’s in industrial engineering from the University of Michigan, and a master’s in public policy from Johns Hopkins with a focus on clean energy. This rigorous educational foundation underscores both his sharp intelligence and his drive. Adam and his wife are raising their two young children here, and one of them attends Havens Elementary. His interest in local government grew from a desire to help Piedmont increase energy efficiency, an initiative that would lower our carbon footprint while boosting property values. Both are critical. While these issues inspired his run, his vision for our city is much broader. While the Hundt family is relatively new to Piedmont, I deeply respect Adam’s commitment to getting involved and sharing his professional expertise. We need the fresh perspectives and energy that young families bring to navigate the complex issues ahead, and I believe Adam Hundt is exactly the kind of leader who will serve our community well. –Pamela Strike Fullerton, Realtor Ramona Ave.
articles.title: Endorsing Adam Hundt for City Council

articles.text: To the Editor: I am writing to support Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council. I have known Nancy for more than a decade, and over the years I have had many opportunities to see firsthand her commitment to our community. I met Nancy through the Piedmont League of Women Voters where she served as President. Nancy put a tremendous amount of time and energy into leading the League. She worked hard to make sure the League provided our community with thoughtful, balanced opportunities to learn about important issues and participate in local government. She was organized, prepared, and consistently went above and beyond in serving our community. Having served on the Piedmont Unified School Board for eight years, I understand the commitment that public service requires. I have seen that same commitment in Nancy. She brings decades of public and community service experience, a willingness to listen and learn, and a genuine commitment to Piedmont and its residents. I know she will bring those qualities to her work on the City Council. I am proud to support Nancy and hope you will join me in voting for her for City Council. THE VALUE OF LOCAL REPRESENTATION: An exceptionally strong class of motivated buyers is fueling heavy demand in Piedmont right now, proving that the fall market remains a fantastic opportunity to sell before the season winds down for winter. This localized window offers sellers a great time to achieve excellent results with careful preparation and local expertise. For buyers, navigating our fast-moving, highly competitive market is always easier with local representation by your side. Working with a local agent brings a few distinct advantages: • Exclusive Insight: Local agents are often the first to know about unique opportunities around town, including quiet, off-market properties. • Intimate Inventory Knowledge: They tour the inventory firsthand and know recent neighborhood sales that make good comparables, often with in-depth knowledge of properties and their condition to help put a new listing’s true value into perspective. • Good Neighbors: Over the years, local agents build real friendships and trust with colleagues across different brokerages. When things get competitive, that mutual respect and track record of smooth closings can be the comfort a listing agent needs to help choose your offer. MORTGAGE MONEY Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: Mortgage rates have moved sharply higher over the past month, and last week the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in more than three years. With inflation heating back up, energy costs rising and the war with Iran continuing, homeowners should be prepared for mortgage rates to stay higher for longer. From my seat as a mortgage lender, higher rates are becoming just as much a seller problem as a buyer problem. I’m talking with more buyers who recognize that when a home needs work, has been sitting, or is priced too aggressively, they have leverage. Instead of simply asking for a lower price, buyers are more frequently negotiating seller credits that can be used to lower their mortgage rate or cover closing costs. This is often the most effective way to bridge the affordability gap. Sellers with the best homes may not need to make these concessions, but everyone else should understand that buyers will increasingly look to sellers for help with the economic pain in the mortgage markets. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Nancy Beninati for City Council To the Editor, I am writing to support Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council. As a 15 year resident of Piedmont, a local real estate agent, and Head Coach of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team, I have had the opportunity to see Nancy’s commitment to Piedmont firsthand through her involvement as a parent/coach with our team. Nancy is smart, hardworking, and dedicated. When she has questions about an issue affecting our community, she asks questions, does her research, and takes the time to understand the full picture. I tremendously respect her thoughtful and responsible approach. I am most proud of the culture of our mountain biking team. A big part of that culture comes from people like Nancy and her family that support and encourage the rest of the community. Culture is built with intentionality, and Nancy knows that full well. I enthusiastically support Nancy for City Council. I believe her experience, judgment, and commitment to Piedmont will make her a strong member of our City Council. Jon Reining Piedmont Bill Reichle for City Council Editor, We proudly support the candidacy of Bill Reichle for City Council. As Piedmont residents for nearly 50 years, we’ve always been grateful for the dedicated service of our elected public offiBonnie Tam Continued from page 1 ence and the judgment to hit the ground running from day one.” As Public Works Director in San Fernando, Tam led a full-service department and oversaw a $46 million Capital Improvement Program, including major infrastructure projects across water treatment, parks, and public facilities. Previously, at the City of Ontario, Tam oversaw a $690 million five-year Capital Improvement Program and led major initiatives including implementing an agency-wide asset management program. Her municipal career also includes service with the cities of Monterey Park and Long Beach. Tam joins Piedmont at an important moment. The City has substantial needs across aging infrastructure and facilities. Meeting cials — the people who step up to run for challenging offices, and the people with the integrity and the competence so critically needed to get important community work done, and done right. Bill Reichle has our enthusiastic support because he represents the finest example of one of those step-up people: Motivated by nothing more than a wish to give back to his community, he accepts no outside donations and is self-funding his campaign. Just as important, he brings to his candidacy a rare set of critical skills for the Council post — an even and generous personality, and an unequaled career background in administrative management. No surprise, then, that Reichle’s candidacy has been endorsed not only by Piedmont’s current mayor, but by eight former mayors, as well. Beyond all that, Bill Reichle has developed a thoughtfully progressive program that emphasizes Public Safety, Fiscal Discipline, and Community Engagement. We urge you to check it out in detail at ReichleforPiedmont.com. Tim and Marian Nelson 237 Scenic Avenue Endorsing Adam Hundt for City Council Editor, I am writing to endorse Adam Hundt for Piedmont City Council. I first met Adam while assisting him with his home search in Piedmont. During that process, I quickly came to appreciate his gentle, thoughtful manner and the respectful way he communicated his priorities, traits that I believe are essential for local leadership. Adam is an exceptional candidate whose unique, highly relevant perspective makes him a strong asset for our city. His impressive academic background includes a bachelor’s degree from Brown, an MBA, a master’s in industrial engineering from the University of Michigan, and a master’s in public policy from Johns Hopkins with a focus on clean energy. This rigorous educational foundation underscores both his sharp intelligence and his drive. Adam and his wife are raising their two young children here, those needs will require careful prioritization, strategic use of local dollars, and maximizing opportunities to leverage outside resources. Tam cites Piedmont’s engaged community as a major factor in her decision, saying “I was drawn to Piedmont because it is a closeknit community where people care deeply about their city and are involved in how it moves forward. My approach is centered on communication and collaboration – listening to residents, working across departments, and identifying and solving problems early.” “I look forward to working with my colleagues and the community to preserve what makes Piedmont special while continuing to elevate the infrastructure and services residents rely on and one of them attends Havens Elementary. His interest in local government grew from a desire to help Piedmont increase energy efficiency, an initiative that would lower our carbon footprint while boosting property values. Both are critical. While these issues inspired his run, his vision for our city is much broader. While the Hundt family is relatively new to Piedmont, I deeply respect Adam’s commitment to getting involved and sharing his professional expertise. We need the fresh perspectives and energy that young families bring to navigate the complex issues ahead, and I believe Adam Hundt is exactly the kind of leader who will serve our community well. –Pamela Strike Fullerton, Realtor Ramona Ave. Support Nancy Beninati for City Council To the Editor: I am writing to support Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council. I have known Nancy for more than a decade, and over the years I have had many opportunities to see firsthand her commitment to our community. I met Nancy through the Piedmont League of Women Voters where she served as President. Nancy put a tremendous amount of time and energy into leading the League. She worked hard to make sure the League provided our community with thoughtful, balanced opportunities to learn about important issues and participate in local government. She was organized, prepared, and consistently went above and beyond in serving our community. Having served on the Piedmont Unified School Board for eight years, I understand the commitment that public service requires. I have seen that same commitment in Nancy. She brings decades of public and community service experience, a willingness to listen and learn, and a genuine commitment to Piedmont and its residents. I know she will bring those qualities to her work on the City Council. I am proud to support Nancy and hope you will join me in voting for her for City Council. articles.text: Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) I support and appreciate the hard work of our police, fire, and city employees. I believe all Piedmont employees should be paid fairly and competitively, consistent with what the City can responsibly afford. The City must carefully evaluate any proposals and the longterm fiscal impacts to make a decision that best serves our community as a whole. While Piedmont has some wealthy residents, the City’s revenue streams are limited and rely heavily on property taxes. Any significant increase in compensation or benefits must be considered in the context of the entire City budget, the needs of all City employees, and other important City priorities. I support Measure GG because it would provide the City with additional ongoing revenue for parks, recreation, infrastructure, maintenance, and other City needs, including employee compensation. But additional revenue does not eliminate the need to make difficult budget choices. As a councilmember, I would support fair compensation while also making sure that any agreement is financially sustainable and treats all of our employees fairly. Ultimately, the Council and City will have to balance competitive compensation with the City’s overall financial constraints and the priorities of the community. Adam Hundt (AdamHundt.com) The City Council should present to the community a comprehensive plan for the police and fire departments. We need to maintain these services for the future in a way that is fair to the union members and ensures that the departments are adequately funded. Currently, overtime salaries are 136% of the amount approved for the budget year (a cost increase of $927,150). This is not sustainable for overtime firefighters or for the city. Is the solution increasing the number of staff, changing the shift schedule, altering the duties (in addition to extinguishing fires, Piedmont firefighters are also trained as EMTs or paramedics), or something else? I believe everyone in the community deserves adequate health care. The plan the Council should produce must assure health benefits for the union and every other city employee. Finally, we should explore ways to provide housing for Piedmont city employees. One way to do this is to work with developers to build below-market-rate units specifically for municipal employees such as firefighters, police, and teachers. I’m eager to work on this plan, and I promise to submit it to the whole community for comment. Sunny Bostrom-Fleming One of the main benefits of living in Piedmont is public safety. Protecting the lives of our families and our pets is our number one priority; our property can be replaced, but the lives we cherish cannot. While we are all very proud of both our police and fire departments, we must maintain a competitive workplace for these fine people. Our current focus is the fire department. Where do we get the operator funds to make sure we are a very competitive community? Every day when they leave their homes they have no guarantee of returning alive or uninjured. Measure GG, which is vital to keeping our community financially sound, could go a long way toward funding the fire department. I want us to consider additional funding, such as the schools have with the Giving Campaign. Seeing how we are surrounded by one of the most dangerous cities in America, Oakland reported 35,096 crimes in 2024: 6,000-plus auto burglaries, 1,100 residential burglaries, and 86 murders. Piedmont had 76 burglaries, one assault, and over 70 stolen cars. Our police and fire professionals are our first line of defense. The officers of Rome who led from the front lines earned their rank through merit and bravery. Tom Ramsey Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com) Piedmont’s first responders are hometown heroes. While many families move here for the schools, we all value our top-quality police and firefighters who keep us safe every day. As a small town, Piedmont is in a tough spot to match compensation packages offered by larger cities or towns that benefit from bigger budgets and commercial tax revenue. For decades, Piedmont navigated this position by determining salary levels through an independent third-party that conducts a salary survey comparing total compensation for each role against 13 Bay Area cities identified as comparable to Piedmont. Pay rates for each role are set based on the median compensation. Recruitment challenges are regional, and responsible budgeting requires balancing new requests such as increased healthcare benefits with existing city obligations, where retiree and current employee medical premiums already cost the city $4 million annually. I acknowledge this process is taking too long, and it weighs heavily on all involved. I am committed to continuing transparent, good-faith dialogue through our established bargaining representatives to reach a sustainable agreement that is both fair to all employees and fiscally responsible to the community.

articles.text: candidates were numbered 1 through 5, and the moderator called on them at random to answer each question. The candidates had a minute and a half to answer each question. The questions were chosen from a public submission form and reviewed to ensure a wide range of topics. The forum asked candidates questions about Piedmont’s community, the budget, capital projects, infrastructure, disaster preparedness, and Automated Licence Plate Reader (ALPR) camera privacy. At the end of the questioning period, each candidates presented a one-minute closing statement describing why Piedmont citizens should vote for them and directed the audience to resources that would inform them of their positions. To watch the full forum and hear the candidates’ responses, readers can go to the LWVP’s YouTube channel: https://www. youtube.com/@lwvpiedmont/ featured. Visit the Election Resources page (https://bit.ly/4ymy5xS) to learn about what’s on the ballot and how, when, and where to vote. Ballots started going out to every registered voter on October 5. Ballot drop-off locations will open October 6. If you have moved or changed your party or your name, you can update your registration online. The last day to register to vote is October 19.

Piedmont had 76 burglaries, one assault, and over 70 stolen cars. Our police and fire professionals are our first line of defense. The officers of Rome who led from the front lines earned their rank through merit and bravery. Tom Ramsey Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com) Piedmont’s first responders are hometown heroes. While many families move here for the schools, we all value our top-quality police and firefighters who keep us safe every day. As a small town, Piedmont is in a tough spot to match compensation packages offered by larger cities or towns that benefit from bigger budgets and commercial tax revenue. For decades, Piedmont navigated this position by determining salary levels through an independent third-party that conducts a salary survey comparing total compensation for each role against 13 Bay Area cities identified as comparable to Piedmont. Pay rates for each role are set based on the median compensation. Recruitment challenges are regional, and responsible budgeting requires balancing new requests such as increased healthcare benefits with existing city obligations, where retiree and current employee medical premiums already cost the city $4 million annually. I acknowledge this process is taking too long, and it weighs heavily on all involved. I am committed to continuing transparent, good-faith dialogue through our established bargaining representatives to reach a sustainable agreement that is both fair to all employees and fiscally responsible to the community. The candidates had a minute and a half to answer each question. The questions were chosen from a public submission form and reviewed to ensure a wide range of topics. The forum asked candidates questions about Piedmont’s community, the budget, capital projects, infrastructure, disaster preparedness, and Automated Licence Plate Reader (ALPR) camera privacy. At the end of the questioning period, each candidates presented a one-minute closing statement describing why Piedmont citizens should vote for them and directed the audience to resources that would inform them of their positions. To watch the full forum and hear the candidates’ responses, readers can go to the LWVP’s YouTube channel: https://www. youtube.com/@lwvpiedmont/ featured. Visit the Election Resources page (https://bit.ly/4ymy5xS) to learn about what’s on the ballot and how, when, and where to vote. Ballots started going out to every registered voter on October 5. Ballot drop-off locations will open October 6. If you have moved or changed your party or your name, you can update your registration online. The last day to register to vote is October 19. articles.text: Honorable Mentions Maddy Huynh earns an honorable mention for making a huge impact on the girls’ tennis varsity roster as a freshman, typically appearing at No. 3 singles, which a few appearances in the No. 2 spot. In September, the freshman won eight matches and lost just twice – both of which went to an extra third set. Dylan Jerez earns an honorable mention for his instant impact on the boys’ water polo team as their starting goalie as a sophomore. He had 12 saves, a steal, and assist in Piedmont’s 14-6 win over Encinal, 10 saves and five assists in a 15-11 win over Bishop O’Dowd on September 4, and nine saves in their 8-7 double overtime loss to James Logan on September 3.

Ruthven won 6-1, 6-2 at the No. 1 spot, while Faith Chin won by the same score, 6-1, 6-2 at No. 2. Huynh won in a 6-0, 6-0 sweep at No. 3, but Sharafi lost 6-2, 6-1 at No. 4. The Highlanders won all three doubles matches. Chan and Silvio won in three sets at the No. 1 spot, 6-4, 6-7 (7-5), 10-6.
